Therefore, regardless of how a string of the form “s1_c_s2s1\_c\_s2s1_c_s2” is divided, at most one of its substrings can produce 0; it cannot form “0=00=00=0.” Note that if either s1s1s1 or s2s2s2 is empty, s1_cs1\_cs1_c and c_s2c\_s2c_s2 are likewise plainly unable to form “0=00=00=0,” so our candidate set must include those cases as well.

  Thanks to the earlier work, we already know every nonzeroable string. Constructing every number of the form “s1+c+s2s1+c+s2s1+c+s2” from them yields a candidate set far smaller than the original one, even though it still contains many zeroable strings. Let CnC_nCn​ be the number of n-digit candidates of this form. Then C8=14456421C_8 = 14456421C8​=14456421, C9=28813930C_9 = 28813930C9​=28813930, C10=24533340C_{10} = 24533340C10​=24533340, C11=8388910C_{11} = 8388910C11​=8388910, C12=920140C_{12} = 920140C12​=920140, C13=45660C_{13} = 45660C13​=45660, and C14=1080C_{14} = 1080C14​=1080. For fifteen digits, the only possible form is “8985898_c_89858988985898\_c\_89858988985898_c_8985898.” Its nine-digit substring “5898_c_89855898\_c\_89855898_c_8985” must be able to produce 0, so every “8985898_c_89858988985898\_c\_89858988985898_c_8985898” can form “898+0=898898+0=898898+0=898.” Hence S15=0S_{15}=0S15​=0. Only 77,159,481 remaining candidates require testing. Add the candidate strings from two through seven digits, and the total is about eighty million, a manageable range for computer verification. There may be a better algorithm, but I was too lazy to find it.

  The computer search found 19,515 unbalanceable strings in all. The largest was 9989858, and not a single unbalanceable number was found from eight through fourteen digits. At last we can breathe easily and state with confidence:

In base ten, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, parentheses, and exactly one equals sign can always be inserted into any integer with eight or more digits to form a true equation.

  One detail still looks slightly awkward: why insist on inserting only “one” equals sign? The string 111 cannot become an equation with one equals sign, but several signs produce “1=1=11=1=11=1=1.” What happens if we remove the word “one”? Cases solvable with one sign do not need several, so the relaxed condition can only expand the conclusion. Is that expansion enough to lower the bound from eight digits to seven or fewer? Fortunately, we can test the 19,515 unbalanceable strings found above, adding only an intersection test for the insertion-value sets of multiple segments. Of those strings, 1,317 can become equations when multiple equals signs are allowed. The largest, 9989858, remains impossible to balance no matter how many signs are inserted. Let us call strings that can never be balanced “strongly unbalanceable,” and those that fail only under the single-sign restriction “weakly unbalanceable.” Fortunately, although the condition is genuinely looser, neither the greatest unbalanceable length nor the largest unbalanceable number changes.

  We may finally announce without reservation:

In base ten, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, parentheses, and equals signs can always be inserted into any integer with eight or more digits to form a true equation.

  An arduous literature search failed to find an earlier result of this kind. Until a predecessor’s version turns up, let us provisionally call this neat result the Silicon–Silence Balance Integer Theorem in honor of the two idle minds who posed and solved the problem.

  At last, we can transmit numerical information through equations without losing sleep, provided the number has at least eight digits or is not one of the 18,198 strongly unbalanceable strings. After all, why would a sophon suspect that an eternally true statement such as “3−5+0=−2×3+43-5+0=-2\times 3+43−5+0=−2×3+4” conceals an unspeakable secret?

entry.title: Heat and Electricity (1) — How Can a Temperature Difference Generate Power?
entry.content:
Can electricity be generated without “boiling water,” using nothing more than a temperature difference? Why should that difference make electric charges move? And how can such a seemingly weak effect power a spacecraft in deep space? This article introduces the Seebeck effect and explains how “heat” can become electricity.

Author: ST
Reviewer: 时光

  When people talk about generating electricity, many describe it as “boiling water”: heat the water, let the steam turn a turbine, and convert mechanical energy into electrical energy. The most obvious example is fossil-fuel power generation, where coal, natural gas, oil, or another fuel is burned to heat water. Nuclear, geothermal, biomass, and even waste-to-energy plants often use the same basic route. Other technologies—wind turbines, photovoltaic cells, hydropower, and fuel cells—do not rely on this kind of “boiling water.”

  Our subject today is different: how heat itself can generate electricity. You may object that boiling water also produces a great deal of heat. It does, but “heat” here means a thermal gradient, or more simply, a temperature difference. Put a metal chopstick in boiling water: the immersed end is clearly hotter than the end in your hand. The temperature difference between those two regions can be understood as a temperature gradient, also called a thermal gradient.

  What does that have to do with electricity? Electricity cannot appear from nowhere. “Boiling-water” generation, for example, relies on Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction: a coil and a magnetic field move relative to one another. Under Faraday’s law, a changing magnetic flux produces an induced electromotive force. The changing field acts like an invisible hand that pushes charges through a wire, converting mechanical motion into electrical energy. In a photovoltaic cell, illumination separates positive and negative charges inside the material and creates a voltage across its terminals. In a fuel cell, a chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidant directs the transfer of electrons and thereby produces a voltage.

  Every method of power generation ultimately requires the directed movement of charge carriers—small particles that can move through a material and carry electric charge. In common metals and semiconductors, those carriers are usually electrons. In plain terms, generating electricity means getting charge carriers to move together in an orderly direction.

  What happens to the carriers in a material with a thermal gradient? Even without any external disturbance, they are not at rest. They undergo continuous random motion. Across the material as a whole, however, the carriers are distributed uniformly and roughly equal numbers move in every direction, so there is no current. If one end of the material is hotter, the carriers there have more energy and move more vigorously. That breaks the balance: they diffuse toward the colder end and accumulate there. Because the carriers themselves are charged, the hot and cold ends develop an unequal distribution of charge, which appears as a voltage. The accumulation cannot continue forever. As more carriers arrive, the cold end increasingly repels them. Eventually, that tendency balances diffusion and produces a stable thermoelectric voltage. This is one kind of thermoelectric effect.

  Now that we understand the most basic mechanism, does it have any practical use? It does. In the 1820s, the German physicist Thomas Johann Seebeck discovered that if two different metals formed a closed circuit and the two junctions were held at different temperatures, a nearby compass needle moved. Seebeck did not realize at the time that a current was flowing, but we now know that the thermal gradient produced an electromotive force. This phenomenon is called the Seebeck effect. For power generation, naturally, a larger voltage is desirable, and the effect depends on the magnitude of the thermal gradient. How can we measure it?

  To express a material’s thermoelectric capability—specifically its Seebeck effect—we define the Seebeck coefficient S as S=−ΔVΔTS=-\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T}S=−ΔTΔV​. Its meaning is straightforward: how much voltage the material produces for each degree of temperature difference between its hot and cold ends. With two materials, the measured voltage is approximately related to the difference between their Seebeck coefficients: V∝(SA−SB)ΔTV \propto (S_A-S_B)\Delta TV∝(SA​−SB​)ΔT.

Figure 1[3]. A: an electric potential difference can produce a thermal gradient—the inverse of the Seebeck effect, known as the Peltier effect. B: diagram of the Seebeck effect. C: a power-generation module based on the Seebeck effect.

  The most obvious application of the Seebeck effect is power generation. Connect many thermoelectric units in series, and they form a thermoelectric generator. As long as one side remains hot and the other cold, the device can continuously produce electrical power.

  Unlike conventional generators, a thermoelectric generator needs no turbine, rotating shaft, or complex mechanical motion. It is quiet, stable, and durable. Its disadvantages are equally clear: thermoelectric conversion is usually inefficient, often around 5%, and the device must maintain a stable temperature difference. Thermoelectric generators are therefore best suited at present to recovering heat that would otherwise be wasted, such as heat from engine exhaust, boiler walls, or electronic equipment.

  For deep-space probes far from the Sun, thermoelectric generation is an important and dependable energy source. Spacecraft such as Voyager, New Horizons, and some Mars rovers carry radioisotope thermoelectric generators. Heat released continuously by radioactive decay establishes a temperature difference across the device, and thermoelectric materials convert part of that thermal energy into electricity. Such generators can operate for many years in harsh environments.

  The Seebeck effect can also be used as a thermometer, in the form of thermocouple thermometry. A thermocouple usually consists of two different metals. If its two junctions are at different temperatures, it produces a tiny voltage that a precise instrument can measure; the temperature can then be calculated from that voltage. In a common type K thermocouple, for example, a temperature change of 1 K changes the voltage by roughly 4.1*10-6 V. That sounds small, but it is readily detectable. Thermocouples are also simple, heat-resistant, and fast to respond, so they are widely used to measure temperature in industrial furnaces, engines, boilers, chemical equipment, and laboratories.

  The Seebeck effect has far more applications than one might expect. Observant readers may have noticed a feature of the thermoelectric effect described here: the voltage is parallel to the thermal gradient. Can a voltage also appear in another direction? Yes. Next time, we will see how a thermal gradient can produce a voltage perpendicular to itself.

References

[1] Seebeck T J. Magnetische Polarisation der Metalle und Erze durch Temperatur-Differenz[J]. Abhandlungen der Königlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1822-1823: 265-373.
[2] Goldsmid H J. Introduction to Thermoelectricity[M]. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer, 2010.
[3] Bell L E. Cooling, heating, generating power, and recovering waste heat with thermoelectric systems[J]. Science, 2008, 321(5895): 1457-1461.
[4] Snyder G J, Toberer E S. Complex thermoelectric materials[J]. Nature Materials, 2008, 7(2): 105-114.
[5] NASA Radioisotope Power Systems Program. Radioisotope Power Systems[EB/OL]. https://rps.nasa.gov/.
[6] Mizuguchi M, Nakatsuji S. Energy-harvesting materials based on the anomalous Nernst effect[J]. Science and Technology of Advanced Materials, 2019, 20(1): 262-275.

entry.title: A Lower Bound for Randomized Sorting: An Introduction to Yao's Principle
entry.content:
The number of comparisons made by a deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm on its worst-case input has a lower bound of Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn). But what about the expected number of comparisons made by a randomized algorithm on its worst-case input? This article introduces Yao’s principle and uses it to analyze the lower bound on comparisons in randomized sorting algorithms.

Author: silverxz
Reviewed by: phy东西

Introduction

  The lower bound of Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn) on the number of comparisons made by a deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm on its worst-case input is a famous result. It appears in textbooks such as Introduction to Algorithms and in most algorithms courses, so readers are probably familiar with it. (This article assumes only an introductory knowledge of algorithms and probability theory. Following the convention in algorithms, lg uses base 222.)

  But what is the expected number of comparisons made by a randomized algorithm on its worst-case input?

  If you have never encountered randomized algorithms, you may suspect that allowing randomness cannot magically make an algorithm better. Yet some randomized algorithms really do seem magical.

  Quicksort is one example. Ordinary quicksort can take Θ(n2)\Theta(n^2)Θ(n2) time on its worst-case input if it chooses pivots by a fixed rule, while choosing pivots at random keeps its expected complexity at O(nlg⁡n)O(n\lg n)O(nlgn) even on the worst input. That example may not seem magical enough, since plenty of other sorting algorithms run in Θ(nlg⁡n)\Theta(n\lg n)Θ(nlgn). A more striking example is Freivalds’ algorithm. It has nothing to do with sorting, but it is so concise and ingenious that it deserves a brief introduction. The algorithm solves the following problem.

Problem: Given three n×nn\times nn×n matrices A,B,CA,B,CA,B,C, determine whether ABABAB equals CCC. In other words, verify whether a matrix multiplication result is correct.

  The most direct approach is, of course, to multiply AAA and BBB and then test whether ABABAB equals CCC. Its computational cost is the cost of matrix multiplication, which is O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) by the naive method. It is hard to imagine doing better than matrix multiplication itself, yet Freivalds found a randomized method that astonishes almost everyone who sees it for the first time.

Lemma (Freivalds’ algorithm)

Let r∈{0,1}nr\in \{0, 1\}^nr∈{0,1}n be a random vector of length nnn with 010101 entries. Then:

  • if AB=CAB=CAB=C, then ABr=CrABr=CrABr=Cr always holds;
  • if AB≠CAB\neq CAB​=C, then Prr∈{0,1}n[ABr=Cr]≤1/2\mathrm{Pr}_{r\in \{0, 1\}^n}[ABr=Cr]\leq 1/2Prr∈{0,1}n​[ABr=Cr]≤1/2.

  To keep the main text shorter, the proof appears in Note 1. It is quite simple, too.

  Using this lemma, independently choose kkk random vectors r1,r2,…,rk∈{0,1}nr_1, r_2, \dots, r_k \in \{0, 1\}^nr1​,r2​,…,rk​∈{0,1}n. Because multiplying a matrix by a vector takes quadratic time, at a cost of O(kn2)O(kn^2)O(kn2) we can compute and compare each ABriABr_iABri​ with CriCr_iCri​, for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,ki=1,…,k. If any pair differs, then AB≠CAB\neq CAB​=C. If all pairs are equal, the algorithm simply declares that AB=CAB=CAB=C. By the lemma, the probability of a false result—the actual case is AB≠CAB\neq CAB​=C, but every ABri=CriABr_i=Cr_iABri​=Cri​ and the algorithm is fooled—is at most 2−k2^{-k}2−k. When kkk is fixed as a constant, this is an O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) algorithm.

  The fastest matrix-multiplication algorithms known today are still a long way from O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2), yet Freivalds’ remarkably simple method sidesteps matrix multiplication altogether. It pays for this with a small error probability, but that is entirely acceptable: just repeat the test a few more times. The error probability falls exponentially and soon becomes lower than the chance of hardware failure, system failure, or the server room exploding (Note 2).

  Does this example make randomized algorithms seem more powerful? Many of them can accomplish, in a very simple way, tasks that are much less straightforward for deterministic algorithms. Similar ideas underlie various hashing algorithms and their extensions, including the Bloom filter, which you may have heard of. In essence, they construct a random “fingerprint” as cheaply as possible and use it to identify or compare objects as reliably as possible.

  This does not mean that randomized algorithms truly have better asymptotic complexity than deterministic ones. In the case of Freivalds’ algorithm, we do not know whether an O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) deterministic matrix-multiplication algorithm exists. In theory, one might. It would give us an O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) deterministic test for whether ABABAB equals CCC, putting the randomized and deterministic algorithms on equal footing. Even if such an algorithm exists, however, it would surely be extremely complicated. The randomized algorithm we just saw is remarkably simple, and that is what makes randomized algorithms so impressive.

  Now return to sorting. Could a randomized algorithm somehow beat the deterministic lower bound, making fewer than Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn) expected comparisons on its worst-case input? There is no need to keep you in suspense: the answer is still no. To prove it, we need a tool that can characterize lower bounds for randomized algorithms—a way to tell us that even randomization cannot produce unlimited miracles.

Yao’s Principle

  The tool we will introduce is Yao’s minimax principle, usually shortened to Yao’s principle. It comes from Andrew Yao’s 1977 work and is one of the oldest and most fundamental tools for lower-bound analysis of randomized algorithms. Its central idea is to view the relationship between an algorithm and its input as a game.

  You may not know what a “game” means in this context, so consider a familiar example: rock–paper–scissors. Let A,X\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}A,X be sets and lll a binary function on them, defined as follows:

A=X={rock, scissors, paper},l(a,x)={win, lose, tie}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{X}=\{\text{rock, scissors, paper}\}, l(a,x)=\{\text{win, lose, tie}\}A=X={rock, scissors, paper},l(a,x)={win, lose, tie}

  The game of rock–paper–scissors has two players—call them Alice and Bob—who each choose an element from A\mathcal{A}A and X\mathcal{X}X, respectively, to decide the outcome. In game-theoretic language, the elements of A\mathcal{A}A are Alice’s strategies (Note 3), while the elements of X\mathcal{X}X are Bob’s strategies. Once they have chosen, the function lll gives the payoff or cost associated with that pair of strategies.

  What does this have to do with algorithms? For the sorting problem, define A\mathcal{A}A as the set of all deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithms, Xn\mathcal{X}_nXn​ as the set of all inputs of size nnn, and l(a,x)l(a,x)l(a,x) as the number of comparisons needed by algorithm a∈Aa\in \mathcal{A}a∈A to sort input x∈Xnx\in \mathcal{X}_nx∈Xn​. Alice and Bob are still playing a game. Think of Alice as an algorithm designer and Bob as an adversary: Alice wants to choose the best possible algorithm aaa and make the number of comparisons l(a,⋅)l(a,\cdot)l(a,⋅) as small as possible, while Bob wants to choose the worst possible input xxx and make l(⋅,x)l(\cdot,x)l(⋅,x) as large as possible.

  A worst-case analysis of a particular algorithm a∈Aa\in \mathcal{A}a∈A—for example, the number of comparisons that a sorting algorithm a∈Aa\in \mathcal{A}a∈A makes in the worst case—allows Bob to attack aaa with the worst input xxx. The maximum number of comparisons can be written as

max⁡x∈Xnl(a,x)\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}_n} l(a, x)x∈Xn​max​l(a,x)

  From this game-theoretic perspective, the familiar lower bound Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn) says that no matter which algorithm aaa Alice chooses, Bob can use that algorithm aaa to find a sufficiently bad input xxx on which algorithm aaa requires l(a,x)>cnlg⁡nl(a,x)>cn\lg nl(a,x)>cnlgn comparisons. Notice the order of play: Alice chooses the algorithm first, and Bob, knowing her choice, can tailor his attack. In symbols, there is a constant c>0c>0c>0 such that, for all sufficiently large nnn,

min⁡a∈Amax⁡x∈Xnl(a,x)>cnlg⁡n\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}}\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}_n} l(a,x) > cn\lg na∈Amin​x∈Xn​max​l(a,x)>cnlgn

  The left-hand side is the number of comparisons required by the best algorithm on its worst input of size nnn. Observe how the expression captures the order just described. If we add parentheses, it becomes

min⁡a∈A(max⁡x∈Xn(l(a,x)))\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \Big( \max_{x\in \mathcal{X}_n} \big(l(a,x)\big) \Big)a∈Amin​(x∈Xn​max​(l(a,x)))

  The inner max⁡x∈Xn\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_n}maxx∈Xn​​ uses the value a∈Aa\in \mathcal{A}a∈A selected in the outer subscript and, according to this aaa, maximizes the function l(a,x)l(a, x)l(a,x). In other words, Bob knows aaa before maximizing l(a,x)l(a, x)l(a,x), which expresses the order of play. This point matters because we will repeatedly encounter interleaved min⁡\minmin and max⁡\maxmax operations.

  So far, we have only restated the familiar result for deterministic algorithms in different language. With a little time, it should be straightforward to follow.

  We have viewed the relationship between deterministic algorithms and inputs as a game. The crucial next question is: what about randomized algorithms?

  First consider what a randomized algorithm is. Unlike a deterministic algorithm, it can generate random numbers and make decisions according to their values.

  If we fix every random number it generates, the randomized algorithm becomes deterministic. For example, if a C program obtains random numbers with rand, fixing the seed passed to srand fixes the sequence produced by rand. This means that we can regard a randomized algorithm as a random variable whose values are deterministic algorithms.

  In case that last sentence sounded obscure, a random variable does not have to take numerical values. If we draw one card uniformly at random from a deck, that draw is a random variable taking values in the deck and following the uniform distribution over its cards. Similarly, a randomized algorithm simply selects one algorithm from the set of all deterministic algorithms, so it is a random variable taking values in that set. In plainer language, a randomized algorithm randomly chooses one algorithm from a collection of deterministic algorithms. We will inevitably use some probability theory below, including this random variable, so it is worth understanding the formulation.

  In mathematical language, let Δ(A)\Delta(\mathcal{A})Δ(A) denote the set of all probability distributions over A\mathcal{A}A. An element R∈Δ(A)R\in \Delta(\mathcal{A})R∈Δ(A) is therefore a probability distribution, and a randomized algorithm is a random variable following some distribution R∈Δ(A)R\in \Delta(\mathcal{A})R∈Δ(A), written A∼RA\sim RA∼R (Note 4).

  Return to the contest between Alice and Bob. We now allow Alice to choose a randomized algorithm. She no longer has to naively choose one fixed algorithm a∈Aa\in \mathcal{A}a∈A and let Bob exploit the weaknesses of aaa. Instead, she can choose a random variable over A\mathcal{A}A, denoted by AAA, representing a randomized algorithm, which makes Bob’s attack more difficult.

  That description alone may not make the benefit obvious, so return to rock–paper–scissors. If Alice can use only a deterministic strategy, Bob always wins. The order of play means that Bob effectively watches Alice make her move before choosing his own. If Alice can instead use a randomized strategy, choosing rock, paper, or scissors with probability 1/31/31/3 each, Bob can no longer target her choice.

  This example should show why a randomized algorithm may have an advantage. The order of play has not changed: Bob can still know Alice’s strategy in advance. But because the strategy itself is random, knowing that “Alice chooses uniformly among rock, paper, and scissors” gives him no way to counter it.

  We already know that the worst-case number of comparisons made by the best deterministic sorting algorithm can be expressed as

min⁡a∈Amax⁡x∈Xnl(a,x)\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}}\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}_n} l(a,x)a∈Amin​x∈Xn​max​l(a,x)

  What, then, is the expected number of comparisons made by the best randomized algorithm on its worst-case input? Since Alice can choose an algorithm at random, the variable beneath min⁡\minmin is no longer a∈Aa\in\mathcal{A}a∈A but

min⁡R∈Δ(A)max⁡x∈XnEA∼R[l(A,x)]\min_{R\in \Delta(\mathcal{A})}\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}_n} \mathbb{E}_{A\sim R}[l(A, x)]R∈Δ(A)min​x∈Xn​max​EA∼R​[l(A,x)]

  Alice specifies a randomized strategy AAA following a distribution R∈Δ(A)R\in\Delta(\mathcal{A})R∈Δ(A). Bob then chooses an input x∈Xnx\in\mathcal{X}_nx∈Xn​ to attack that strategy, and we calculate its expected cost EA∼R[l(A,x)]\mathbb{E}_{A\sim R}[l(A,x)]EA∼R​[l(A,x)].

  This expression is plainly difficult to evaluate. We do not even know all the deterministic algorithms, let alone all the distributions RRR over them. Yao’s principle, however, can transfer the randomness from Alice’s side to Bob’s. That makes the problem much simpler because we know exactly what Xn\mathcal{X}_nXn​ contains: all permutations of 111 through nnn. We can now state the theorem.

Theorem (Yao’s minimax principle)

Let A,X\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{X}A,X be two finite sets and let l:A×X→Rl:\mathcal{A}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}l:A×X→R. For every random variable over A\mathcal{A}A, denoted by AAA, and every random variable over X\mathcal{X}X, denoted by XXX,

max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]≥min⁡a∈AEX[l(a,X)]\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)] \geq \min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X}[l(a,X)]x∈Xmax​EA​[l(A,x)]≥a∈Amin​EX​[l(a,X)]

Proof

The proof is simple, so we will finish it before explaining what the theorem means.

max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]≥EXEA[l(A,X)]=EAEX[l(A,X)]≥min⁡a∈AEX[l(a,X)]\begin{aligned}\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)] &\geq \mathbb{E}_X \mathbb{E}_A[l(A,X)]\\&=\mathbb{E}_A\mathbb{E}_X[l(A,X)]\\&\geq \min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X}[l(a,X)]\end{aligned}x∈Xmax​EA​[l(A,x)]​≥EX​EA​[l(A,X)]=EA​EX​[l(A,X)]≥a∈Amin​EX​[l(a,X)]​

The first and last lines use the elementary inequality

max⁡z∈Zf(z)≥EZ[f(Z)]≥min⁡z∈Zf(z)\max_{z\in \mathcal{Z}} f(z) \geq \mathbb{E}_{Z} [f(Z)] \geq \min_{z\in \mathcal{Z}} f(z)z∈Zmax​f(z)≥EZ​[f(Z)]≥z∈Zmin​f(z)

The maximum is at least the average, which is at least the minimum. Straightforward, isn’t it? Such a basic inequality rarely yields anything useful on its own. The crucial step here is the exchange of the order of expectation in the second line. The theorem assumes that A,X\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}A,X are finite, so these expectations are finite double sums whose order can be exchanged. That completes the proof.

In fact, the proposition does not require both sets A,X\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{X}A,X to be finite. Finiteness was used only to exchange the expectations in the second step, and it is enough for one of the two sets to be finite, because a finite sum and an integral can be interchanged. The lower-bound proof for sorting later in this article actually uses this version, in which one set is infinite and the other finite. Writing it as a separate theorem would be cumbersome, so we will not do so (Note 5).

If both sets are infinite, conditions such as l≥0l\geq 0l≥0 allow the integrals to be exchanged using Tonelli’s theorem. Yao’s principle can therefore be extended, but we will not need that version. Readers without a mathematical background can safely ignore it.

  The proof is remarkably simple, but the important question is not how it is proved; it is what the theorem says. In the statement, A,X\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}A,X are merely abstract sets without any specified meaning, and lll is an abstract function. To understand them, give them their usual interpretation: this is still the game between algorithm designer Alice and adversary Bob. The set A\mathcal{A}A contains every deterministic algorithm Alice may choose, X\mathcal{X}X contains every concrete input Bob may choose, and l(a,x)l(a,x)l(a,x) is the cost paid by algorithm aaa on input xxx, such as total running time or number of comparisons. Alice wants the best algorithm against Bob’s input and tries to make lll small; Bob wants the worst input against Alice’s algorithm and tries to make lll large.

  As discussed above, the random variable over A\mathcal{A}A denoted by AAA is one of Alice’s randomized algorithms. The left-hand side, max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)]maxx∈X​EA​[l(A,x)], is the strongest attack Bob can mount against the randomized algorithm AAA: he chooses the input with expected cost EA[l(A,x)]\mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)]EA​[l(A,x)] as large as possible, denoted by xxx. By contrast, the random variable over X\mathcal{X}X denoted by XXX is a random input. Bob’s input is randomized, and Alice then finds the best deterministic algorithm for that random input. The expected cost of this algorithm is the right-hand side, min⁡a∈AEX[l(a,X)]\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X}[l(a,X)]mina∈A​EX​[l(a,X)].

  Once we understand the two sides, we understand the inequality itself. To lower-bound the expected cost of a randomized algorithm AAA on its worst input—the left-hand side—we may instead analyze the expected cost of the best deterministic algorithm under a random input XXX—the right-hand side. The latter is a lower bound for the former. More concretely, suppose we want to prove max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]>nlg⁡n\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)] > n\lg nmaxx∈X​EA​[l(A,x)]>nlgn. The inequality tells us that it is enough to prove min⁡a∈AEX[l(a,X)]>nlg⁡n\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X}[l(a,X)] > n\lg nmina∈A​EX​[l(a,X)]>nlgn, after which

max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]≥min⁡a∈AEX[l(a,X)]>nlg⁡n\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A,x)] \geq \min_{a\in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X}[l(a,X)] > n\lg nx∈Xmax​EA​[l(A,x)]≥a∈Amin​EX​[l(a,X)]>nlgn

  Readers who have followed this far may wonder whether this method analyzes only one randomized algorithm AAA. Our original goal was a lower bound for every randomized sorting algorithm, not merely one particular algorithm. Those sound very different. But the theorem allows arbitrary AAA and XXX, so we immediately obtain the following corollary.

Corollary

Let A,X\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{X}A,X be two finite sets and let l:A×X→Rl:\mathcal{A}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}l:A×X→R. Then

min⁡R∈Δ(A)max⁡x∈XEA∼R[l(A,x)]≥max⁡D∈Δ(X)min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]\min_{R\in \Delta(\mathcal{A})}\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A\sim R}[l(A, x)] \geq \max_{D\in \Delta(\mathcal{X})}\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a,X)]R∈Δ(A)min​x∈Xmax​EA∼R​[l(A,x)]≥D∈Δ(X)max​a∈Amin​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]

In particular, for any random input—that is, any random variable over X\mathcal{X}X, denoted by XXX—

In practice, finding a sufficiently difficult XXX is often the hard part of applying Yao’s principle. The harder the distribution you construct, the tighter the lower bound you obtain. Yao’s principle is not a theorem that can be applied mechanically; it often appears only as the final step of a larger proof.

  This equality follows directly from the von Neumann minimax theorem in game theory. Its proof is unrelated to our subject, so we will omit it. The equality need not hold in the infinite case. This also explains the name “Yao’s minimax principle.”

A Lower Bound on Comparisons in Randomized Comparison-Based Sorting

  We can now answer the question posed at the beginning. First, let us review the most basic result because we will use the same decision-tree model. The review will be brief; it is only meant to refresh a memory that may have faded.

Theorem

The number of comparisons made by a deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm has a lower bound of Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn).

Proof

“Comparison-based” means that the algorithm cannot directly use the specific values of the elements. It can learn their ordering only by asking questions of the form xi<xj ?x_i < x_j\ ?xi​<xj​ ?. In sorting problems, we ordinarily assume that no two elements are equal.

Consider a deterministic sorting algorithm. Since the algorithm is deterministic, its comparison strategy is completely fixed: which two elements it compares next depends entirely on the outcomes of all earlier comparisons.

We can therefore unfold the algorithm’s entire execution into a binary tree called a decision tree. Each node represents the comparison the algorithm makes when it reaches that point. For example, the root might be xi<xj ?x_i < x_j \ ?xi​<xj​ ?, meaning that the algorithm begins by comparing xi,xjx_i, x_jxi​,xj​. If the root’s left child is xk<xl ?x_k < x_l\ ?xk​<xl​ ?, then after finding xi<xjx_i < x_jxi​<xj​, the algorithm next compares xk,xlx_k, x_lxk​,xl​. If the root’s right child is xm<xn ?x_m < x_n\ ?xm​<xn​ ?, then after finding xi>xjx_i > x_jxi​>xj​, it next compares xm,xnx_m, x_nxm​,xn​. Because the algorithm is deterministic, its behavior uniquely determines the whole tree.

The algorithm follows the left or right child after each comparison and continues downward. When it stops, it makes no further comparisons and has reached a leaf of the decision tree, where it outputs one fixed ordering. Thus, every leaf corresponds to one permutation. If the algorithm is correct, inputs with different orders cannot reach the same leaf; otherwise, at least one of them would receive the wrong output. There are n!n!n! possible orders, so the decision tree has at least n!n!n! leaves.

Let the decision tree have height hhh. A binary tree of height hhh has at most 2h2^h2h leaves, so

2h≥n!2^h \geq n!2h≥n!

By Stirling’s formula,

h≥lg⁡(n!)=nlg⁡n−O(n)=Ω(nlg⁡n)h \geq \lg (n!) = n\lg n- O(n) = \Omega(n\lg n)h≥lg(n!)=nlgn−O(n)=Ω(nlgn)

The permutation corresponding to a deepest leaf therefore requires the algorithm to make at least Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn) comparisons before it can be sorted.

  That completes the review. We now want to analyze randomized algorithms, for which the decision-tree model no longer seems applicable. One important reason the model works for deterministic algorithms is that their comparison strategy is fixed. Whenever all previous comparison outcomes are the same, the next pair of elements to compare is fully determined, allowing the execution to be expanded into a binary decision tree. A randomized algorithm breaks this property: its next comparison may itself be chosen at random.

  This is precisely where Yao’s principle helps. It shifts the randomness from the algorithm to the input, making the algorithm deterministic again and restoring the decision-tree model. We have laid enough groundwork, so let us proceed directly to the proof.

Theorem

The expected number of comparisons made by a randomized comparison-based sorting algorithm on its worst-case input has a lower bound of Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn).

Proof

Recall Yao’s principle: we need a distribution DDD over random inputs that makes the problem difficult for every deterministic algorithm. We noted that constructing DDD is often the hard part. Here, however, there is a natural choice that readers have probably already guessed: the uniform distribution. In sorting, all elements and all permutations have equal standing. There is no reason to favor one over another, so trying the uniform distribution is the most natural approach.

Let A=\mathcal{A}=A={ all deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithms }, X=\mathcal{X}=X={ all permutations of 1 through n }, and let l(a,x)=l(a,x)=l(a,x)= the number of comparisons algorithm a makes to sort input x. Let DDD be the uniform distribution over X\mathcal{X}X. To apply Yao’s principle, we must lower-bound min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]\min_{a\in A}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a,X)]mina∈A​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]: the expected number of comparisons made by a deterministic algorithm under the uniform distribution. This is exactly the domain of decision trees.

For a deterministic algorithm a∈Aa\in\mathcal{A}a∈A, consider its decision tree again. The n!n!n! distinct inputs reach n!n!n! distinct leaves. Let the depths of these n!n!n! leaves be d1,d2,…,dn!d_1,d_2,\dots,d_{n!}d1​,d2​,…,dn!​. The expected number of comparisons made by aaa on this random input is the average of all these depths:

EX∼D[l(a,X)]=1n!∑k=1n!dk\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a, X)]=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{k=1}^{n!} d_kEX∼D​[l(a,X)]=n!1​k=1∑n!​dk​

Estimating the right-hand side requires only a little mathematics. First, we have the Kraft inequality

∑k=1n!2−dk≤1\sum_{k=1}^{n!} 2^{-d_k} \leq 1k=1∑n!​2−dk​≤1

Do not be alarmed; its intuitive proof is simple. Imagine first a full binary tree, in which every node has either two children or none. Assign every leaf at depth ddd the value 2−d2^{-d}2−d. Then repeatedly merge pairs of sibling leaves, as in the game Synthetic Watermelon: remove two sibling leaves, each worth 2−d2^{-d}2−d, and assign their parent—which becomes a new leaf—the value 2−d+12^{-d+1}2−d+1. Keep merging until only a bare root with value 111 remains. Thus, for a full binary tree, the leaf depths satisfy ∑2−di=1\sum 2^{-d_i}=1∑2−di​=1. In a binary tree that is not necessarily full, some nodes have only one child. Contract each such edge by merging the node with its only child, making the tree full. That edge only increased the depths of the leaves, so the original sum on the left can only be smaller. Hence ∑k=1n!2−dk≤1\sum_{k=1}^{n!}2^{-d_k}\leq1∑k=1n!​2−dk​≤1.

One final bit of mathematics remains. Jensen’s inequality says that if, on R\mathbb{R}R, the function f(x)f(x)f(x) is convex, positive real numbers a1,…,am>0a_1,\dots,a_m>0a1​,…,am​>0 satisfy ∑i=1mai=1\sum_{i=1}^m a_i = 1∑i=1m​ai​=1, and x1,…,xm∈Rx_1,\dots,x_m\in \mathbb{R}x1​,…,xm​∈R, then

Here 1/n!1/n!1/n! plays the role of aia_iai​ in the inequality, and dkd_kdk​ plays the role of xix_ixi​. Since the result holds for every algorithm aaa,

min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]≥lg⁡n!=Ω(nlg⁡n)\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a, X)]\geq \lg n! = \Omega(n\lg n)a∈Amin​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]≥lgn!=Ω(nlgn)

Yao’s principle now gives

min⁡R∈Δ(A)max⁡x∈XEA∼R[l(A,x)]≥min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]=Ω(nlg⁡n)\min_{R\in \Delta(\mathcal{A})}\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A\sim R}[l(A, x)] \geq \min_{a\in\mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a,X)] =\Omega(n\lg n)R∈Δ(A)min​x∈Xmax​EA∼R​[l(A,x)]≥a∈Amin​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]=Ω(nlgn)

In other words, every randomized algorithm AAA has some sufficiently bad input xxx on which its expected number of comparisons is also of order nlg⁡nn\lg nnlgn.

Randomized Sorting Algorithms That May Err

  At this point, the problem appears to be fully resolved, though the answer is a little disappointing: no miracle occurs, and randomized algorithms cannot break the Ω(nlg⁡n)\Omega(n\lg n)Ω(nlgn) barrier.

  Careful readers may still have a question. Freivalds’ algorithm, our opening example, permits a small probability of error, and that is a major reason for its excellent performance. Although our proof seemed to cover every randomized algorithm, it did not: it covered only randomized algorithms that never err. The random algorithm AAA is a random variable over A\mathcal{A}A, and A\mathcal{A}A consists of correct deterministic algorithms that never err. No matter how they are randomized, AAA therefore never errs either. Could a randomized algorithm become miraculously better if we allowed some probability of error? As an encore, this section will answer that question as well. It is slightly more complicated than what came before, but not substantially more difficult.

  The preceding analysis missed randomized algorithms that may err because A\mathcal{A}A did not contain incorrect deterministic algorithms. Our first step should therefore be to enlarge A\mathcal{A}A so that it includes them.

  The problem is that a deterministic algorithm in this larger set may be spectacularly wrong. Consider a simple and rather foolish randomized algorithm: with probability ε\varepsilonε, it returns the input unchanged; with probability 1−ε1-\varepsilon1−ε, it invokes a correct deterministic sorting algorithm such as merge sort. This is certainly a randomized sorting algorithm that may err, and its error probability is at most ε\varepsilonε. To include it, A\mathcal{A}A must contain the “return the input unchanged” algorithm, which is wrong almost all the time. Yet that algorithm makes no comparisons at all. If it belongs to A\mathcal{A}A, then

min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]=0\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a, X)]=0a∈Amin​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]=0

  which tells us nothing.

  The underlying problem is that we want the randomized algorithm’s error probability to be controlled, and the number of sorting comparisons should depend on that error probability. A randomized algorithm with controlled error may nevertheless correspond to deterministic algorithms that are wildly inaccurate, while our cost function lll records only the number of comparisons and says nothing about error.

  Yao’s-principle framework allows only one function lll. We seemingly cannot use two separate functions for comparisons and error. What can we do? Readers familiar with optimization may recognize a standard device: Lagrangian relaxation. This technique lets us combine two quantities whose joint optimization we want to constrain.

  Let A\mathcal{A}A be the set of all deterministic algorithms, whether or not they correctly sort. Leave X\mathcal{X}X unchanged as the set of all inputs of size nnn, namely the n!n!n! permutations. Redefine lll as a function with a hyperparameter λ>0\lambda>0λ>0:

l(a,x)=c(a,x)+λe(a,x)l(a, x) = c(a, x) + \lambda e(a, x)l(a,x)=c(a,x)+λe(a,x)

  Here c(a,x)c(a,x)c(a,x) is our original l(a,x)l(a,x)l(a,x), the number of comparisons made by algorithm aaa on input xxx, while e(a,x)e(a,x)e(a,x) is defined by

e(a,x)={1,sorting result is incorrect,0,sorting result is correct.e(a, x)=\begin{cases}1, & \text{sorting result is incorrect}, \\0, & \text{sorting result is correct}.\end{cases}e(a,x)={1,0,​sorting result is incorrect,sorting result is correct.​

  Thus, we combine the comparison count ccc and the error indicator eee using a coefficient λ\lambdaλ and put them together in lll. By error probability at most ε\varepsilonε for a randomized algorithm AAA, we mean that the algorithm satisfies

∀x∈X, PrA[e(A,x)=1]≤ε\forall x\in\mathcal{X}, \ \mathrm{Pr}_{A}[e(A,x)=1]\leq \varepsilon∀x∈X, PrA​[e(A,x)=1]≤ε

  Let us apply the same Yao’s-principle analysis to these definitions of A,X,l\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}, lA,X,l.

  Again choose the uniform distribution over X\mathcal{X}X, denoted by DDD, and consider the performance of a deterministic algorithm a∈Aa \in\mathcal{A}a∈A under this random input. Suppose algorithm aaa correctly sorts, among all N=n!N=n!N=n! inputs, a fraction qqq—that is, it correctly sorts qNqNqN of them.

  Allowing q=0q=0q=0 creates a minor nuisance, so first exclude algorithms that are wrong on every input. We may therefore discard the case q=0q=0q=0 and assume q>0q>0q>0.

max⁡x∈XEA[l(A,x)]≥min⁡a∈AEX∼D[l(a,X)]≥min⁡q=1N,…,1(qlg⁡(qN)+λ(1−q))\max_{x\in \mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}_{A}[l(A, x)] \geq \min_{a\in\mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[l(a,X)] \geq \min_{q=\frac 1 N, \dots, 1} (q\lg(qN)+\lambda(1-q))x∈Xmax​EA​[l(A,x)]≥a∈Amin​EX∼D​[l(a,X)]≥q=N1​,…,1min​(qlg(qN)+λ(1−q))
