  Suppose five flip-flops are connected in this way and all begin in state “0.” We can write the state of the group as “00000.” After the first pulse is fed into the rightmost flip-flop, that device changes to state “1.” Because it produces no response pulse, the four devices to its left remain in state “0,” giving the combined state “00001.” On the second input pulse, the rightmost flip-flop returns to state “0” and sends a response pulse to its neighbor. That neighboring flip-flop changes to state “1,” while all the others, having received no response pulse, remain in state “0.” The combined state is now “00010.” When the third pulse arrives, the rightmost flip-flop changes back to state “1” without producing a response pulse; the other states remain unchanged, yielding “00011.” Continuing the cycle produces the following data:

  If we interpret these states as binary numbers and convert them to decimal, we obtain 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and so on. Connected flip-flops can therefore “count” external pulse signals—and they do so in a distinctive way.

  Binary represents every number using “0” and “1.” Unlike decimal notation, each place in a binary number is worth 2 times the place to its right, rather than 10 times as much. To convert a binary number to decimal, multiply each digit by 2 to the power n, where n denotes its place, and add the results. For example, converting the binary number “10011” gives 1 × 2^0 + 1 × 2^1 + 0 × 2^2 + 0 × 2^3 + 1 × 2^4 = 19.

  Each flip of the device—that is, each input pulse—takes only a few hundred-millionths of a second. Modern counting flip-flops can “count” more than ten million pulses in one second, whereas the human eye needs about 0.1 seconds to distinguish a changing signal. Compared with a person, the device is nearly one million times faster.

  Next, let us see how flip-flops can perform addition. Connect three rows of flip-flops as shown in Figure 3. The first row represents the augend, the second the addend, and the third their sum. Whenever a flip-flop in either of the upper rows is in state “1,” it sends a pulse to the corresponding device in the third row.

Figure 3

  In Figure 3, the first two rows store the binary numbers 101 and 111. The first flip-flop in the third row receives one pulse from each of the first devices in the two upper rows, for a total of two. As explained above, it remains in state “0” and sends one response pulse to the second flip-flop in the third row. In addition to this response pulse, the second flip-flop receives a pulse from the second device in the second row. It therefore receives two pulses in all, remains in state “0,” and sends a response pulse to the third device in its row. Besides that response pulse, the third flip-flop receives one pulse from each of the first and second rows, for a total of three. It ends in state “1” and also produces a response pulse. The fourth flip-flop in the third row receives only that one response pulse and therefore enters state “1.” This is binary addition; written vertically, the calculation is the one shown in Figure 4:

Figure 4

  Converting the binary values in Figure 4 to decimal gives 5 + 7 = 12. The response pulses from the third row serve as the carries in column addition. With 20 or more flip-flops in each row, the circuit can add numbers in the millions or even tens of millions. A modified version of the same design can perform not only addition and subtraction, but multiplication and division as well.

Reference: Recreational Algebra

entry.title: The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics
entry.content:
Entangled States—from Theory to Technology

Alain Aspect, John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger conducted groundbreaking experiments using entangled quantum states. In such states, two particles behave as a single unit even when separated. Their results cleared the way for new technologies based on quantum information.

The once-ineffable effects of quantum mechanics are beginning to find practical applications. They are now the subject of a major research field that includes quantum computers, quantum networks, and secure quantum-encrypted communication.

A key to this progress is the way quantum mechanics allows two or more particles to exist in what is known as an entangled state. What happens to one particle in an entangled pair determines what happens to the other, even when the two are far apart.

For a long time, scientists debated whether this correlation arose because the particles in an entangled pair contained hidden variables—instructions telling them which result to produce in an experiment. In the 1960s, John Stewart Bell formulated the mathematical inequality that bears his name. It showed that if hidden variables existed, the correlations among the results of many measurements could never exceed a certain value. Quantum mechanics, however, predicted that a particular kind of experiment would violate Bell’s inequality and produce stronger correlations than would otherwise be possible.

John Clauser developed John Bell’s ideas into a practical experiment. His measurements clearly violated Bell’s inequality, supporting quantum mechanics. This meant that quantum mechanics could not be replaced by a theory based on hidden variables.

Some loopholes remained after John Clauser’s experiment. Alain Aspect refined the setup to close an important one. He could switch the measurement settings after an entangled pair had left its source, so the settings in place when the particles were emitted could not affect the outcome.

Using sophisticated instruments and a series of experiments, Anton Zeilinger began working with entangled quantum states. His group also demonstrated a phenomenon known as quantum teleportation, which makes it possible to transfer a quantum state from one particle to another across a distance.

“It has become increasingly clear that a new kind of quantum technology is emerging. We can see that the laureates’ work with entangled states is of great importance, even beyond the fundamental questions about the interpretation of quantum mechanics,” said Anders Irbäck, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.

Translation: DeepL
Proofreader: Shiguang
Original: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/press-release/

entry.title: The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
entry.content:
Introduction

Humanity has always been curious about its origins: Where do we come from? How are we, Homo sapiens, related to the other humans who came before us? What makes Homo sapiens different from other humans?

Through his pioneering research, Professor Svante Pääbo accomplished something seemingly impossible: sequencing the genome of an extinct human relative, the Neanderthal. He also made the sensational discovery of a previously unknown human group, the Denisovans. Crucially, Pääbo found that genes from these now-extinct groups were transferred to Homo sapiens after our ancestors left Africa about 70,000 years ago. This ancient genetic legacy remains physiologically significant in people today, affecting, for example, how our immune systems respond to infection.

Pääbo’s groundbreaking work gave rise to an entirely new discipline: paleogenomics. By revealing the genetic differences that distinguish all living humans from extinct human groups, his discoveries laid the foundation for exploring what makes Homo sapiens uniquely human.

Where Do We Come From?

Questions about where we come from and why we are unique have occupied humanity since ancient times. Paleontology and archaeology are essential to the study of human evolution. Evidence from these fields indicates that anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, first appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Our closest known relatives, the Neanderthals, developed outside Africa and inhabited Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 30,000 years ago, after which they became extinct. Around 70,000 years ago, groups of Homo sapiens migrated from Africa to the Middle East and then spread across the rest of the world. Homo sapiens and Neanderthals therefore coexisted across much of Eurasia for tens of thousands of years. But how much do we know about the relationship between Homo sapiens and the extinct Neanderthals? Genomic information might provide clues. By the late 1990s, almost the entire human genome had been sequenced. This major achievement later enabled scientists to investigate the genetic relationships among different human populations. Studying the relationship between people alive today and extinct Neanderthals, however, required the sequencing of genomic DNA extracted from ancient human specimens.

A Seemingly Impossible Task

Early in his scientific career, Svante Pääbo became fascinated by the possibility of using modern genetic methods to study Neanderthal DNA. He soon recognized the daunting technical challenges. Over time, chemical reactions break DNA down into short fragments. After thousands of years, only trace amounts remain, and those remnants are heavily contaminated by DNA from bacteria and present-day humans (Figure 1). As a postdoctoral student of Allan Wilson, a pioneer in evolutionary biology, Pääbo began developing methods for studying Neanderthal DNA—an effort that would continue for decades.

Figure 1. DNA is located in two different compartments within the cell. Nuclear DNA contains most of the genetic information, while the much smaller mitochondrial genome is present in thousands of copies. After death, DNA degrades over time until only small amounts remain. It also becomes contaminated by DNA from sources such as bacteria and present-day humans.

In 1990, Pääbo joined the University of Munich. As a newly appointed professor, he continued his work on ancient human DNA and decided to analyze Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA. Mitochondria are organelles that contain their own DNA. Although their genome is small and accounts for only a tiny fraction of the cell’s genetic information, thousands of mitochondria can be found in a sample, greatly improving the chances of success. Using his methods, Pääbo succeeded in sequencing a region of mitochondrial DNA from a 40,000-year-old bone. For the first time, a sequence from an extinct human relative was available. Comparisons with present-day humans and chimpanzees showed that Neanderthals were genetically distinct.

Sequencing the Neanderthal Genome

Because analysis of the small mitochondrial genome provided only limited information, Pääbo took on the formidable challenge of sequencing the Neanderthal nuclear genome. At this point, he was offered the opportunity to establish a Max Planck Institute in Leipzig, Germany. At the new institute, Pääbo and his team steadily refined their methods for isolating and analyzing DNA from ancient human remains. They took advantage of new technological advances that made DNA sequencing highly efficient. Pääbo also recruited key collaborators with expertise in population genetics and advanced sequence analysis. His efforts succeeded: Pääbo completed the seemingly impossible task and published the first Neanderthal genome sequence in 2010. Comparative analyses indicated that the most recent common ancestor of Neanderthals and Homo sapiens lived around 800,000 years ago.

Figure 2. A. Pääbo extracted DNA from skeletal specimens of extinct humans. He first obtained a bone fragment from the Neander Valley in Germany, which gave Neanderthals their name. Later, he used a finger bone from Denisova Cave in southern Siberia, after which the Denisovans were named. B. The phylogenetic tree shows the evolution of and relationships between Homo sapiens and extinct human groups. It also illustrates the gene flow discovered by Pääbo.

Pääbo and his colleagues could now investigate the relationship between Neanderthals and modern humans from different parts of the world. Comparative analyses showed that Neanderthal DNA sequences were more similar to those of present-day people of European or Asian descent than to those of present-day people of African descent. This meant that Neanderthals and Homo sapiens had interbred during the thousands of years in which they coexisted. In modern people of European or Asian ancestry, approximately 1–4% of the genome comes from Neanderthals (Figure 2).

A Sensational Discovery: The Denisovans

In 2008, a fragment of a 40,000-year-old finger bone was discovered in Denisova Cave in southern Siberia. The bone contained exceptionally well-preserved DNA, which Pääbo’s team sequenced. The result caused a sensation: compared with all known sequences from Neanderthals and present-day humans, the DNA sequence from the finger bone was unique. Pääbo had discovered a previously unknown human group, which was named the Denisovans. Comparisons with sequences from present-day people in different parts of the world showed that gene flow had also occurred between Denisovans and Homo sapiens. This relationship was first identified in populations in Melanesia and elsewhere in Southeast Asia, whose genomes contain up to 6% Denisovan DNA.

Pääbo’s discoveries transformed our understanding of evolutionary history. When Homo sapiens left Africa, at least two now-extinct human populations inhabited Eurasia. Neanderthals lived in western Eurasia, while Denisovans occupied the continent’s eastern regions. As Homo sapiens expanded beyond Africa and migrated eastward, they encountered and interbred not only with Neanderthals but also with Denisovans (Figure 3).

Paleogenomics and Its Relevance

Professor Svante Pääbo’s pioneering research established an entirely new scientific discipline: paleogenomics. Following his initial discoveries, his group completed analyses of the genome sequences of several other extinct human groups. Pääbo’s discoveries created a unique resource that scientists have used extensively to gain a better understanding of human evolution and migration. Powerful new sequence-analysis methods indicate that ancient humans may also have interbred with Homo sapiens in Africa. However, because ancient human DNA degrades more rapidly in tropical climates, no genome from an extinct African human group has yet been sequenced.

Thanks to Pääbo’s discoveries, we now know that ancient genetic sequences inherited from our extinct relatives continue to influence people today. One example is the Denisovan gene EPAS1, which confers an advantage for survival at high altitudes and is common among present-day Tibetans. Other examples include Neanderthal genes that affect our immune responses to different kinds of infection.

Figure 3. Pääbo's discoveries provide important information about the world's human populations when Homo sapiens migrated out of Africa and spread across the globe. Neanderthals lived in western Eurasia and Denisovans in the east. As Homo sapiens spread across the continent, the groups interbred, leaving traces that remain in our DNA.

What Makes Us Uniquely Human?

Homo sapiens created diverse cultures and great art, and developed the ability to cross oceans and reach every part of the planet (Figure 4). Neanderthals also lived in groups and had large heads (Figure 4). They, too, used tools, but those tools developed very slowly over hundreds of thousands of years. The genetic differences between Homo sapiens and our closest extinct relatives remained unknown until Pääbo’s groundbreaking work identified them. Professor Pääbo’s ongoing research focuses on analyzing the functional effects of these differences, with the ultimate goal of explaining what makes us uniquely human.

Figure 4. Pääbo's pioneering work provides a foundation for explaining what makes us uniquely human.

Translation: DeepL
Proofreader: Shiguang
Original: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/press-release/

entry.title: Variational Inference and Generative Models
entry.content:
Author: I Am Zhang Yixian
Author’s Zhihu profile: Thinker

Variational Inference

The basic idea is this: in probabilistic models, we often need to approximate probability distributions that are difficult to calculate. Inference about any unknown quantity can be regarded as posterior-probability inference, because Bayes’ theorem can be used to construct it:

p(x)=∑p(x∣z)p(z)p(x) = \sum p(x|z)p(z)p(x)=∑p(x∣z)p(z)

For large datasets, Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are too slow, so we need variational inference.

We frequently encounter two kinds of variables here: real data, xxx, and latent data, zzz​.

The resulting inference problem is to determine the posterior conditional probability distribution p(z∣x)p(z|x)p(z∣x)​​ of the input data. Using the ELBO method, we hope to find a concrete distribution q(z)q(z)q(z) that can approximate and replace the true posterior distribution p(z∣x)p(z|x)p(z∣x)​.

We therefore need to optimize their KL divergence:

q∗(z)=argminq(z)∈QKL(q(z)∣∣p(z∣x))q^*(z) = argmin_{q(z)∈Q}KL(q(z)||p(z|x))q∗(z)=argminq(z)∈Q​KL(q(z)∣∣p(z∣x))

The KL divergence can be rewritten further. All expectations below are with respect to q(z)q(z)q(z):

KL(q(z)∣∣p(z∣x))=E(log⁡q(z))−E(log⁡p(z∣x))=E(log⁡q(z))−E(log⁡p(x,z))+log⁡p(x)KL(q(z)||p(z|x)) =E(\log q(z)) - E(\log p(z|x))\\=E(\log q(z)) - E(\log p(x,z))+ \log p(x)KL(q(z)∣∣p(z∣x))=E(logq(z))−E(logp(z∣x))=E(logq(z))−E(logp(x,z))+logp(x)

We can therefore define the evidence lower bound, or ELBO:

ELBO(q)=E(log⁡p(z,x))−E(log⁡q(z))ELBO(q) = E(\log p(z,x)) - E(\log q(z))ELBO(q)=E(logp(z,x))−E(logq(z))

The q(z)q(z)q(z)​ above can of course be replaced by q(z∣x)q(z|x)q(z∣x); the equation then needs only a small adjustment. ​

Whether in a VAE, GAN, or NF, one inequality is always especially important:

  • Make pθ(z∣x)p_\theta(z|x)pθ​(z∣x) and qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z|x)qϕ​(z∣x) as close as possible

    DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z∣x))=log⁡(pθ(x))−∑zqϕ(z∣x)log⁡(pθ(x,z)qϕ(z∣x))=log⁡(pθ(x))−L(θ,ϕ;x)D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z|x))= \log(p_\theta(x)) - \sum_zq_{\phi}(z|x)\log(\frac{p_{\theta}(x,z)}{q_{\phi}(z|x)})\\=\log(p_\theta(x)) - L(\theta,\phi;x)DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z∣x))=log(pθ​(x))−z∑​qϕ​(z∣x)log(qϕ​(z∣x)pθ​(x,z)​)=log(pθ​(x))−L(θ,ϕ;x)

    This equation seeks to make DKLD_{KL}DKL​​ as close to 0 as possible, which means making the two distributions as close as possible. Continuing the transformation gives:

    L(θ,ϕ;x)=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡(pθ(x∣z))]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z))L(\theta,\phi;x) = E_{q_{\phi}(z|x)}[\log(p_{\theta}(x|z))] - D_{KL}(q_{\phi}(z|x)||p_{\theta}(z))L(θ,ϕ;x)=Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[log(pθ​(x∣z))]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z))

    Combining the two equations gives:

    log⁡(pθ(x))−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z∣x))=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡(pθ(x∣z))]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z))\log(p_\theta(x)) - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z|x)) = E_{q_{\phi}(z|x)}[\log(p_{\theta}(x|z))] - D_{KL}(q_{\phi}(z|x)||p_{\theta}(z))log(pθ​(x))−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z∣x))=Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[log(pθ​(x∣z))]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z))

    Our objective is to make DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z∣x))D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z|x))DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z∣x))​ as close to 0 as possible, so we obtain the equation from the paper:

    log⁡(pθ(x))≥Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡(pθ(x∣z))]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z))=−F(x)\log(p_\theta(x)) ≥ E_{q_{\phi}(z|x)}[\log(p_{\theta}(x|z))] - D_{KL}(q_{\phi}(z|x)||p_{\theta}(z)) = -F (x)log(pθ​(x))≥Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[log(pθ​(x∣z))]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z))=−F(x)

    The formula above captures the key idea of variational inference. Here, FFF is called the ELBO bound.

VAE (Variational Autoencoder)

A VAE seeks to make the ELBOELBOELBO​​ derived above as large as possible. It introduces SGVB and the reparameterization method.

The VAE network architecture is shown below:

Put simply, it takes real data xxx as input and uses the generative networks h,gh,gh,g to produce the desired μx,σx\mu_x,\sigma_xμx​,σx​:

μx=g(x)σx=h(x)\mu_x = g(x) \\\sigma_x = h(x)μx​=g(x)σx​=h(x)

It then introduces Gaussian noise N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) and combines the two to construct the latent variable zzz​—the reparameterization trick, which makes backpropagation possible:

z=σxζ+μxz = \sigma_x \zeta + \mu_xz=σx​ζ+μx​

The decoder then decodes zzz into x^\hat{x}x^:

x^=f(z)\hat{x} = f(z)x^=f(z)

Note that when training a VAE, we must ensure that zzz follows a normal distribution. This is a major difference between a VAE and an AE: it gives the latent space a degree of regularity—continuity and completeness.

The VAE loss function is:

L(θ,ϕ;x)=ELBO=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡(pθ(x∣z))]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z))L(\theta,\phi;x) = ELBO \\=E_{q_{\phi}(z|x)}[\log(p_{\theta}(x|z))] - D_{KL}(q_{\phi}(z|x)||p_{\theta}(z))L(θ,ϕ;x)=ELBO=Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[log(pθ​(x∣z))]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z))

The first term can be understood as reconstruction loss, and the second as regularization loss.

Applying maximum likelihood to the first term gives:

(f∗,g∗,h∗)=argmax(f,g,h)∈F×G×H(Ez qx(−∣∣x−f(z)∣∣22c)−KL(qx(z)∣∣p(z)))(f^*,g^*,h^*) = argmax_{(f,g,h)∈F\times G \times H} (E_{z ~ q_x}(-\frac{||x-f(z)||^2}{2c}) - KL(q_x(z)||p(z)))(f∗,g∗,h∗)=argmax(f,g,h)∈F×G×H​(Ez qx​​(−2c∣∣x−f(z)∣∣2​)−KL(qx​(z)∣∣p(z)))

How do we handle the second term? We can integrate it directly:

−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∣∣pθ(z))=∫qθ(z)(log⁡pθ(z)−log⁡qθ(z))dz=12∑j=1J(1+log⁡((σj)2)−μj2−σj2) - D_{KL}(q_{\phi}(z|x)||p_{\theta}(z)) = \int q_{\theta}(z)(\log p_{\theta}(z)-\log q_{\theta}(z))dz \\ = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^J (1+\log((\sigma_j)^2)-\mu_j^2-\sigma_j^2)−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣∣pθ​(z))=∫qθ​(z)(logpθ​(z)−logqθ​(z))dz=21​j=1∑J​(1+log((σj​)2)−μj2​−σj2​)

(Note that because we want the distribution of zzz​​ to be as close as possible to N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1)​, the mean of the distribution of zzz​​ is 0 and its variance is 1. For qϕ(z∣x)q_{\phi}(z|x)qϕ​(z∣x), the distribution is N(μ,σ)N(\mu,\sigma)N(μ,σ).​)

The second term means making qϕ(z∣x)q_{\phi}(z|x)qϕ​(z∣x) approach N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1)​ as closely as possible. The first term is the MSE between the generated x^\hat{x}x^ and xxx; this is the term that also appears in an AE. The second is equivalent to a regularization term.

To generate a completely new image, sample zzz directly and feed it into the decoder network. The output will be a new image.

GAN (Adversarial Learning)

A GAN consists of a generator network G and a discriminator network D:

A GAN can be understood as using the cross-entropy formula to determine the similarity between distributions:

H(p,q)=−∑ipilog⁡qiH(p,q)=-\sum_{i}{p_i \log q_i}H(p,q)=−i∑​pi​logqi​

This resembles a binary-classification problem. The data either comes from the real dataset or is produced by randomly generating noise and passing it through the generator. The discriminator must then decide whether it is real or fake:

The discriminator says only “right” or “wrong.” It is a binary-classification network.

Suppose is the distribution of correct samples. The corresponding is then the distribution of generated samples. represents the discriminator, so represents the probability that it classifies a sample as correct, while corresponds to the probability that it classifies a sample as incorrect.

Implementing this with cross-entropy gives:

Let the sample generated by the generator be x^\hat{x}x^~G(z)G(z)G(z), where zzz follows the distribution of the noise fed into the generator. xxx​ is a real sample point.

Extending this to infinity, we rewrite it in integral form.

Here is the formal procedure:

We first fix G—that is, choose an arbitrary G—and then seek V(G,D)V(G,D)V(G,D):

V(G,D)=∫∞pdata(x)log⁡D(x)dx+∫∞pz(z)log⁡(1−D(g(z)))dz=∫∞(pdata(x)log⁡(D(x))+pg(x)log(1−D(x)))dxV(G,D) = \int _\infin p_{data}(x)\log D(x) dx + \int _\infin p_z(z) \log (1-D(g(z))) dz\\ = \int _\infin (p_{data}(x)\log(D(x)) + p_g(x)log(1-D(x)) )dxV(G,D)=∫∞​pdata​(x)logD(x)dx+∫∞​pz​(z)log(1−D(g(z)))dz=∫∞​(pdata​(x)log(D(x))+pg​(x)log(1−D(x)))dx

Differentiating the expression inside the integral gives the maximum V(G,D)V(G,D)V(G,D), which is the point at which DDD performs best:

At this point:

D∗(x)=pdata(x)pdata(x)+pg(x)D^*(x) = \frac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x)+p_g(x)}D∗(x)=pdata​(x)+pg​(x)pdata​(x)​

That is:

V(G,D)=Ex−>pdata[pdata(x)pdata(x)+pg(x)]+Ex−>pg[pdata(x)pdata(x)+pg(x)]V(G,D) = E_{x->p_{data}}[ \frac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x)+p_g(x)}]+E_{x->p_{g}}[ \frac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x)+p_g(x)}]V(G,D)=Ex−>pdata​​[pdata​(x)+pg​(x)pdata​(x)​]+Ex−>pg​​[pdata​(x)+pg​(x)pdata​(x)​]

We must then keep training the generator network so as to minimize max⁡DV(G,D)=V(G,D∗)\max_D V(G,D) = V(G,D^*)maxD​V(G,D)=V(G,D∗)​: C(G)=min⁡GV(G,D∗)C(G) = \min_G V(G,D^*)C(G)=minG​V(G,D∗).

Thus, when pg=pdata=1/2p_g = p_{data} = 1/2pg​=pdata​=1/2​—the Nash equilibrium, at which point it can no longer tell which is which—we obtain the minimum:

min⁡Gmax⁡DV(G,D)=min⁡GV(G,D∗)=−log⁡4\min_G\max_D V(G,D) = \min_G V(G,D^*) = -\log 4Gmin​Dmax​V(G,D)=Gmin​V(G,D∗)=−log4

Substituting their minimum values and rewriting gives:

C(G)=−log(4)+KL(pdata∣∣pdata+pg2)+KL(pg∣∣pdata+pg2)=−log(4)+2JSD(pdata∣∣pg)C(G) = -log(4) + KL(p_{data}||\frac{p_{data}+p_g}{2})+ KL(p_{g}||\frac{p_{data}+p_g}{2}) \\= -log(4)+2JSD(p_{data}||p_g)C(G)=−log(4)+KL(pdata​∣∣2pdata​+pg​​)+KL(pg​∣∣2pdata​+pg​​)=−log(4)+2JSD(pdata​∣∣pg​)

When JSD is 0, pdatap_{data}pdata​​ and pgp_gpg​ are considered equal and can no longer be distinguished from one another. At this point, C* = -log4.​​

NF (Normalizing Flow)

A normalizing flow is another kind of generative network, based on a change-of-variables theorem.

Suppose the generative network is still G, zzz is a standard normal distribution—the latent variable—and x is real data.

Z−>Generator...−>xZ->Generator...->xZ−>Generator...−>x

We therefore want the distribution of the generated x to be as close as possible to the original distribution of x.

Suppose {x1,x2,...,xm}\{x^1,x^2,...,x^m\}{x1,x2,...,xm} is a sample from pdata(x)p_{data}(x)pdata​(x)​.

We want pG(x)p_G(x)pG​(x) and pdata(x)p_{data}(x)pdata​(x) to be as close as possible, giving the target:

G∗=argmaxG∑i=1mlog⁡PG(xi)≈argminGKL(pdata(x)∣∣pG(x))G^* =argmax_G \sum_{i=1}^m \log P_G(x^i) \\≈ argmin_G KL (p_{data}(x)||p_G(x))G∗=argmaxG​i=1∑m​logPG​(xi)≈argminG​KL(pdata​(x)∣∣pG​(x))

Several mathematical formulas matter here: the volume after a linear transformation equals the determinant of the transformation matrix.

In other words, the determinant can be regarded as the local linear rate of volume change under the transformation .

The input and output sizes of an NF must be the same. This distinguishes it from the other two, which accept arbitrary inputs.

Now suppose that it consists of a series of flow networks.

We modify the original network accordingly:

log⁡pK(xi)=log⁡π(zi)+∑h=1Klog⁡∣det(JGK−1)∣\log p_K (x^i) = \log \pi(z^i) +\sum_{h=1}^K \log|det(J_{G_K^{-1}})|logpK​(xi)=logπ(zi)+h=1∑K​log∣det(JGK−1​​)∣

We seek the maximum value of the left-hand side—that is, the maximum log likelihood.

To calculate it, we can consider the process in reverse and feed x through the G−1G^{-1}G−1​ network to generate z.

Because the expression above is too computationally expensive, we need the following treatment:

1. Coupling Layer: – > used in NICE and Real NVP

It sends the first 1:d dimensions directly from z to x. For the remaining d+1:D dimensions, the earlier data passes through the F and H networks to obtain βd+1:D\beta_{d+1:D}βd+1:D​ and γd+1:D\gamma_{d+1:D}γd+1:D​, followed by a linear combination:

xd+1:D=βd+1:D×zd+1:D+γd+1:Dx_{d+1:D} = \beta_{d+1:D} \times z_{d+1:D} + \gamma_{d+1:D}xd+1:D​=βd+1:D​×zd+1:D​+γd+1:D​

After the coupling layer, the Jacobian matrix becomes a triangular matrix:

​`

The upper portion is copied directly, so it is 1:1, while the values along the lower-right diagonal (D>i>d+1) are the βi\beta_iβi​ values.

The determinant of the Jacobian can therefore be written as:

det(JG)=1×1×...×1×βd+1×...×βDdet(J_G) = 1\times 1 \times ...\times 1\times \beta_{d+1}\times ...\times \beta_{D}det(JG​)=1×1×...×1×βd+1​×...×βD​

But if every network is processed this way, would the first d terms not remain unchanged?

They must therefore be processed in an interleaved manner. Each network randomly selects d terms, and the size of d must also vary. Only then will stacking the networks have an effect.

  1. 1x1 Convolution

In addition to coupling layers, we can use a 1x1 convolution. This was proposed in GLOW and works especially well.

Suppose we are processing an image with three channels—the R, G, and B channels. The 1x1 convolution uses a 3x3 matrix WWW:

The size does not change after the 1x1 convolution, and this WWW matrix is in fact det(JG)det(J_G)det(JG​):

x=f(z)=W×zx = f(z) =W\times z x=f(z)=W×z

\begin{equation} % begin mathematical environmentJ_f = \left( % left parenthesis \begin{array}{ccc} % the matrix has three centered columns w_{11} & w_{12} & w_{13}\\ % first-row elements w_{21} & w_{22} & w_{23}\\ % second-row elements w_{31} & w_{32} & w_{33}\\ \end{array}\right) = W % right parenthesis\end{equation}

As long as W is easy to solve, the result is easy to calculate:

The result is therefore the product of the W matrices on the diagonal:

(det(W))d×d(det(W))^{d\times d}(det(W))d×d

Substituting into the formula:

log⁡pK(xi)=log⁡π(zi)+∑h=1Klog⁡∣(det(W))d×d∣\log p_K (x^i) = \log \pi(z^i) +\sum_{h=1}^K \log|(det(W))^{d\times d}|logpK​(xi)=logπ(zi)+h=1∑K​log∣(det(W))d×d∣

This simplifies the complex computation.

References:
[1] Hung-yi Lee, Machine Learning
[2] Su Jianlin

entry.title: Paradox Interactive: Game Worlds and (Political) Social Simulation
entry.content:
Author: Enthusiastic A-Jiang
Reviewer: Saito Shin

  Everyone has played a game by “Paradox,” right? (Figure 1 shows Paradox’s official logo.) Anyone who enjoys historical strategy or simulation games will know the famous company. Headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden, Paradox has created many classic game series. Its games go on sale every year from April to May, so if you have not played one yet, now is the time. You may find something you like.

(Figure 1: Paradox logo)

  Why is Paradox so famous? Its players are said to be the most inhuman people in gaming history. Search for “Paradox players,” and you will see descriptions such as “demons” and “perverts.” But why are they considered inhuman? Take Stellaris as an example. Ordinary players fly spaceships through space, make friends with aliens, and discover unfamiliar civilizations. Paradox players capture aliens for food and purge alien species at the slightest disagreement. Every Paradox player has probably eliminated populations numbering in the hundreds of millions. In Cities: Skylines, meanwhile, they flood the world with sewage. In short, every Paradox player is an “Old Man of Ten Perfections” (Complete the old man).

  The rest of this article will focus on two Paradox series that I think you will find interesting.

I. The Stellaris Series

  First is Stellaris, a science-fiction epic comparable in scope to The Three-Body Problem and addictive from the first playthrough. Stellaris has moderate difficulty and is extremely open-ended. You can develop freely in a galaxy of almost any size. The entire Milky Way forms its setting, and the vast universe contains almost everything. You are not alone: the galaxy is home to other empires with different systems of government, species, and ideologies. You can expand, declare sovereignty, colonize Earth, develop technology, conduct diplomacy with other empires, sign agreements, wage war, and enslave or exterminate other species. You can instead coexist peacefully, establish a federation with other empires, encounter alien civilizations, and translate their languages. All of this can happen in Stellaris. The most exciting events, however, are the three late-game crises: Void Demons, the Extradimensional Invasion, and the Contingency.

  (Interested readers can look them up on Baidu.)

(Figure 2: Stellaris gameplay screenshot 1)

  If you are a science-fiction fan with plenty of time, you really, truly should play Stellaris. Even if you do not know how to play, you can still admire the vastness of the universe. Trust me: you will not regret it.

Beginner-Level Gameplay

  Players say that Stellaris is a game about exploration. At the start, you first configure the civilization you have imagined—in plain terms, you create its character. It looks roughly like Figure 3 below (hhhhhh).

(Figure 3)

  Once you finish creating it, the system assigns your civilization a personality based on the points you selected. The most common setup is a machine civilization (Mechanical civilization): an advanced defense system that continues to operate after the apocalypse of its original creators. (This makes the game much smoother, almost like playing Anipop: anyone with hands can do it.) The game then automatically divides the system into sectors, though there are also choices such as Skynet, Earthnet, and defense systems.

  Take my own game as an example. I originally set my defense system as a Determined Exterminator, which meant that ideologically I had to wipe out every biological (organic) species. But while preparing to eliminate a civilization forgotten by love, I discovered that my system had mastered the hyperdrive long ago, which meant that I could not exterminate other organisms. A black hole near the home system, however, had a peculiar gravitational field that distorted the hyperlane between that system and the main galaxy. Even with hyperspace-jump technology, the civilization could not use it normally and remained trapped in the system like a prisoner. Since the system contained many planets, a civilization could begin on only one planet, then explore space and invade the life-forms on other worlds—the aliens of our real life.

  The two original powers on the planet had been at war without end, and centuries of hatred had sunk into their bones. One of them was Li Shanchang. Its hyperspace technology had brought its black-hole and wormhole teleportation systems close to completion, and it was on the verge of leaving that godforsaken place for the vast galaxy. In a system dominated by a mechanical civilization, however, hostile powers will destroy your defense systems and level everything you have built. It feels like losing all your progress overnight, but the experience is still very nice. Most importantly, the game presents a realistic simulation of the universe. Many scenes from The Three-Body Problem appear in it, making the experience comparable to dozens of American blockbusters.

(Figure 4: Stellaris gameplay screenshot 2)

II. The Victoria Series

  This is a relatively uncommon kind of economic and social-structure simulation, in which every social class has different economic and political demands. In Victoria, a policy cannot be implemented merely by clicking a button. It is unlike a single-player-like mobile online game such as Honor of Kings, where you can switch off your brain for an entire session. (I am not talking about Honor of Kings itself, of course, but about a brainless player like this editor. Boo-hoo! Have you ever suffered through nineteen consecutive losses? Do not follow my example and get so used to being reported.) Instead, policies receive support or resistance from different interest groups. Those groups may be pursuing private gain, or the livelihoods of a million grain-transport workers may depend on the issue.

  Supporting and opposing interest groups exert their influence and compete with one another. The stronger the opposition, the more likely a reform is to become mired in argument and stagnation. For example, if the Qing gentry’s interest group is too influential, changing the education system to make private academies focus primarily on science becomes very difficult. Workers may want an eight-hour day while capitalists demand a twelve-hour one. Amid this endless exploitation, capital in the game rivals capital in real life.

  (Here are a few examples everyone will know. At Foxconn, national regulations prescribe an eight-hour workday and treat anything beyond it as overtime. Yet the company uses twelve-hour shifts that rotate between night and day. I experienced this firsthand during the winter break of my first year at university; it was hell on earth and a miniature version of the game. Having looked at the bottom tier, consider the middle: the “Chrysanthemum Factory” should be familiar to everyone. I had the chance to intern there in my second year. “996” may be only a label; more than two-thirds of the time, the schedule was 9 a.m. to 11 p.m.—a full fourteen hours. Yes, really. Some people will say that the pay is high, and it certainly is… But that is not our focus. The point is to introduce the appeal we can find in the game. I think students of politics, management, and finance will enjoy the Victoria series.)

(Figure 5: Victoria gameplay screenshot)

  In the game, the player acts as the ruler, holding supreme power but also bearing the greatest responsibility and mission: serving the people, promoting the establishment of labor laws, and enabling people to live in peace. Because wealthy capitalist interest groups wield excessive influence, however, labor laws can be difficult to pass. The game lets players experience the enormous efforts that historically late-industrializing countries made to protect the growth of their domestic industries during the early stages of industrialization. At times it feels less like a game simulation than a miniature version of reality.

  In many games, technology simply means domestic development and strength, and building a factory immediately produces money. The Victoria series does not present modern industrialization so simplistically. Its ideas are more advanced because they come from both our past and our present. Different buildings in the series have different statistics and effects, allowing the game to simulate populations more realistically. To operate, for example, a factory needs raw materials, workers, and customers. From the workers’ perspective alone, inadequate education may leave the factory unable to recruit enough literate employees. Independent farmers with stable lives may be so accustomed to that stability that they refuse factory work no matter how high the wages. If production exceeds demand and the products cannot be sold, the factory may also fail after exhausting its cash reserves.

  The Victoria series sold poorly and received an average response when it was first released. Perhaps because of the era, the series was discontinued. Later, as time passed, the world economy recovered, and education in China gradually improved, more players discovered the distinctive framework and central ideas of the games, and the series slowly gained recognition.

Victoria’s Materialist View

  Compared with Paradox’s earliest titles, Victoria II no longer constructs its world according to a historical timeline. Instead, it tries to identify the logic behind history. If Britain had not done so, could another feudal country have become the first to complete an Industrial Revolution by resolving its own problems? After the Industrial Revolution, everyday goods became scarcer than ever before, the population surged, and advancing industrialization put large numbers of artisans out of work. Might that country have begun migrating to the New World in the Americas before Britain in order to solve its population problem? The Industrial Revolution also produced too many goods. When a crisis emerged, might this country have sought to resolve it by dumping those goods (The Opium War of 1840 was Britain’s attempt to dump goods into China), and gone to war with a self-sufficient country that had not completed a modern industrial revolution? Once the world market had been fully divided, might imperialist wars have broken out among industrial countries? The game’s distinctive framework and materialist conception of history contain a fascinating internal logic that builds a complete virtual world.

Advice for Readers Who Want to Play Victoria

  Victoria 3 is now available. It makes detailed changes to the earlier games, such as reducing their historicity, leaning further toward today’s diverse society, and fixing known bugs. The results are quite good. I am an engineering student who has played Victoria for three years, so if your budget is tight, I suggest waiting before buying it because it is rather expensive. Another option is to look for a “mirrored” version on certain shopping or secondhand platforms.

  All right, that is the end of this installment!!

entry.title: A Brief Lecture on Traditional Chinese Philosophy
entry.content:
Author: Silicon-Based
Reviewer: Xian’e

  I wrote this lecture while my school was under a pandemic lockdown. I had already reached the library’s borrowing limit, and the books in which I had taken notes were far away at my home in southern China. Almost everything here was written from my rather unreliable memory, so this account of traditional Chinese philosophy will inevitably contain major omissions and errors. Please read it with appropriate caution and a critical eye.

  Traditional Chinese philosophy generally refers to the Chinese philosophical systems—or “Eastern philosophy”—that occupied a dominant ideological position in East Asia from the Hundred Schools of Thought in pre-Qin China until Marxism entered China. Compared with its counterpart, “Western philosophy,” traditional Chinese philosophy displays many distinctive traits: it emphasizes moral injunctions and social forms while giving less weight to the systems and methods of natural science; stresses unity more than particularity; values people more than things; accepts the actual existence of a supreme order and seeks harmony and unity between human beings and the external world; and has a strong strain of rudimentary dialectical thinking. Over more than a thousand years of practice in feudal society, this philosophy shaped what is now called the “spirit of the Chinese nation” and left modern China with enormous cultural inertia. Studying traditional Chinese philosophy can help readers understand China’s current intellectual landscape and trace contemporary Chinese social and cultural phenomena back to their roots.

  Traditional Chinese philosophy first began to emerge during the pre-Qin Hundred Schools of Thought. Before that period, ancient China had a primitive philosophy composed of early beliefs and morality: the seed of traditional Chinese philosophy. As the productive forces developed, the slaveholding relations of production under the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, together with their political and cultural superstructure, reached the limits imposed by those forces. More advanced feudal relations of production demanded more centralized authority. The result was the long and frequent warfare of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, which destabilized society and severely damaged production. In this turbulent age, advanced thinkers reflected on, systematized, and developed the sparse philosophy of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou, giving rise to many outstanding schools of thought;

  For the landowning ruling class, perceptive rulers in different regions recognized that the unsystematized primitive ideas of the past could no longer meet the needs of governance, development, and the struggle for supremacy. The political philosophies represented by Confucianism, Legalism, the School of Military Strategy, and the School of Diplomacy consequently formed communities of shared interests with this ruling class. At this stage, each side supported and advanced the other.

  For the broad civilian population, social upheaval severely damaged both production and daily life. The people’s simple wish for solidarity combined with their advanced productive forces. Under the leadership of the brilliant Mozi, it produced an organized, disciplined, and united proto-political collective: the Mohist school. Meanwhile, the desire of both the peasantry and the ruling class to restore production, together with advances in agricultural production, gave rise to the technical philosophy of the Agriculturalist school.

  Because Mohism and Agriculturalism responded to concrete needs in the development of the productive forces, they developed early forms of technology and science. Daoism, meanwhile… The childlike ideals inherited from primitive morality collided with the harsh reality of the period’s social turmoil, leaving Laozi, a member of the lower bureaucracy, with a profound spiritual void. This gave him both a desire to “withdraw from the world” and an ideal of “engaging with the world.” From that great contradiction emerged a precocious philosophy of extraordinary transcendence. From the standpoint of the supreme rule, the “Dao,” it constructed new moral and cognitive systems. By adopting a position beyond its own age, it escaped the immediate moment and found spiritual grounding in the eternal and the vast (“Heaven and earth are not humane; they treat the myriad things as straw dogs”). Zhuangzi later inherited these moral and cognitive systems and used them to construct a philosophy of self-exploration and a free spiritual world. Other schools—including the School of Names, the Yin-Yang School, the School of Minor Talks, and the Miscellaneous School—served different classes and groups. Their independence was relatively weak: some were assimilated through continuing conflict and exchange with larger schools, while others later declined into purely technical bodies of knowledge. Even so, their independent thinking and defiant stance in struggle greatly advanced the maturation and development of early Chinese philosophy and made a major historical contribution.

  By the late Warring States period, the hard-line philosophies of governance represented chiefly by Qin Legalism and military thought had achieved enormous success in maintaining stability and competing for hegemony through force and violence. This success gave the ruling class, Legalists, and military strategists the mistaken impression that the philosophy and methods of intense struggle could be applied directly to governance and construction after the struggle for rule had ended. The Qin dynasty consequently collapsed after only two emperors. This was a severe blow to the School of Military Strategy, which declined into an independent and abstract body of technical knowledge rather than remaining an autonomous philosophical school. The clearest sign of this change was that later periods had many “generals” but very few “military thinkers.” Legalism, unable to meet the ruling class’s growing demand for centralization, was reshaped and absorbed by Han Confucianism. Most of the other schools met a similar fate, epitomized by the call to “suppress the Hundred Schools and exalt Confucianism alone.” Only Daoism, grounded in a more profound and expansive supreme order, retained a degree of independence. Political and academic pressure nevertheless drove it to merge with ancestral religious worship and develop into a singular phenomenon in the world of religion: religious Daoism.

  The turmoil on which the Hundred Schools of Thought depended did not disappear until Qin unified the country. Qin Shi Huang’s burning of books and burying of scholars produced a tool of centralized rule that represented the new relations of production: “unified thought.” After the Qin fell, Liu Bang won popular support by opposing its harsh Legalism through his “Three Rules of Law.” He did not, however, abandon the basic principles of “unified thought” and “centralized authority.” Stable rule over a country as vast and populous as China made them inevitable. Qin’s failure also made the ruling class aware of the disastrous consequences of mistaken ideas and helped prompt Dong Zhongshu’s “suppression of the Hundred Schools” during the reign of Emperor Jing of Han. In practice, this meant critically absorbing the various schools and recombining them into a more complete “New Confucianism.” Confucianism already served the ruling class, and this new synthesis better satisfied its need for centralized authority. New Confucianism inherited the basic framework of moral education, benevolent rulers, and mutual love between ruler and people. It also integrated into that framework the insights from Legalism and Daoism that helped stabilize rule, constructing a social order that served the long-term interests shared by the ruling class and Confucian scholars. This successful intellectual transformation sustained the exceptionally long rule of three Han reigns and established Confucianism at the center of Chinese philosophy for the next thousand years.

  Confucianism called for monarchy. The ruler of the state was always the focus of Confucian reform: the ruler was expected to practice “benevolent government,” while the system cultivated an ethical model and ideal, the junzi or “exemplary person.” This model was used to teach the people to follow a system of social morality in which “the ruler is a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, and the son a son.” The original logic of Confucian political governance ran as follows: “The ruler practices benevolent government and loves the people; the people will in turn love a benevolent ruler. Moral education and ritual music teach the people, while family ethics arrange social relations and organize production. Initiated from above, this creates a stable top-down society in which everyone occupies the proper place.”

  Under Dong Zhongshu’s reforms, Confucianism retained morality as its core principle while incorporating effective methods and ideas from many other schools. It adopted, for example, the Legalist use of written law to limit a ruler’s power and regulate social customs, as well as the Daoist policy of rest and recuperation when production had suffered severe damage. This more complete form of Confucianism protected the rule of the ruling class more effectively.

  Confucianism sought to maintain the stability of feudal society primarily through moral instruction, emotional norms, and ties of blood. In its understanding of the productive forces and relations of production, however, it remained at the reactionary and passive level of “emphasizing agriculture and suppressing commerce.” This limitation was inevitable.

  Because Confucianism made “emphasizing agriculture and suppressing commerce” an important principle of rule, China’s bourgeoisie developed extremely slowly. The overall structure of philosophical thought remained at the level of feudal society for a long period, without major breakthroughs. During the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern dynasties, scholar-officials confronted political darkness and social turmoil by turning to Daoism for spiritual support, thereby developing the Wei-Jin school of xuanxue, or “arcane learning.” More generally, the pattern was roughly Confucianism in orderly times and Daoism in troubled ones.

  By the Tang dynasty, rulers continued to value the Buddhist thought that had developed since the Northern and Southern dynasties, allowing it to flourish and introducing a distinctive and powerful new current into the earlier contest between Confucianism and Daoism. The Tang’s commercial economy also grew, politics remained stable, and its rulers were clear-minded; governance and culture consequently prospered. China was then a global center of culture, where innumerable ideas and religions met in the East. Chang’an even had a Zoroastrian, or fire-worshipping, temple, which gives some sense of the cultural splendor of the time.

  In this age of cultural exchange, Chinese philosophy reached a turning point. Material resources were becoming richer, and a bourgeoisie was beginning to emerge; propelled by the age, new ideas collided and took shape. After several periods of turmoil from the Southern dynasties through the Sui and into the early Tang, the transcendent Buddhist worldview of rebirth, reincarnation, and the convergence and dispersal of karmic conditions offered comfort amid real hardship. Its beautiful vision of a future life won followers tormented by suffering in the present. Different rulers nevertheless held different attitudes toward Buddhism. Some believed in it, so it expanded dramatically, at times producing the spectacle of “one temple, one cooking pot, a hundred monks.” Yet an excessively large religious community did not engage in production. This held society back and created a corrupt community in which religion and politics merged. Other rulers recognized Buddhism’s drawbacks or embraced a traditional reverence for antiquity and rejection of foreign influences. They launched movements to “eradicate” or “ban” Buddhism, repeatedly forcing it to submit to political power. Before the Tang, Buddhism’s uneven development gave it a broad popular base while also compelling it to become localized in China. During Wu Zetian’s reign, the appearance of Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, definitively marked the completion of Buddhism’s Sinicization. Buddhism as a religion also became “Buddhist philosophy.”

  Daoism transformed from an intellectual and political force into a religious one. Buddhism followed the opposite path in China: it arrived as a purely religious form, then gradually moved beyond religious influence through its difficult process of localization and became an intellectual force within Chinese philosophy. The clearest evidence is that one can read Buddhist scriptures without being a Buddhist, accept and apply their knowledge and wisdom, and find in them ideas unavailable in the Confucianism and Daoism of the time.

  Buddhism initially brought the Chinese an alien otherworld. There was no register of gods decreed by Jiang Ziya; instead, anyone could practice and become a Buddha. Nothing in this life was accidental, only the necessity of reincarnation. Most importantly, Buddhism placed human suffering and its solution at the center of its thought. Everything, including suffering, was an empty phenomenal form. Material things gathered and dispersed according to causes and conditions, while the spirit moved through cycles of reincarnation. Material needs, or desire, were described as the source of all suffering and as meaningless attachments. Buddhist philosophy therefore pursued “the emptiness of the four elements” as its highest end, while practice meant “breaking attachments” and “breaking through appearances.” Once even “attachment to the self” had been broken, the self itself could cease to exist. One could then enter a transformed state of pure spirit and return to the most innocent, lucid, compassionate, and benevolent condition: “Originally there was not a single thing; where could dust alight?”

  The various Buddhist schools are distinguished mainly by how they interpret the scriptures and how they practice. Their overall values are consistent.

  Buddhism and Daoism have similar temperaments, but essential differences remain. No matter how much Daoism withdraws from society and seeks purity and stillness, its central concern is solving problems in this world. What matters most is how to live freely here and now. It neither postpones happiness and prosperity to an illusory otherworld nor denies the existence of the self. Before Buddhism was Sinicized, its faith in the otherworld and in attaining Buddhahood was extremely firm. Records even describe groups of monks sitting in meditation on high mountains until they died of hunger and cold. This was wholly incompatible with China’s secular traditions.

  In the process of Sinicization, Buddhism therefore became less religious and more secular. One famous story about Wang Yangming, “persuading an old monk to return to lay life,” also reflects this process. We may find the existence of “Buddhist extremists” in India today difficult to understand precisely because the Buddhism familiar to us has long been Sinicized and secularized. A comparison with the Esoteric tradition of Tibetan Buddhism, which was relatively isolated from the culture of the Central Plains, supports the same judgment.

  Traditional Chinese Confucian and Daoist philosophy ultimately centers on this world. “The Master did not speak of strange phenomena, feats of strength, disorder, or spirits,” and not one sentence in the Dao De Jing discusses another world, the underworld, or where life and death come from. These philosophical systems are not inherently religious. Superstition and ancestral worship created later religious concepts such as the “underworld,” “Lingxiao Palace,” “Supreme Lord Lao,” and the “Jade Emperor.” Even these concepts developed from earlier forms of worldly moral instruction. Like heaven and hell in the West, they were intended to regulate conduct in this life. As a result, Confucian and Daoist philosophy ultimately could not explain certain basic questions scientifically, such as the “origin of the spirit” or the “essence of human beings.” They either avoided such questions entirely or appealed to mystery. A proper understanding of Chinese philosophy requires us both to separate out its religious elements when discussing its actual ideas and to consider those elements when discussing the limits of its thought.

  The introduction and Sinicization of Buddhist philosophy therefore addressed transcendent questions that Confucianism and Daoism lacked or neglected, while also bringing an entirely new set of values. Even Laozi’s Dao De Jing never left behind the “ruler,” “people,” “water,” and “infant” of real life. Like Confucianism, it could not escape politics. From their origins, both Confucianism and Daoism were closely tied to the ruling class’s needs in governance. The philosophical systems they formed could not in practice be separated from politics. For the ruling class, both were ultimately forms of learning directed toward political ends, which is why they endured throughout feudal society. For the broad civilian population, such learning was unnecessary. If ordinary people studied it, they did so to sit examinations and become officials, which still amounted to the ruling class maintaining itself.

  Buddhist philosophy, by contrast, could genuinely break away from politics and spread among ordinary people. It addressed their spiritual needs regardless of class and used religious means to comfort the population as a whole. Chan Buddhism in particular taught that one could “see one’s nature and become a Buddha” and relied on “no written words,” greatly lowering the threshold for ordinary people to study Buddhist thought. Once Sinicized, Buddhism could also provide the social and moral education needed by the ruling class. By the Tang, a Chinese philosophical system centered on “Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism” had therefore begun to take shape. After this round of conflict and integration, and propelled by the developmental needs of the bourgeoisie, Chinese philosophy was poised to enter a new stage.

  In the Song and Ming dynasties, Zhou Dunyi, Zhu Xi, the Cheng brothers, and the Lu-Wang school advanced Confucian-centered Chinese philosophy by a major step. Confucianism developed in two broad directions during this period. One was a further extension of the highly systematized union of scholarship and politics: Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism. The other combined Buddhist and Daoist ideas and returned philosophy to the people: the Lu-Wang School of Mind.

  Traditional Chinese philosophy was essentially mature by this stage. The philosophy developed by Huang Zongxi and others who represented new bourgeois currents had acquired certain modern features, including political ideas such as “democratic demands” and the “free market.” Its basic methods did not leave the category of traditional Chinese philosophy, an inevitable limitation, although the thought itself did move beyond the ordinary system of traditional Chinese philosophy. My knowledge is too limited to offer a sound conclusion, so I will leave the subject there.

  The central figures of Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism were the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi. They continued earlier Confucian learning and emphasized “orthodoxy.” Academic assessments of the school are relatively low today, but for the ruling class it was an almost ideal tool of ideological control. It represented a nearly perfected final form produced as intellectuals and the ruling class adapted to each other within a community of shared interests. The Neo-Confucianism reshaped by the three thinkers began to advocate “preserving heavenly principle and extinguishing human desires,” intensifying moral discipline to its extreme. The result included forms of oppression against women such as the so-called “chaste martyrs” and “chastity arches,” along with horrifying stories such as “Guo Ju Buries His Son” from The Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars. Zhu Xi’s Collected Commentaries on the Four Classics also allowed “revering the ancient and rejecting the new” and strained interpretations to flourish in later ages. This was probably why Li Zongwu once concluded: “Western learning was simple at first and then grew increasingly rigorous and complete; Chinese learning began at an extremely high level and then became progressively worse.” Although Neo-Confucian scholars controlled moral judgment, the scholar-official class itself was often highly dissolute, until its halls eventually became filled with hypocrites. The three Cheng-Zhu thinkers possessed high levels of moral and scholarly learning. Yet the survival and development of their intellectual synthesis ultimately depended on its community of interests with the ruling bloc, and an autocratic feudal monarchy was ultimately bound to become corrupt. No number of great Cheng-Zhu scholars could rescue it.

  The Lu-Wang School of Mind, especially Wang Yangming’s thought, can be described as Confucianism’s final peak. It genuinely absorbed the finest ideas of Buddhist philosophy and Daoism, although Wang himself denied doing so, and brought a Confucianism that appealed to the “Way of Heaven” back to human beings and the human mind—to subjective agency. “Human beings” here did not mean only the scholar-official class, but every person in the fullest sense. Emperors, kings, generals, and ministers had to study Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism, yet they found it tiresome. It was a body of learning alienated by the community of interests between Neo-Confucianism and imperial power. It alienated people by extracting human value and assigning it to an elusive “Way of Heaven”: beside that Way, one’s life counted for nothing. Wang Yangming, however, proposed that “the mind is principle.” Heavenly principle was not an abstract, external, eternal object beyond the world that only a handful of sages could master. It existed in the “mind” of every person, from emperors and generals to porters and common laborers. Morality arose from the human mind. It was neither external nor dictated by sages; it belonged to each person. This was a Confucian philosophy for the people. It continued to revolve around the central ideas of “morality” and “benevolence,” but its character changed fundamentally. First, “the mind is principle,” like “seeing one’s nature and becoming a Buddha,” greatly lowered the threshold. It genuinely addressed the people’s need to learn, rather than being locked away and serving only the ruling class. This explains the popular esteem and welcome Wang received at the time. Second, “the mind is principle” dissolved the existence of an external and abstract “Way of Heaven.” Only morality arising from within remained. There was no “Way of Heaven” apart from concrete human beings and no external Other that could impose such a Way upon you; the “Way of Heaven” was in your own mind. This returned to human beings the meaning that the Way had taken from them. It emphasized subjective agency and the effect of individual will on collective will. In this sense, Wang Yangming’s breakthrough somewhat resembled Marx’s dialectical transcendence of Feuerbach. Yet traditional Chinese philosophy, centered on Confucianism, had long depended on a scholar-official class that did not engage in production. It was not expressed with precision through practice and scientific methods and never formed a rigorous scientific methodology. What separated it from Marx, in the end, was scientific rigor.

  During the Qing dynasty that followed, the highest degree of centralization brought even stricter central control. Literary inquisitions and restrictions on thought almost halted the development of Chinese philosophy, while selecting officials through the “eight-legged essay” severed the roots from which traditional philosophy might have developed under the Qing. Only when the thunder of modern artillery approached and Western ideas gradually entered China did the country’s intellectual world begin another round of breakthroughs. By then, however, it had left the domain of traditional philosophy.

  The seeds of primitive ancient morality were scattered across the land of China. As the climate warmed and rain became plentiful, the Hundred Schools of Thought sprouted in profusion. After a long and fierce struggle, only two trees—Confucianism and Daoism—grew tall. Confucianism occupied the richest soil and water. It flourished, growing tall and luxuriant, although its wood was soft. Defiant Daoism grew from bare rock beside a cliff. It was neither tall nor thick, and its leaves were sparse, but it was hard and resilient. The seasons turned for thousands of years. When the climate was favorable, birds gathered in the Confucian tree. When it became harsh, they sheltered in the Daoist one. During a particularly delightful spring, a bird from far away brought a seed called Buddhism. Unlike the other short-lived, stunted seeds, Buddhism began growing wildly as soon as it took root in the Central Plains. Botanists explained that a metabolic waste product, which neither the Confucian nor Daoist tree could recycle, had accumulated in the soil and happened to be ideal fertilizer for Buddhism. To stop Buddhism from overgrowing and seizing its ecological niche, Confucianism repeatedly crowded it until its growth was finally checked. Through conflicts large and small, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism became the collective name for the three great local trees. As the soil grew richer and the climate improved, all three continued to grow and compete. They discovered that each could learn from the others and take what it needed. Through competition and cooperation, the three trees grew strong and formed a harmonious ecological relationship. This, in broad outline, was the evolution of the community called “traditional Chinese philosophy.”

  [End of Part One: An Overview of the History of Traditional Philosophy]

entry.title: Stars Are Not Fixed: How Their Positions Change
entry.content:
Author: 丛雨
Reviewer: 白烟

  If you have excellent eyesight, you may see more than 2,500 stars on a clear, dark night, while nearly 6,000 stars are visible to the naked eye across the entire celestial sphere. Ancient observers noticed that, unlike the five planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, the relative positions of most celestial objects seemed eternally unchanged. This gave rise to the Chinese term for a star, literally a “constant star.” We now know that stars only appear fixed because their great distances make their motion across the celestial sphere difficult to perceive. This article briefly introduces three ways in which stars move relative to the celestial background:

  • Parallax
  • Proper motion
  • Aberration of light

Parallax

  Hold one finger upright in front of your eyes and close first one eye, then the other. The finger plainly changes position relative to the objects behind it. This illustrates parallax: a difference in the observed direction of the same object when viewed from different positions. The line joining the two observing points is the parallax baseline, and the angle between the lines from those points to the target is the parallax angle. Once that angle has been measured, calculating the distance is a simple problem in triangle geometry, which is why parallax is also called trigonometric parallax.

  Earth’s continually changing position as it revolves around the Sun creates the conditions needed for stellar parallax. The Earth–Sun distance is known, and stellar parallax measured with the mean Earth–Sun distance of 1 AU as its baseline is called annual parallax. As Figure 1 shows, stars are generally so distant that their parallax π is extremely small, making tan π ≈ π. We need only find, in the plane of Earth’s orbit—the ecliptic plane—a parallax baseline perpendicular to the star’s direction, and its distance follows readily: d = a / π. By definition, an object with an annual parallax of 1 arcsecond (″) lies at a distance of 1 parsec (pc), approximately 3.262 light-years. The practical value of this definition has made the parsec one of astronomy’s most commonly used units of distance. In these units, taking the reciprocal of the annual parallax in arcseconds directly gives the stellar distance in parsecs. Because parallax becomes less conspicuous with distance, accurate parallax measurements are possible only for relatively nearby targets. The Gaia telescope, which entered service in 2013, nevertheless achieves precision on the order of 10 microarcseconds and can measure the parallaxes of stars thousands of parsecs away.

Annual stellar parallax

  For an arbitrary star in space, the line joining it to the Sun will in practice make an angle with the ecliptic plane. That angle is its ecliptic latitude β in the heliocentric ecliptic coordinate system. As Earth travels around its circular orbit, the line from Earth to the star traces an ellipse on the celestial sphere. The annual-parallax track of a star on the ecliptic is a line, while that of a star near the north ecliptic pole is a circle. The semimajor axis of this parallax ellipse is the annual parallax and corresponds to the parallax baseline. By symmetry, we need wait no more than any six-month interval to reconstruct the entire ellipse and then use parallax to calculate the star’s distance.

The parallax ellipse of a star in space

  Parallax is useful not only for measuring stars beyond the Solar System, but also for objects within it. During a transit of Venus, for example, observers at two locations on Earth see Venus in different positions against the Sun’s disk. That difference can be used to calculate Venus’s distance and orbital radius. The Sun itself also exhibits parallax when viewed from different parts of Earth; using Earth’s radius as the baseline, solar parallax is approximately 8.8″.

Proper Motion

  Like the Sun, the Milky Way’s hundreds of billions of stars are in motion. Suppose a star’s velocity relative to the Sun is v. It can be resolved orthogonally into radial velocity v_r and tangential velocity v_t. The tangential component reflects the direction in which we see the star move, while its proper motion μ, usually measured in arcseconds per year, describes the magnitude of that movement.

A star’s space velocity and proper motion

  Once proper motion and distance are known, the tangential velocity is easy to calculate. If the radial velocity is measured as well, we obtain the star’s true space velocity relative to the Sun. Measuring radial velocity relies on the Doppler effect: motion changes the wavelength of electromagnetic waves emitted by a light source. A receding source shifts to longer wavelengths, a redshift, while an approaching one shifts to shorter wavelengths, a blueshift. Comparing the lines in a star’s spectrum with their wavelengths at rest therefore gives both the magnitude and direction of the radial velocity.

  Barnard’s Star has the greatest known proper motion. This red dwarf, approximately 6 light-years away, moves across the celestial background at 10.3″ per year. Figure 3 shows how its position changed between 1985 and 2005.

The proper motion of Barnard’s Star

Aberration of Light

  Light has a finite speed, so an observer in motion sees it arriving from a direction different from the one seen by a stationary observer. This is the aberration of light. A familiar analogy is a person walking through rain. Although the raindrops fall vertically, a runner experiences them as slanting down from ahead. Aberration works similarly, except that the relevant transformation is not the classical addition of velocities but the Lorentz transformation.

  Earth is constantly moving: it rotates, revolves around the Sun, and follows the Sun through the Milky Way. All these motions produce aberration when we observe distant light sources. The largest practical effect is annual aberration caused by Earth’s revolution. As Figure 3 shows, θ is the angle between the direction of motion and the direction of the light source. Earth’s motion changes the observed angle to φ, so the aberration is θ - φ.

Direction of motion and the aberration of light

  Earth revolves around the Sun at approximately 29.8 km / s. When a speed v is much smaller than the speed of light c, aberration can be calculated simply as v sin θ / c. When the velocity is perpendicular to the light, annual aberration reaches its maximum of 20.5″. Diurnal aberration caused by Earth’s rotation is two orders of magnitude smaller, while the aberration due to the Solar System’s orbit around the Milky Way, though larger, has such a long period—200 million years—that it can be ignored over short timescales.

  Like parallax, a star’s annual-aberration track is an ellipse with a one-year period, produced by the periodic change in Earth’s direction of motion. For stars at different ecliptic coordinates, the track ranges from a circle to a line segment. The maximum positional swing of 20.5 arcseconds is also far greater than stellar parallax. Parallax, proper motion, and aberration combine to make a star’s path across the celestial sphere look complicated and irregular. Fortunately, their periodic and systematic behavior makes it relatively easy to separate and analyze their effects.

entry.title: Car Design and Aerodynamics
entry.content:
Author: 未名
Reviewer: 未名

Introduction

  In 1886, Karl Benz built the world’s first three-wheeled automobile powered by an internal-combustion engine. Its main difference from a horse-drawn carriage was the powertrain, while the basic form of the modern four-wheeled car came from Daimler’s ideas. Over the following century and more, car bodies changed continually as people demanded greater mobility and aesthetic tastes evolved. From the Beetle through the ponton body to the wedge shape, designers consistently sought forms that combined lower drag with visual appeal. This article offers a brief look at the relationship between automotive styling and aerodynamics.

Car Design and Aerodynamic Drag

  At constant speed on a level road under normal atmospheric pressure, a car's aerodynamic drag consists of pressure drag and skin-friction drag. Depending on their proportions and the part of the vehicle involved, aerodynamic drag can be further divided into form drag, induced drag, roughness and interference drag, and internal-flow drag. About 69% of a car's fuel is used to overcome air resistance, and form drag accounts for 58% of aerodynamic drag. Body shape is therefore crucial to reducing resistance. We can define the drag coefficient as Cw=F_drag/(ρ/2 v_∞² A), where v_∞ is the relative velocity between the car and the uniform airflow far upstream, and A is the vehicle's frontal area. Figure 1-1 gives the aerodynamic drag coefficients of several body shapes moving at the same constant speed through the same horizontal, uniform, ideal airflow. The differences among vehicle types are substantial.
Figure 1-1
  We will now look briefly at each of these forms of aerodynamic drag.

Form Drag

  Pressure drag accounts for 80–90% of a car's form drag, while air friction contributes only 10–20%. Figure 1-2 shows the pressure drag on several shapes in the same ideal fluid:
Figure 1-2
  For a bluff body such as a flat plate placed across the flow or a rectangular block, pressure rises sharply near the object's largest cross-section. The flow separates, forming a wake of vortices behind the body. This makes the pressure distribution across the surface asymmetric and creates pressure drag. Rounding a corner can keep the flow from separating as it passes an edge. Delaying separation in this way reduces pressure drag. The same reasoning applies to pressure drag on a car.
  Now consider skin-friction drag:
Figure 1-3
  The velocity gradient and molecular viscosity within the boundary layer create wall shear stress τw at every point on the surface. The sum of the components of that stress in the direction of flow is skin-friction drag.
  When the flow does not separate, friction can account for a large share of total drag; when separation is extensive, its share is small. This is why the dimples on a golf ball allow it to travel farther. On a streamlined body, including some vehicles, skin-friction drag makes up a much larger proportion of the whole.
  All liquids and gases have viscosity. When adjacent parcels of fluid move at different speeds, friction acts between them. Viscosity also causes fluid next to a solid surface to adhere to it. These attached parcels slow the fluid moving past them and form a friction-producing boundary layer. Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer interacts less strongly with the body's surface, reducing frictional drag and energy absorption. This is why friction represents a comparatively large share of the drag on streamlined bodies.
  The car's surface therefore needs a smooth finish.

Induced Drag

  Induced drag results from the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces of the body, though it is not itself lift. That pressure difference superimposes a vertical component on the horizontal freestream. Air moves around the sides of the body to equalize the pressure, creating vortices that travel downstream along the vehicle. The continuous production of vortices absorbs energy and therefore produces induced drag. Induced drag is related to aerodynamic lift, a point we will return to below.
Figure 2-1. Induced drag around a car

Roughness and Interference Drag

  Roughness and interference drag include resistance created by surface discontinuities and accessories that protrude through the boundary layer around the car. Chassis and suspension components, wheels, mirrors, auxiliary lights, and windshield wipers all contribute.
  Interference drag may be positive or negative; as the names suggest, the two have opposite effects. Positive interference drag arises between nearby or connected objects. Taking the car as the main body, a side mirror disturbs its original flow field, causes the air to separate earlier, and increases aerodynamic drag. Negative interference drag arises because every object in a flow has a slower-moving region behind it. Another object inside that region experiences less resistance than it would in the undisturbed flow. For example, when two discs are placed one behind the other at a suitable separation, their combined drag is lower than the sum of their drag when tested separately (Figure 2-2). The same principle appears in tractor-trailers: an aerodynamically optimized tractor can reduce the overall drag of the combination.
Figure 2-2

Internal-Flow Drag

  Internal-flow drag, also called internal drag, is produced when air passes through the vehicle for engine cooling and ventilation. It includes momentum lost where the air exits and pressure lost as it moves through the radiator and engine compartment. These processes consume additional energy. Internal-flow drag accounts for about 5–12% of total air resistance.

Car Design and Aerodynamic Lift

  A car's aerodynamic lift comes from its distinctive shape (Figure 3-1).
