Figure 3-1
  Under ideal conditions, Bernoulli's equation gives:
  Combining this with the car's shape, in the ideal case:
F_top ＜ F_bottom
  The result is aerodynamic lift.
  In reality, the underbody also matters. Figure 3-2 shows simplified two-dimensional inviscid and viscous flows and pressure distributions around a car:
Figure 3-2
  A car's rolling resistance is proportional to the normal force on its wheels. Increasing aerodynamic lift reduces that normal force and therefore reduces rolling resistance. At first, this seems to suggest that lift can lower the vehicle's total resistance. Yet greater lift also reduces traction and stability, while producing additional induced drag that may greatly exceed the reduction in rolling resistance. Increasing lift to reduce drag is therefore a poor trade. A large rise in lift weakens high-speed stability and creates a safety hazard. Above 70 km/s, for example, some cars may begin to feel “light” as aerodynamic instability reduces the driver's sense of contact with the road, potentially contributing to rollover or skidding.
  This led to the wedge-shaped car. These aerodynamically optimized bodies, many of them sports cars, may also use spoilers to generate downforce. Their aerodynamic lift can even be negative, greatly improving stability at high speed.

(Some of the text and figures in this article draw on Aerodynamics of Road Vehicles.)

entry.title: The Philosophy and Theology of Saint Augustine
entry.content:
The Philosophy and Theology of Saint Augustine

Author: Михaїл-А-Булгáкoв☦️
Reviewed by: 观复·钧天

  Saint Augustine was an extraordinarily prolific writer whose works dealt mainly with theological questions. His polemical writings addressed issues of the day and, once they had served their purpose, generally lost all significance. Some of them, however—especially those concerning the Pelagians—have continued to exert a real influence into modern times. I do not intend to cover everything he wrote. Instead, I will examine the works and arguments that seem to me intrinsically or historically important:
  • First, his pure philosophy, especially his theory of time
  • Second, the philosophy of history presented in The City of God
  • Third, the theory of salvation developed in opposition to Pelagianism

Pure Philosophy

  In general, Saint Augustine did not devote himself single-mindedly to pure philosophy, but when he did engage with it, he displayed exceptional ability. Many thinkers throughout history have allowed the demands of scriptural conformity to shape their speculative views, and Augustine stands at the head of that long line. This was not yet true of early Christian philosophers such as Origen. In Origen's writings, Christianity and Platonism coexist without penetrating each other. In Augustine's work, by contrast, original philosophical thought was stimulated by the fact that Platonism was, in certain respects, inconsistent with *Genesis*.
  Among Saint Augustine's writings, Book XI of Confessions is his finest work of pure philosophy. Some ordinary editions of *Confessions* contain only ten books because the material after Book X is considered dull. It is dull precisely because it is no longer autobiographical and instead contains a great deal of philosophy. Book XI addresses this question: if creation occurred as described in the first chapter of *Genesis*, as Augustine maintained against the Manichaeans, why did it not happen sooner? He imagines an opponent raising this objection and develops his argument in response.
Excerpt from *Confessions*
  To understand his discussion, one must first recognize that the Old Testament idea of creation out of nothing was wholly foreign to Greek philosophy. When Plato spoke of creation, he imagined primordial matter given form by God; Aristotle held a similar view. Their God was less a creator than a designer or architect. They believed matter to be eternal and uncreated, with only its form arising from the will of God. Against this view, Saint Augustine maintained—as every orthodox Christian had to—that the world was created not from any preexisting matter, but out of nothing. God created matter itself; he did not merely order and arrange it.
  The Greek conviction that nothing could be created from nothing reappeared intermittently during the Christian era and gave rise to pantheism. Pantheism holds that God and the world cannot be distinguished and that everything in the world is part of God. This view was fully developed in the writings of Spinoza and appealed to almost every mystic. Throughout the Christian centuries, mystics had difficulty remaining orthodox because they found it hard to believe that the world existed outside God. Augustine had no difficulty on this point. *Genesis* was perfectly clear, and that was enough for him. His view of the issue had important consequences for his theory of time.
  Why was the world not created sooner? Because there was no “sooner.” Time was created together with the world. God is eternal in the sense of being outside time: in God there is no before and after, only an eternal present. God's eternity is independent of temporal relations; for God, all time is present. He did not precede the time he created, for that would mean that he himself existed in time. In reality, God stands eternally outside the stream of time. This led Augustine to formulate a highly admirable theory of the relativity of time.
  “What, then, is time?” he asked. “If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.” A number of difficulties perplexed him. What really exists, he said, is neither the past nor the future, but only the present. Yet the present is only an instant, while time can be measured only as it passes. Even so, past and future time plainly do exist, which seems to leave us with a contradiction. Augustine found only one way around it: past and future can be conceived only as present. The “past” must be identified with memory, and the “future” with expectation; both memory and expectation are facts that exist now. He said there are three times: “a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future.” “The present of things past is memory; the present of things present is sight; the present of things future is expectation.” (To speak simply of three times—past, present, and future—is merely a loose expression.)
  He also understood that this theory did not actually solve every problem. “My mind longs to understand this most intricate riddle,” he wrote. He prayed that God would enlighten him and assured God that his concern did not arise from idle curiosity. “Lord, I confess to you that I still do not know what time is.” The central point of his answer, however, is that time is subjective: “Time exists in the mind that expects, attends, and remembers.”
  Thus, if there were no created beings, there could be no time; it is therefore meaningless to speak of time before creation.
  I do not agree with this theory that makes time a product of the mind. It is nevertheless plainly a remarkable theory and deserves serious consideration. I would go further: it is a great advance on any theory of time found in Greek philosophy. Its account is also more complete and explicit than Kant's subjective theory of time, a theory widely accepted by philosophers since Kant.
  The view that time is merely an aspect of thought is an extreme form of subjectivism. As we have seen, this subjectivism had gradually grown in antiquity since the age of Protagoras and Socrates. Its emotional aspect was an idea haunted by sin, though this developed later than its intellectual aspect. Saint Augustine advanced two forms of subjectivism. They made him not only a precursor of Kant's theory of time, but also of Descartes' “I think” (cogito). In his Soliloquies, Augustine wrote: “You who wish to know—do you know that you exist? I know it. Where do you come from? I do not know. Do you think yourself simple or composite? I do not know. Do you think that you move? I do not know. Do you know that you think? I know it.” This passage contains not only Descartes' cogito, but also Gassendi's reply, “I walk, therefore I am” (ambuloergosum). Augustine accordingly deserves a high place as a philosopher.

The City of God

  When Rome was sacked by the Goths in 410 CE, pagans naturally blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the ancient gods. While Rome worshiped Jupiter, they said, it had remained powerful. Now that the emperors no longer worshiped him, he no longer protected the Romans. This pagan argument demanded an answer. The City of God, written in stages between 412 and 427, was Saint Augustine's response. As the work progressed, however, its scope broadened until it became a complete Christian outline of past, present, and future history. It exerted enormous influence throughout the Middle Ages, particularly in the Church's struggles against secular rulers. Like some other great works, it leaves a better impression in the reader's memory than it does upon rereading. Much of its content is unacceptable to any modern reader, and its central thesis is obscured by factors of little importance today. Yet the broad contrast between the earthly city and the City of God has continued to inspire many people, so much so that it can still be restated in non-theological terms.
The first page of a manuscript of *The City of God*, written in 1470
  Any introduction to this work that omits the details and concentrates on its central idea will praise it too highly. Any account that concentrates on the details, however, will inevitably miss its finest and most important features. I will try to avoid both errors by first describing some of its details and then discussing its general ideas in the order of their historical development.
  The book begins with reflections prompted by the sack of Rome and attempts to show that even worse events had occurred before the Christian era. Pagans often blamed disasters on Christianity, the saint says, yet many of them sought refuge in churches during the sack. The Gothic invaders were Christians and respected the churches. When Troy was sacked, by contrast, Juno's temple not only failed to shelter the people, but the gods did not protect the city from destruction. The Romans had never spared the temples of conquered cities, yet Rome received comparatively lenient treatment when it was sacked, and that leniency was due to Christianity.
  For several reasons, the Christians who suffered during the sack had no right to complain. Wicked Goths might enrich themselves at the Christians' expense, but they would suffer in the next life. If every sin were punished on earth, there would be no need for the Last Judgment. If the Christians were virtuous, their suffering must improve their virtue. To a saint, losing worldly possessions does not mean losing anything of value. Even if their bodies received no burial, it did not matter, for ravenous beasts could not prevent the resurrection of the flesh.
Two Gothic soldiers
  He then turns to the rape of devout virgins during the sack. Some evidently believed that these women had lost the crown of virginity through no fault of their own. Saint Augustine very sensibly rejected this view. “Away with the thought! Another person's lust cannot defile you.” Chastity is a virtue of the mind and cannot be lost through rape; a sinful intention, even when never carried out, can make you lose it. He suggests that God permitted these rapes because the victims had been excessively proud of their continence. Suicide to escape rape is sinful. This leads to a long discussion of Lucretia, who, in his view, should not have killed herself, because suicide is always a sin.
  His defense of virtuous women who have been raped includes one reservation: they must not have enjoyed it, or they are guilty.
  He next discusses the wickedness of the pagan gods. “Those stage plays of yours, those displays of filth, those licentious pagan deities, were not first introduced into Rome by human corruption; they arose by the direct command of your gods.” Worshiping a virtuous man such as Scipio would be more edifying than worshiping these immoral gods. Christians need not be troubled by the sack of Rome because they have a place of refuge in “God's pilgrim city.”
  In this world, the two cities—the earthly city and the heavenly city—are intermingled. In the next world, God's predestined elect will be separated from the reprobate. In the present life, we cannot know who, even among those who seem to be our enemies, will ultimately be one of the elect.
  He tells us that the most difficult part of the book is its refutation of the philosophers, since Christians and certain eminent philosophers agree to a considerable extent—for example, on the immortality of the soul and the doctrine that God created the world.
  The philosophers did not renounce belief in the pagan gods, but because those gods were wicked, their moral teaching was worthless. The book does not suggest that the pagan gods were merely fictions. Saint Augustine believed that they existed, but that they were all demons. They wished to harm humankind and were therefore willing to spread obscene stories about themselves. For most pagans, Jupiter's deeds were more influential than Plato's principles or Cato's opinions. “Plato excluded poets from a well-governed city; this shows that he himself was worthier than the gods who wished to be honored with stage plays.”
  He says that Rome had been thoroughly wicked ever since the Romans raped the Sabine women. Augustine devotes several chapters to the grave sins of Roman imperialism. The claim that Rome never suffered before becoming Christian is false: its sufferings during the Gallic invasion and the civil wars equaled or exceeded those inflicted by the Goths. Astrology is not merely wicked but false, as the different fates of twins born at the same moment demonstrate. The Stoic view of fate, which is connected with astrology, is wrong because angels and human beings possess free will. God foreknows our sins, but we do not sin because he foreknows them. The idea that virtue brings misfortune, even in this world, is likewise false. Virtuous Christian emperors are happy even when they meet with adversity; Constantine and Theodosius were both quite fortunate. Moreover, the Jewish kingdom endured for as long as the Jews remained faithful to religious truth.
Statue of Constantine the Great
  The book contains a passage highly sympathetic to Plato, whom Augustine places above every other philosopher. All philosophers, he thinks, should yield to Plato: “Let Thales depart with his water, Anaximenes with the air, the Stoics with fire, and Epicurus with his atoms.” All these thinkers were materialists; Plato was not. Plato held that God is not a corporeal thing, but that all things derive their being from God and from something constant and immutable. He was right that perception is not the source of truth. The Platonists excelled in logic and ethics and came closest to Christianity. “Plotinus, who lived not long ago, is said to have understood Plato best.” Aristotle, though inferior to Plato, stood far above the other philosophers. Yet both Plato and Aristotle said that all the gods were good and deserved worship. The Platonists were right about God but wrong about the other gods, and they were also wrong not to acknowledge the Incarnation.
  Saint Augustine opposed the Stoic condemnation of every passion. A Christian's passions, he held, might become causes of virtue; anger and pity should not be condemned in themselves. We must examine what causes them.
  The book includes a lengthy discussion of angels and demons that is connected with the Neoplatonists. Angels may be good or evil, but demons are always evil. For angels, knowledge of worldly things—though they possess such knowledge—is base. Both Saint Augustine and Plato considered the sensible world inferior to the eternal world.
  Book XI begins its account of the nature of the City of God, which is the society of the elect. Knowledge of God can be obtained only through Christ. Some things, as certain philosophers demonstrate, can be discovered by reason, but for all further religious knowledge we must rely on Scripture. We must never try to understand the time and space before the world was created: there was no time before creation and no space where there was no world. Everything blessed is eternal, but not everything eternal is blessed; hell and Satan, for example, are eternal. God foresaw the sins of the demons but also foresaw their role in improving the universe as a whole, rather like an antithesis in rhetoric.
  Origen was wrong to think that bodies were given to souls as punishment. If that were so, evil souls would have evil bodies. Yet demons, including the most wicked demons, have ethereal bodies, which are superior to our own.
  God created the world in six days because six is a perfect number—that is, it equals the sum of its proper divisors.
  There are good angels and bad angels, but even bad angels have no nature contrary to God. They are God's enemies not by nature, but by will. An evil will has no efficient cause, only a deficient cause; it is not an effect but a defect.
  Fewer than six thousand years have passed since creation. History is not cyclical, as philosophers suppose: “Christ died for our sins only once.”
  If our first parents had not sinned, they would not have died. Because they did sin, all their descendants must die. Eating the apple brought not only natural death, but eternal death—that is, everlasting punishment. Porphyry was wrong to believe that the saints in heaven have no bodies. The saints will have bodies better than Adam's before the Fall. Their bodies will be spiritual, but not spirits, and will have no weight. Men will have male bodies and women female bodies; those who died in infancy will be resurrected with adult bodies.
  Adam's sin brought eternal death—everlasting punishment—to almost all humankind, but God's grace rescues many from it. Sin comes from the soul, not the body. The Platonists and the Manichaeans were both wrong to blame sin on bodily nature, though the Platonists' error was less grave than that of the Manichaeans. The punishment imposed on all humanity for Adam's sin was just, because that offense reduced beings who might have possessed spiritual bodies to minds ruled by carnal desire.
  This question leads to a long and tedious discussion of sexual desire. According to Augustine, our subjection to lust forms part of the punishment for Adam's sin. The discussion is important for what it reveals about ascetic psychology, so it must be summarized. Although Saint Augustine himself admits that the subject is absurd, we must discuss it for the same reason. His doctrine is as follows. Sexual intercourse within marriage must be considered innocent when undertaken to produce children. Yet even within marriage, a virtuous person cannot manage it without lust. The fact that people wish to conceal intercourse shows that they consider it shameful even in marriage, because “this lawful act of nature has, since our first parents, been accompanied by the shame of sin.” The Cynics believed that no one ought to feel shame. Diogenes wished to free himself from shame completely and to behave like a dog in every respect, but after trying once, even he abandoned this extreme shamelessness in practice. Lust is shameful because it is not subject to the will. Before the Fall, Adam and Eve might have had intercourse without lust, though in fact they did not. Craftsmen feel no lust when they move their arms to perform their work; likewise, had Adam stayed away from the apple tree, he might have performed the sexual act without the emotions now required. The sexual organs might have obeyed the will like every other part of the body. The need for lust in intercourse is one punishment for Adam's sin. Otherwise, sexual desire and pleasure might have gone their separate ways. Apart from certain physiological details, which the English translator of this book judiciously left in the appropriate obscurity of the original Latin, this is Saint Augustine's theory of sexual desire.
  The ascetic's aversion to sexual desire plainly arises from the fact that desire does not obey the will. Morality requires the will to control the body completely, but such control would make the sexual act impossible. Sexual activity therefore appears incompatible with a morally perfect life.
  After Adam's sin, the world was divided into two cities. One would reign eternally with God; the other would suffer everlasting torment with Satan. Cain① belonged to the city of the devil, Abel to the City of God. By divine grace and predestination, Abel was a pilgrim on earth and a citizen of heaven. The twelve patriarchs also belonged to the City of God. A discussion of Methuselah's death led Augustine into the disputed comparison between the Septuagint and the Latin Bible. According to the Septuagint's chronology, Methuselah must have lived for fourteen years after the Flood. That was impossible because he had not entered Noah's Ark. The Latin Bible, following the original Hebrew, records that Methuselah died in the year of the Flood. Saint Augustine concluded that Saint Jerome and the Hebrew text must be right on this point. Some claimed that hostility toward Christians had led the Jews to falsify the Hebrew Bible deliberately, but Augustine rejected this hypothesis. On the other hand, the Septuagint must also have been divinely inspired. The only possible conclusion, therefore, was that Ptolemy's copyists had made an error while copying it. Discussing the various Old Testament translations, Augustine wrote: “The Church has accepted the Septuagint as though no other translation existed, just as many Greek Christians know only this version and do not know whether there is another. Our Latin version was likewise translated from the Septuagint. Yet a learned monk and great linguist, Jerome, translated this Bible directly from Hebrew into Latin. Although the Jews confirmed the accuracy of his accomplished translation and said that the Septuagint contained many errors, the churches of Christ judged that no single man should be preferred to those many translators, especially since the high priest had chosen them for this task.” He accepted the story that the seventy translators worked separately yet arrived at a miraculous agreement, regarding this as evidence that the Septuagint was inspired by the Holy Spirit. But the Hebrew Bible was equally inspired. That conclusion left the authority of Jerome's version unresolved. Augustine might have sided more decisively with Jerome had the two saints not quarreled over Saint Peter's tendency toward duplicity.
Palma il Giovane — Cain and Abel
  Augustine compared the chronology of sacred and secular history. According to this comparison, Aeneas arrived in Italy while Othniel was judge in Israel. The final persecution would be led by the Antichrist, though its date was unknown.
  After an admirable chapter opposing judicial torture, Saint Augustine refuted the New Academics, who believed that everything should be doubted. “Because the Church of Christ possesses the most certain knowledge of the things it understands, it rejects these doubts as madness.” We ought to believe the truth of Scripture. He went on to argue that there can be no true virtue apart from true religion. Pagan virtue is “defiled by the power of obscene demons.” What is virtue in a Christian becomes vice in a pagan. “Some things which she [the soul] regards as virtues and on which she prides herself, if they are not entirely related to God, ought in truth to be called vices rather than virtues.” Those outside this society—the Church—will suffer eternal misery. “In the struggles of our present life, either suffering conquers and death then drives away the capacity to feel it, or nature conquers and drives suffering away. But there, suffering will torment forever and nature will suffer forever. Both will endure an unending punishment.” (Chapter 28).
  There are two resurrections: the resurrection of the soul after death and the resurrection of the body at the Last Judgment. After discussing the difficulties surrounding Christ's thousand-year reign and the subsequent actions of Gog and Magog①, Augustine turns to a passage in 2 Thessalonians (Chapter 2, verses 11 and 12): “God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.” It might seem unjust for an omnipotent God first to deceive them and then punish them for being deceived, but Saint Augustine saw nothing surprising in this. “They are deluded because they have been condemned, and condemned because they have been deluded. Yet their delusion comes from the secret judgment of God, a judgment at once secretly just and justly secret, which he has continued since the creation of the world.” Saint Augustine believed that God divides people arbitrarily into the elect and the reprobate, not according to human merit. Everyone equally deserves eternal punishment, so the reprobate have no grounds for complaint. The passage from Saint Paul quoted above suggests that people are wicked because they are reprobate, rather than reprobate because they are wicked.
  It is not surprising that, after the resurrection of the body, the bodies of the condemned will burn without end yet never be consumed; salamanders and Mount Etna provide examples of this. Demons, though incorporeal, can be burned by corporeal fire. The torments of hell do not purify people and cannot be reduced through the intercession of the saints. Origen was wrong to think that hell was not eternal. Heretics and deeply sinful Catholics will suffer everlasting punishment.
  The book ends with Saint Augustine's vision of God in heaven and the eternal happiness of the City of God.
Modern artistic cover of The City of God
  The preceding summary may not yet make the work's importance clear. One influential feature is its separation of Church and State, with the definite implication that a State can form part of the City of God only by submitting to the Church in every religious matter. This claim thereafter remained a principle of the Church. Throughout the Middle Ages, during the gradual rise of papal power and the successive conflicts between popes and emperors, Saint Augustine supplied the theoretical basis for the Western Church's policy. The Jewish state was a theocracy both in the legendary period of the Judges and in the historical period after the return from the Babylonian captivity. Christian states should imitate it in this respect. The weakness of Roman emperors and most medieval rulers in Western Europe greatly helped the Church realize the ideal of the City of God. No such development occurred in the Eastern Roman Empire, where the emperors were strong, and the Eastern Church was far more subordinate to the State than the Western Church.
  The Reformation, which revived Saint Augustine's doctrine of salvation, rejected his theocratic theory and moved toward Erastianism, mainly because of the practical demands of its struggle against Catholicism. Protestant Erastianism, however, lacked fervor, and the most religious Protestants remained under Saint Augustine's influence. The Anabaptists, Fifth Monarchy Men, and Quakers inherited part of Augustine's doctrine but placed less emphasis on the Church. Augustine upheld predestination while also maintaining that baptism was necessary for salvation. These two principles do not fit together very well, and some radical Protestants abandoned the latter. Their eschatology nevertheless retained Augustine's principles.//①Erastianism is the doctrine that the Church must submit to the State.
  *The City of God* contains very little original theory. Its eschatology came from the Jews and entered Christianity chiefly through the Book of Revelation. Predestination and the doctrine of the elect are Pauline, though Augustine developed them more fully and logically than Saint Paul's epistles had done. The distinction between sacred and secular history is already explicit in the Old Testament. Augustine merely combined these elements and related them to the history of his own time, enabling Christians to adapt to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the chaotic period that followed without too severe a trial of their faith.
  The Jewish way of understanding past and future history appeals powerfully, in every age, to the oppressed and unfortunate. Saint Augustine applied it to Christianity; Marx applied it to socialism. To understand Marx psychologically, we should use the following dictionary:

Yahweh = dialectical materialism; Messiah = Marx; the elect = the proletariat; the Church = the Communist Party; the Second Coming = the revolution; hell = punishment of the capitalists; Christ’s thousand-year reign = the communist commonwealth

  The terms on the left carry the emotional content of those on the right. It was this emotional content, long familiar to Christians and Jews, that gave Marx's eschatology the value of a faith. A similar dictionary could be drawn up for the Nazis, but their concepts were closer to the Old Testament and less close to Christianity than Marx's. Their Messiah resembled the Maccabees more than Christ.

The Pelagian Controversy

  The most influential part of Saint Augustine's theology arose from his attack on the Pelagian heresy. Pelagius was Welsh; his original name was Morgan, meaning “man of the sea,” which is also the meaning of the Greek word “Pelagius.” He was a mild and courteous monk, not a fanatic like many of his contemporaries. He believed in free will, questioned the doctrine of original sin, and held that human virtue resulted from people's own moral effort. If people behaved properly and belonged to the orthodox faith, they would enter heaven as a reward for their virtue. Though these views sound commonplace today, at the time they caused a major upheaval and were declared heretical largely because of Saint Augustine's opposition. For a time, however, they enjoyed considerable success. Augustine had to write to a church elder in Jerusalem, warning him against this cunning founder of a heresy who had persuaded many Eastern theologians to adopt his mistaken views. After Augustine's condemnation, a group known as the Semi-Pelagians advocated Pelagian doctrine in a milder form. Augustine's relatively pure doctrine did not win a complete victory until much later, especially in Gaul, where Semi-Pelagianism was finally condemned as heresy at the Council of Orange in 529 CE.
  Saint Augustine taught that Adam possessed free will before the Fall and could have avoided sin. But when he and Eve ate the apple, moral corruption entered them and was inherited by all their descendants. Their descendants could no longer avoid sin through their own power. Only God's grace could make a person virtuous. Because we have all inherited Adam's original sin, we all deserve eternal punishment. Everyone who dies unbaptized, even an infant, goes to hell and suffers endless torment. Since we are all wicked, we have no right to complain. (In *Confessions*, Saint Augustine lists the sins he committed in infancy.) Yet by God's freely given grace, some of the baptized will be admitted to heaven. These are the elect. They do not enter heaven because they are good; all of us are corrupt except insofar as God's grace, granted only to the elect, saves us from corruption. There is no reason why some are saved while the rest are damned. It is simply God's unmotivated choice. Eternal punishment demonstrates God's justice; salvation demonstrates his mercy. Both equally display his goodness.
Adam and Eve eating the forbidden fruit
  Arguments supporting this cruel doctrine can be found in the writings of Saint Paul, especially the Epistle to the Romans. The doctrine was revived by Calvin and has since been abandoned by the Catholic Church. Augustine treated these writings as a lawyer treats the law. His interpretation was powerful, and he pressed the text for every possible implication. One is ultimately led to suppose that Saint Paul's faith was not quite what Augustine inferred, though certain passages, considered in isolation, do suggest Augustine's meaning. The claim that the eternal punishment of unbaptized infants, far from being horrifying, comes from a benevolent God may seem preposterous. Yet Augustine was so deeply ruled by a conviction of sin that he genuinely regarded newborn babies as limbs of Satan. Many exceptionally cruel features of the medieval Church can be traced to Augustine's dark sense of universal guilt.
  Only one intellectual difficulty truly troubled Saint Augustine. It was not the thought that creating humanity might have been regrettable because most people were destined for eternal torment. What troubled him was this: if original sin, as Saint Paul taught, was inherited from Adam, then the soul, like the body, must be generated by the parents, since sin belongs to the soul rather than the body. He found this doctrine difficult. But because Scripture never addressed the question, he said that a correct view of it could not be necessary for salvation, and he left the matter unresolved.
  It is truly strange that the last outstanding intellectuals before the beginning of the Dark Ages, instead of concerning themselves with preserving civilization, expelling the barbarians, or reforming political abuses, enthusiastically preached the value of virginity and the eternal punishment of unbaptized infants. Once we understand that these were among the prejudices the Church passed on to converted barbarians, however, it becomes easy to see why the following age surpassed almost every recorded period in cruelty and superstition.

entry.title: Procedural Art—Drawing a Black-and-White Checkerboard with Code
entry.content:
Author: Shiguang
Reviewed by: Dongda

  Many readers probably first encountered “procedural art” in an elementary-school information technology class, where the textbook introduced a fascinating program called Turtle Graphics. Think back: how did we make the little turtle move? With code. In 1996, Seymour Papert and Wally Feurzig invented Logo, a language designed to teach children programming, and we used it to direct a turtle as it drew on the screen. As technology has evolved, however, Logo has gradually faded from view, and mainstream approaches to drawing have changed as well.
  This article explains how to use a shader language—referred to below simply as Shader—to draw a 3*3 checkerboard. I use UE4 for the demonstration. If you are interested, you can try the algorithm presented here in Unity or on an online rendering site such as ShaderToy.
  Why begin a series on procedural art with a checkerboard? Drawing a checkerboard is one of the more basic tasks in procedural art: the algorithm is simple, and its result can be worked out easily. That makes it approachable for readers who are interested in Shader but do not know it well. Because the article does involve some technical terms, however, it is recommended for readers with some background in computer graphics. With that said, let's begin.

Getting Started

  Open UE4's powerful Shader Graph and get ready to draw. The first step is to connect the texcoord node—a set of texture coordinates—to base color on the output root node. The result looks like this:


  What exactly are we looking at, and how was it produced? (It really does resemble some kind of fruit.) First, remember that the texcoord node stores a set of texture coordinates ranging from 0 to 1. If we take the upper-left corner of the rectangle in Figure 1 as the origin and point the y-axis downward, texcoord's coordinate (0, 0) refers to the upper-left corner, while (1, 1) refers to the lower-right. We have also connected the texcoord node to base color, which expects a Vector3 variable—the three components of RGB—as its output. Texture coordinates are Vector2 values, so one component is missing. Fortunately, the engine automatically supplies 0 as the third component. The color at the upper-left is therefore (0, 0, 0), or black, while the color at the lower-right is (1, 1, 0), or yellow.
  To check this idea, we can manually set the third component to “1.” When this value is fed into base color, we get the result shown below. Here, the output at the upper-left is (0, 0, 1), while the output at the lower-right is (1, 1, 1), just as expected.


Mathematical Processing

  Our data is now perfectly continuous. To produce distinct checkerboard squares, we need to turn that continuous data into discrete “steps.” We can do this by introducing the Floor function to round the coordinates down. Floor rounds decimal values down and gives us one segment of data. But we need three rows and three columns. Multiplying by 3 produces three segments, as shown below:


  The result does not look quite right. That is because any color component above 1 is treated as 1, making several regions appear identical. The data for the lower-right square is actually (2, 2, 0), but its displayed output is (1, 1, 0), which is yellow. Dividing the data by 2 gives all nine squares distinct colors, as shown below:


  We are now close to the final result. Look at the current board. The data for each square is:
  You have probably spotted the interesting pattern. If we output only the R-channel value of each square, we get vertical stripes in black, gray, and white, as shown below. If we output only the G-channel value of each square, we get horizontal stripes in those same three colors:


  Could we create the checkerboard by adding the R and G channels? No—we would get the result shown below:


  The result is disappointing because every component above the limit is automatically clamped to 1. Our checkerboard draft also contains gray blocks, while we want a black-and-white board whose final output can only be (0, 0, 0) or (1, 1, 1). How can we achieve that? At this point, the mathematical result for the nine-square grid looks like this:


  Taking only the fractional part now gives us a fairly good “gray-and-white checkerboard.” To turn it into a black-and-white checkerboard, we simply multiply the gray value (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) by 2. The final result is shown below. To increase the number of rows and columns, multiply texcoord by a larger value before applying the floor operation.

entry.title: A Brief History of Fluorescent-Protein Research and the Mechanisms of Fluorescence
entry.content:
A Brief History of Fluorescent-Protein Research and the Mechanisms of Fluorescence

Author: 极地冰川
Reviewed by: 未名

Abstract

  Green fluorescent protein (GFP), discovered and isolated from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria in 1962, and the red fluorescent protein drFP583, discovered in 1999 in corals of the genus Discosoma, are now among the most widely used proteins across biological research. They are nontoxic to organisms, efficiently emit characteristic fluorescence when excited by light of specific wavelengths, have low molecular weights, are readily incorporated into vectors, and can be expressed in many organisms. These properties give them broad potential in numerous fields. Many fluorescent proteins are already used in practical research.

History of Fluorescent-Protein Research

  Green fluorescent protein was the first fluorescent protein to be discovered. In 1962, the Japanese scientist Osamu Shimomura first discovered and isolated GFP from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria. At first, it appeared as a by-product of Shimomura's extraction of aequorin. It looked green in sunlight, appeared intensely yellow under tungsten light, and fluoresced bright green under ultraviolet light. Through biochemical and spectroscopic studies, Shimomura made an initial determination of GFP's fluorescence mechanism and fluorophore[1]. Yet he did not realize that his discovery would transform modern biotechnology three decades later. Before long, he discontinued further work on GFP and moved into other areas of research.
  Between 1985 and 1992, Douglas Prasher successfully determined the gene and protein sequences of GFP and, on that basis, cloned the GFP gene in 1992. Martin Chalfie of Columbia University was the first to use GFP in biological research. In 1994, Chalfie used molecular biology techniques to introduce GFP cDNA into model organisms, including nematodes, and successfully expressed it, revealing GFP's enormous potential as a reporter gene. That same year, Roger Tsien's team elucidated GFP's fluorescence mechanism and modified GFP through mutation, producing variants with greater fluorescence intensity, a single absorption peak, and more efficient conformational folding, such as GFP-S65T[2].
  In 1999, a second type of fluorescent protein after GFP was first reported: the red fluorescent protein drFP583. Matz and his colleagues purified this tetrameric protein from corals of the genus Discosoma in the Pacific; it fluoresces red under ultraviolet illumination. Its long emission wavelength, high sensitivity, and high signal-to-noise ratio made it a valuable complement to GFP-based studies in vivo. The shortcomings of drFP583 itself, however—including oligomerization, slow maturation, and cellular toxicity—limited its use. In practice, researchers now more often use E57-NA, an engineered mutant produced by Clontech and sold under the name DsRed, which has lower cytotoxicity, a reduced tendency to oligomerize, and faster maturation. As DsRed has continued to be modified and improved, its range of applications has grown. In combination with GFP, it provides a new and rapid detection method for research in molecular biology, cell biology, and related fields[3].

How Fluorescent Proteins Produce Fluorescence

Fluorescent-Protein Structure

Structure of Green Fluorescent Protein

  The primary structure of wild-type green fluorescent protein has been inferred from its corresponding cDNA sequence. Its primary sequence contains 238 amino-acid residues, and its molecular mass is approximately 27 kDa[2]. Analysis of X-ray diffraction images from prepared crystals[4] shows a cylindrical secondary structure approximately 4 nm high and 3 nm in diameter.
  The wall of the cylinder consists of 11 β-strands wrapped into a barrel. The β-strands pack tightly against one another and form regular bands of hydrogen bonds. A short α-helix caps one end, producing a densely packed structure with a single opening known as a β-barrel.
Figure 1. Secondary structure of GFP[4]
  At the same time, the α-helix that closes one end extends inward along the central axis and serves as a scaffold for the chromophore. The chromophore lies at the core of the structure, protected by the surrounding β-sheet layers. This architecture makes the overall structure highly stable and greatly increases the central chromophore's resistance to heat, acids, bases, denaturants, and other factors[5]. The same compactness, however, makes it difficult for enzymes or cofactors to enter GFP and catalyze chromophore formation. The chromophore must therefore form by autocatalysis.
Figure 2. Structural relationship between the GFP chromophore and the β-barrel[6]
  The GFP chromophore forms from the Ser–Tyr–Gly triad at residues 65–67. Autocatalytic cyclization of the triad produces the 4-(p-hydroxybenzylidene)imidazolin-5-one structure that constitutes GFP's central chromophore.
Figure 3. Structure of the GFP chromophore, with the remaining amino-acid residues omitted
  Chromophore formation[7] is an autocatalytic cyclization process that requires no enzyme or cofactor. Ser65 and Gly67 first cyclize rapidly to form an imidazolin-5-one intermediate. O2 then slowly oxidizes the Tyr66 side chain to form a double bond. This slow step often takes several hours. Gly67 is essential for chromophore formation; no other amino acid can replace it. The reaction is also temperature-sensitive, and its yield falls above 30 ℃. This may be related to the low temperature of the jellyfish's natural habitat. Once formed, the chromophore itself is highly resistant to heat and is thermally stable.
Figure 4. Formation of the GFP chromophore[7]
  Experiments have shown[7] that amino acids 2–232 in GFP's primary structure are required to maintain fluorescence. Truncating more than seven amino acids from the C terminus or more than two from the N terminus completely eliminates fluorescence. The final seven residues are disordered and do not form part of the protein's specific structure, so deleting or adding residues in this region does not affect its overall function. The N-terminal residues help form the “cap” at one end of the β-barrel. This indispensable structure protects the chromophore, though extending the peptide chain at the N terminus does not disrupt the protein. When GFP forms a fusion protein with certain other proteins, the loss of some C-terminal residues does not eliminate fluorescence, although it still affects the spectral properties to some extent[5].
  GFP can dimerize in crystals or in solutions with ionic strength below 100 mmol／L. Dimerization facilitates energy transfer between GFP and the jellyfish photoprotein under natural conditions.

Structure of Red Fluorescent Protein (DsRed)

  DsRed consists of 225 amino-acid residues and has a relative molecular mass of approximately 25.9 KDa. This coral fluorescent protein has little primary-sequence homology with GFP from Aequorea victoria—only about 23%. Their secondary structures, however, are highly similar. Like GFP, DsRed forms a β-barrel.
Figure 5. Secondary structure of DsRed, shown as a tetramer[8]
  The DsRed chromophore is formed from Gln66–Tyr67–Gly68 and is structurally very similar to the GFP chromophore. During in vitro maturation, its initial excitation and emission wavelengths are 475 nm and 499 nm, respectively, producing green fluorescence. The green fluorescence reaches maximum intensity after about 7 hours and then begins to decay. After 2 days, the green fluorescence disappears completely, after which red fluorescence slowly begins to emerge. Analysis shows that formation of the DsRed chromophore first requires a structure essentially identical to the GFP chromophore, followed by further oxidation to form the DsRed chromophore. Compared with its GFP counterpart, the DsRed chromophore contains an imine group[9]. The imine double bond further extends the chromophore's conjugated system, shifting its emission toward longer wavelengths.
Figure 6. Formation of the DsRed chromophore passes through a GFP-like chromophore intermediate[9]
  Crystallographic analysis shows that DsRed normally exists as a tetramer. Experiments further indicate that its chromophore can form and function only after oligomerization. Alkaline, acid, and guanidine denaturation experiments show that the DsRed chromophore forms through several folding steps and that oligomerization plays an important role in maturation[3].

Mechanism of Fluorescence

  Existing research has established that the fluorescent proteins discovered so far produce fluorescence through broadly similar mechanisms. GFP was the first such protein discovered and studied, and research on its mechanism is now relatively mature. This section therefore focuses on how GFP produces fluorescence.
  In Aequorea victoria, fluorescence from GFP is coupled to another luminescent protein, aequorin.
  Aequorin uses coelenterazine as a prosthetic group and, in the presence of calcium ions, can emit blue light at 460–470 nm.
Figure 7. Coelenterazine
Figure 8. Aequorin[10]
  In the presence of calcium ions, aequorin is oxidized by oxygen and emits blue light. Through Förster resonance energy transfer, this energy reaches the GFP chromophore, which is excited and then emits GFP's characteristic green fluorescence at 509 nm.
  GFP fluorescence is now generally believed to involve a process called excited-state proton transfer (ESPT)[11]. The key lies in the phenolic group on the Tyr66 side chain in the chromophore. Because a phenol is weakly acidic, it interconverts between neutral and ionic forms. Under ordinary conditions, the neutral form predominates, and the two occur in a ratio of approximately 6:1. However, when the chromophore
Figure 9. Interconversion between the neutral and ionic forms of the chromophore's phenolic group
  is excited by light, the acidity of the group increases greatly. Changes in the hydrogen-bond network formed jointly by amino-acid side-chain groups and by those side chains with water molecules in the chromophore's microenvironment play a decisive role in this process[12].
  Crystallographic analysis shows that, in the unexcited state, the Tyr66 phenolic hydroxyl is neutral. Electrostatic repulsion from the Glu222 carboxyl group, together with hydrogen bonds involving the bound water molecule Wat304 and the side-chain oxygen of Ser205, maintains this state. The interaction between Glu222 and Ser65 stabilizes it further.
  Upon excitation, Glu222 transmits a negative charge to the chromophore's phenolic hydroxyl through the hydrogen-bond network formed with Wat304 and Ser205, while the hydroxyl proton is transferred away. In most cases, the chromophore that accepts the charge undergoes photoisomerization and then returns to the ground state by emitting radiation at 504 nm, after which it becomes neutral again.
Figure 10. Model of the GFP fluorescence mechanism[12]
  In a minority of cases, however, changes in the hydrogen-bond network stabilize the chromophore in its ionic form. A new network forms: the His148 side chain hydrogen-bonds to the Tyr66 phenolic oxygen (Oη), while Wat304 interacts with Tyr66 Oη and the side-chain oxygens of Thr203 and Ser205, thereby stabilizing the chromophore. At the same time, the hydrogen bond between Glu222 and Ser205 breaks, and the carboxyl oxygen of Glu222 may undergo cis–trans isomerization.
Figure 11. Chromophore conformations in different GFP states[12]

Engineering Fluorescent Proteins

  Wild-type fluorescent proteins have several shortcomings, including low fluorescence intensity, temperature-sensitive folding, delayed fluorescence, and, for drFP583, cytotoxicity. Most fluorescent proteins used today have therefore been engineered. Such engineering generally centers on the chromophore and follows two basic approaches. The first directly alters the chromophore chemically, thereby changing its photochemical properties. The second replaces amino acids in the chromophore's microenvironment, using the altered surroundings to modify fluorescence. Several common engineered fluorescent proteins are introduced briefly below[11].

Enhanced Blue Fluorescent Protein (EBFP)

  In wild-type GFP, Tyr66 is replaced with His, substituting an imidazole group for the original phenolic group. This mutation blue-shifts the excitation and emission spectra relative to GFP (excitation wavelength: 383 nm; emission wavelength: 445 nm). Val150 is also mutated to Ile and Val224 to Arg, filling the cavity left by replacing tyrosine with histidine and increasing chromophore stability.
Figure 12. Structure of the EBFP chromophore

Enhanced Cyan Fluorescent Protein (ECFP)

  Cyan fluorescent protein follows the same engineering strategy as blue fluorescent protein. Replacing Tyr66 with tryptophan introduces an indole group into the chromophore. Its excitation and emission wavelengths then fall between those of the neutral and ionic phenolic forms of wild-type GFP, producing characteristic blue-green fluorescence (Ex: 439 nm; Em: 476 nm). In addition, replacing His148 with aspartic acid eliminates the interaction between Tyr145 and His148, stabilizing the protein's first conformational state. Replacing Tyr145 with Ala further increases the mutant's fluorescence intensity. The S72A mutation plays an important role in accelerating chromophore maturation.
Figure 13. Structure of the ECFP chromophore

Enhanced Yellow Fluorescent Protein (EYFP)

  EYFP was produced mainly by engineering the microenvironment around the wild-type GFP chromophore. The largest change relative to avGFP is the replacement of Thr203 with tyrosine. When the fluorescent protein folds, the Tyr203 phenolic group extends into the internal cavity and forms a π–π stacking interaction with the chromophore's phenolic group. This mutation stabilizes the excited-state dipole moment of the chromophore, red-shifting both the absorption and emission spectra of GFP by approximately 20 nm. The Gln69-to-Lys mutation also increases chromophore ionization and shifts the emission wavelength another 1–2 nm toward the red.
Figure 14. Structure of the EYFP chromophore

Superfolder GFP

  Superfolder GFP combines nine point mutations: S30R, Y39N, F99S, N105T, Y145F, M153T, V163A, I171V, and A260V. Compared with wild-type GFP, Superfolder GFP is more stable, has more efficient folding kinetics, can fold efficiently at 37 ℃, and is brighter than EGFP. It also tolerates acids and bases better than other members of the GFP family.

Orange Fluorescent Protein (mOrange)

  mOrange belongs to the mFruit family of fluorescent proteins and has characteristic absorption and emission wavelengths of 548 nm and 562 nm, respectively. Engineered from the red fluorescent protein DsRed, the mFruit family has the relative advantages of being monomeric, having low toxicity and high brightness, and maturing quickly. mOrange fluoresces orange because an oxazole ring forms at Thr66 during chromophore formation. Formation of the oxazole ring reduces the conjugation of the carbonyl group at residue 65, blue-shifting the absorption and emission spectra relative to the wild type.
Figure 15. Structure of the mOrange chromophore

Commentary

  From the single green fluorescent protein first discovered to today's diverse range of proteins with different spectral properties, fluorescent proteins can fairly be said to have transformed biological research. They have given life scientists exceptionally effective tools and marked a turning point for the field. As excellent new labels, fluorescent proteins are now widely used throughout biology. Further research will undoubtedly open still broader prospects for their application.

Main References

[1] Zhu Yun, Li Chaowei. Green Fluorescent Protein[J]. Biology Teaching, 2010, 35(6): 62.

[2] Wang Yupeng. The Story of Fluorescent Proteins[J]. Biology Teaching, 2019, 44(5): 73-74.

[3] Hao Limei, Li Tangdi. Advances in Red Fluorescent Protein Research[J]. Foreign Medical Sciences: Pharmacy, 2006, 33(2): 131-133.

[4] Liu Mofang, Wang Enduo. Green Fluorescent Protein[J]. Progress in Biochemistry and Biophysics, 2000, 27(3): 238-243.

[5] Liu Zuqiang, Hu Min, Qi Yipeng. The Structure, Fluorescence Mechanism, and Applications of Green Fluorescent Protein[J]. Journal of Wuhan University, 2000, 46(2): 211-214

[6] Remington, S.J., Saif, M. Crystal structure of GFP S205A/T203V at 2.2 A resolution [DB/OL]. www.pdbus.org/structure/4OGS, 2014-05-14/2021-12-20.

[7] Ma Jinshi. Green Fluorescent Protein[J]. Chemistry Bulletin, 2009, 3: 243-250.

[8] Tubbs, J.L., Tainer, J.A., Getzoff, E.D. High Resolution Crystal Structure of the Discosoma Red Fluorescent Protein (DsRed) [DB/OL]. www.pdbus.org/structure/1ZGO, 2005-08-02/2021-12-20.

[9] Fan Jinyu, Cui Zongqiang, Zhang Xian’en. Spectral Diversity and In Vitro Molecular Evolution of Red Fluorescent Proteins[J]. Progress in Biochemistry and Biophysics, 2008, 35(10): 1112-1120.

[10] Head, J.F., Inouye, S., Teranishi, K., Shimomura, O… Crystal Structure of Aequorin[DB/OL]. www.pdbus.org/structure/1EJ3, 2000-05-31/2021-12-21.

[11] Sample V, Newman R H, Zhang J, et al. The structure and function of fluorescent proteins[J]. Chemical Society Reviews, 2009, 38(10): 2852-2864.

[12] Wang Wei, Liu Xianglin, Li Jiudi. The Fluorescence Mechanism of Green Fluorescent Protein[J]. Chemistry of Life, 1999, 19(6): 275-279.

entry.title: The Phases of Earth as Seen from the Moon
entry.content:
The Phases of Earth as Seen from the Moon

Author: Congyu
Reviewed by: Yuandao and Shiguang

  What does Earth look like from the Moon? If you know something about Earth, the Moon, and lunar phases, you may readily notice that something is amiss in this image. The screenshot comes from Horizon Lunar Colony, a map in the game Overwatch. Setting its artistry and visual impact aside, we will begin with Earth and the Moon and introduce a few basic ideas about the phases of celestial bodies.
Figure 1: Screenshot from Overwatch. The image greatly exaggerates Earth's apparent size. From the Moon, Earth has an apparent diameter of about 1.9 degrees, only 3.6 times that of the Sun.

  The phase of a celestial body is determined by the relative positions of the Sun, the body, and the observer. It reflects how much of the body's sunlit portion we can see. Take the familiar phases of the Moon. Because the distance from the Sun to Earth is far greater than the distance from Earth to the Moon, we can use the Sun–Earth–Moon angle—that is, the angular separation between the Sun and Moon—as a simple measure of how much of the Moon's illuminated face is visible. As the angular separation between the Moon and Sun changes, the lunar phases follow this sequence: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent, and new moon. A quarter moon is separated from the Sun by about 90 degrees, while a full moon is about 180 degrees from it.
  A Moon at a given phase occupies a definite position relative to the Sun. You can use the Moon's direction in the sky to infer the Sun's position and then estimate the local time. For example, if we ignore the inclination between the Moon's orbit and the ecliptic, a first-quarter moon must rise or set six hours after the Sun, while a last-quarter moon does so six hours before it.
Figure 2: The relationship between the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon and the lunar phases. The diagram also shows why the sidereal month and synodic month have different lengths.

  The same rules apply to the “phases of Earth” observed from the Moon. Look at Earth's terminator in the opening game screenshot (Figure 1). Earth appears to be in a waning gibbous phase close to last quarter, yet its angular separation from the Sun at upper left is clearly less than 90 degrees. This means that most of its illuminated side lies on the far side of Earth, out of view, so it should appear as a waning crescent.
  The angle used to describe a celestial body's phase accurately is actually the Sun–Moon–Earth angle, known as the phase angle. As Figure 3 shows, it ranges from 0° to 180°, and the illuminated portion corresponds to an angle of 180°-ψ. Seen from a distance, the terminator separating the bright and dark sides of a celestial body is an elliptical arc—one half of an ellipse divided along its major axis. The extremely curved crescents seen in some animated films and other screen works do not occur as normal phases of celestial bodies. During a lunar eclipse, moreover, the curvature of the edge obscuring the Moon differs from the curvature of a lunar phase. Near the Moon's orbit, the radius of Earth's umbra is 2.6 times the Moon's radius, so the obscuring edge is less strongly curved than the Moon itself.
Figure 3: In the left-hand diagram, ∠SME is the phase angle ψ and is readily seen to equal ∠AMB. The right-hand diagram shows the illuminated and dark sides from the observer's perspective.

  The Moon is not the only Solar System body with phases; every other body has them as well. The inner planets pass through a complete set of phases, but in the reverse order to the Moon: inferior conjunction corresponds to new moon, greatest western elongation to last quarter, superior conjunction to full moon, and greatest eastern elongation to first quarter. Their respective phase angles are 180°, 90°, 0°, and 90°. Because the outer planets orbit beyond Earth, their phase angles never exceed 90°. By analogy with greatest elongation for an inner planet, it is easy to see that when Earth is at greatest elongation relative to an outer planet, that planet's phase angle as observed from Earth reaches its maximum. We therefore cannot see an outer planet in a crescent phase from Earth. Even Mars, whose orbit lies closest to ours, presents at least 84% of its illuminated face.
  Finally, let us admire the haunting view of Earth photographed in 1968 by Apollo 8 from lunar orbit. The astronauts aboard Apollo 8 marveled as Earth appeared to “rise” above the Moon's horizon outside their window. It is worth noting that such earthrises and earthsets would be difficult to see from the lunar surface rather than lunar orbit. The Moon is tidally locked to Earth and always keeps the same side facing us. To someone stationed on the Moon, Earth would therefore remain suspended at a fixed altitude and direction in the sky, moving only slightly because of lunar libration.
Figure 4: A digitally remastered image of Earth. The original was a black-and-white photograph taken by Apollo 8.

entry.title: Early Greek Philosophy
entry.content:
Early Greek Philosophy

Author: Михaїл-А-Булгáкoв☦️
Reviewer: Nancy

  Early Greek philosophy belonged to Greek culture as a whole and to all Greeks, not only to city-states such as Athens and Sparta. Its thinkers shared the use of ancient Greek for thought, expression, and exchange. They shifted humanity's perspective on the world away from the divine focus of early civilization and toward a human-centered outlook intended to educate and cultivate—regardless of whether the earlier authority came from the gods of Babylon, Assyria, Egypt, or Greece's own Olympus.
  Early Greek philosophy reached the Stoics through the selective interpretations of Socrates, Plato, and especially Aristotle. In the hands of the Greek and Latin Church Fathers, it later met Neoplatonism and entered Christian teaching. Heraclitus's *logos*, for example, appears at the beginning of the Gospel of John. Its ability to encompass reason, truth, speech, and the way also made it a foundational theological concept. Yet early Greek philosophy as a whole, like most of Aristotle's writings, remained largely unknown in medieval Europe. Only in the later Middle Ages and the Renaissance did it reenter the Western scholarly world, as Greek texts returned and Arabic works were translated into Latin.
  Early Greek philosophy entered modern scholarship in earnest only at the end of the nineteenth century. The German historian of philosophy Eduard Zeller published *A History of Greek Philosophy*, while the British historian of ancient philosophy and classicist John Burnet published *Early Greek Philosophy*. Over several decades, the German historian and classical scholar Hermann Diels compiled *Doxographi Graeci* and *The Fragments of the Pre-Socratics*, finally giving scholars collections of early Greek philosophical texts that met modern academic standards.
  Among the world's early civilizations, the Greeks of the Archaic period were relatively early to abandon theological explanations that used the supernatural powers of myth and religion to account for real events and natural processes. They used rational inference independent of supernatural forces to think critically about natural phenomena, disasters, society, and human relationships, explaining such questions through nature itself. This turn produced not only the philosophical thought of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, but also a system of dependable knowledge: science.
  Early Greek thinkers investigated nature and natural phenomena independently, critically, and seriously. They asked about the basic constituents and overall composition of everything in the world, the ways and laws governing the cosmos and individual action, and the properties and causes behind them. In doing so, they posed philosophical questions that still matter today: Did the universe have a beginning? How did that beginning begin? Do the basic components of things and their transformations follow discoverable laws? Is the world a unity? How do we know, and how can we possess knowledge?
  On the relationship between philosophy and science, early Greek thinkers offered cosmogonies rooted in empirical observation. The world arose neither from nothing nor through divine creation. Everything came from a single entity or unified state, combining into the things of the world under natural laws and following those laws through generation and destruction. Each thinker had a distinct set of terms and explanations, yet those ideas could be discussed, exchanged, corrected, and developed. They could explain and judge particular natural events and facts while also grasping and interpreting the world systematically as a whole. In this way, they formed the earliest rational worldview.
  As for the subject matter of philosophical thought, early Greek thinkers first focused on the reality of all things: their origin and governing principle. Thales, for example, proposed that “water is the origin of all things.” These thinkers also set cosmological change beside the eternal logic of epistemology, seeking at the level of language and thought to reconcile the differences and opposition between natural reality and human reflection. Heraclitus held that “everything flows” while proposing the “order and harmony” of the law of *logos*. Parmenides, beginning from “eternal, unchanging truth,” was the first to bring being, thought, and language into unity.
  From these two realms—the realities of nature and thought—early Greek thinkers went on to explore the human soul and the possibility of its search for knowledge. Starting respectively from change and changelessness, Heraclitus and Parmenides both moved toward knowledge's “eternal truth.” The atomists investigated the fundamental material composition of nature while also considering human sensation and experience, explaining the lawful operation of the world through a unity of nature and mind. Early Greek thought thus opened philosophical questions about first principles, cosmic order, being and what a thing is, and the ethical relationship between gods and humans.
  On philosophical discourse and terminology, the British scholar Barnes identifies several concepts as the most important categories of early Greek thought. Cosmos (universe) means both the world as a whole and order itself. As a verb, it means arranging the generation, operation, and coordination of things according to an order. As a noun, it denotes the ordered world as a whole—the totality of things. Physis (nature) stands in contrast to what is made or artificial. A natural thing, true to its nature, can grow by itself; this was humanity's first conceptual distinction between nature and artifice. Alongside the *cosmos*, *physis* refers specifically to the distinctive nature that each thing in the world possesses, rather than its accidental or random features. It marks the particular natures that distinguish diversity within the unity of the whole *cosmos*. In this sense, if the world as a whole is treated as one individual, its *physis* is its *cosmos*. This meaning of *physis* survives in many fields of study today. Early Greek inquiry into *physis*, however, also concerned the beginning and operative principle of all things and the world. This leads to the next fundamental term. Arche (beginning) is both the origin or starting point of all things and the world, and the initial principle by which the world operates—in other words, the first principle.  The Greeks held that things and worlds capable of growing according to their own nature must have an origin and root, together with rules governing their growth or operation. *Arche* therefore reflects on the mode and course by which naturally constituted things—and the world itself—operate within a *cosmos*. Beyond *cosmos* and *physis*, it searches for their external foundation. The concept has several levels: How did the world and its contents begin? What is the first principle of their growth and operation? What basic elements constitute the world? How do those elements compose individual things, their structures, and the world as a whole? These first three terms concern objective knowledge of the external world. Early Greek thinkers also reflected on human knowledge and its expression: *logos*. *Logos* is rational thought and speech, distinguished from empirical observation of the world. It represents one of the earliest distinctions in human thought between sensation and reason. Guided by *logos*, early Greek thinkers emphasized reasoning from causes, the use of rationality, argument, and inference rather than dogmatic judgment and unsupported conclusion.
  Early Greek thought laid the first foundations for scientific method and its working principles. It used humanly constructed terms to name the basic elements of nature, employed observation to infer or posit mechanisms by which things arise and operate, and reduced the world's complex diversity to simpler forms of order and principle. Compared with modern scientific knowledge, many of its particular conclusions and inferences now appear amusing or naïve. Yet their mode of producing knowledge already displayed the essential features of science. Early Greek thought created the basic concepts of Western science and philosophy and began a scientific—or rational—way of seeing the world. It continues to shape how people establish confidence in knowledge and conduct scholarly research today.

entry.title: The Basics of Mineral Description: How to Read a Rock
entry.content:
The Basics of Mineral Description: How to Read a Rock

Author: 约翰史密斯

  Hello, everyone. Today we will introduce some common terms used to describe the many properties of minerals.
  First, why do we need to learn how to describe minerals? The Earth contains an extraordinary variety of mineral deposits. Some specimens that look completely different are actually the same mineral, while others that look remarkably alike have entirely different compositions.
  Consider what happens if we judge a specimen only by its most obvious appearance. Take the famous “fool’s gold,” for example:

  It may glitter with a golden-yellow shine, but it has nothing to do with gold: it is simply pyrite. And even among iron ores, there are hematite, magnetite, limonite, and many others. A systematic description of a mineral therefore helps us compare specimens later and determine what mineral each one actually is.
  To describe a mineral, we need to examine it from many angles:

  • Color: What color does it appear overall? Is the color uniform or mixed?

  • Transparency: Is it transparent, translucent, or opaque?

  • Luster: Does it look metallic or waxy? Does it sparkle?

  • Cleavage: Does it split along straight, flat surfaces? Are those surfaces continuous or discontinuous?

  • Fracture: What shape does the broken surface have? Is it conchoidal or rough? Does it follow a regular pattern?

  • Twinning: Is the crystal twinned? If so, what type of twinning does it exhibit?

  • Density: Self-explanatory.

  • Hardness: Self-explanatory.

  • Streak: What color is the powder produced by rubbing the mineral, and does it have any distinctive properties?

  • Magnetism: Self-explanatory.

  • Optical activity: Does a thin section rotate the plane of polarized light? What is the period of that rotation?

  • Fluorescence: Does it glow under ultraviolet light or at a particular wavelength?

  • Environment: In what setting was the mineral found—in igneous, metamorphic, or sedimentary rock? Was there anything unusual about that environment?

entry.title: How to Use Color Well
entry.content:
How to Use Color Well

Author: 时光

  How do you “do color” properly? Did that wording send your mind somewhere questionable? No—this is an entirely respectable science article. So let me show you a color picture. Very proper, isn't it? The charming little object below is called a color wheel. It will be the main character in what follows, so take a moment to remember what it looks like.
  This article introduces the fundamentals of color and several common ways of building a palette.

Color Theory and Color Schemes

How Do Humans See Color?

  In nature, light travels from a source to the surface of an object. Most illuminated objects absorb part of that light and reflect the rest into our eyes. The reflected light becomes the color we see. If an object absorbs none of the light falling on it—in other words, if it reflects all of that light unchanged—it looks white. At the other extreme, an object that absorbs all incident light looks black.
  This way of producing color is called subtractive color mixing and corresponds to the CMYK model in multimedia. In everyday life, it is widely used by printers and in other situations where color must appear on an object that does not emit light. The object cannot shine by itself, so the color we see comes from light reflected by the ink.
  The other model, RGB, works in the opposite way. You probably know more about RGB than CMYK. Its initials stand for red, green, and blue, the three primary colors of light. The RGB model mixes those colors in different proportions to create new ones. It is widely used in light-emitting devices such as televisions, computers, and phones.
  Now that you know the two most basic color models, how can you combine colors into a successful palette? Let us begin by looking at several established approaches.

Monochromatic Color Scheme

  A monochromatic scheme may be the most harmonious of all. In the example, the colors barely clash at all; the entire image feels balanced and fresh.
  That harmony comes from using one base color, or hue, and deriving the others through changes in lightness and darkness, as the color wheel shows. No additional hue intrudes, so the result looks simpler, cleaner, and more refined. The weakness is just as obvious: a monochromatic palette offers little variation.

Complementary Color Scheme

  If monochromatic color feels clean, spacious, and harmonious, the next scheme is far more energetic. Can anyone guess what it is? Type your answer in the group chat.
  This is complementary color, also called a contrasting scheme. Complementary colors create a powerful sense of collision. They sit opposite each other on the color wheel, which means their warm–cool qualities and the impressions they produce are also opposed. Place them together, and their conflict immediately commands attention. Used well, that conflict can be striking.
  UI designers often use complementary colors to highlight information they want users to notice. Paintings can exploit the same tension to lead the viewer's eye straight to the intended focal point. The disadvantage is equally clear: too many competing contrasts can become dazzling and chaotic.

Split-Complementary Color Scheme

  Next comes the split-complementary scheme. As the diagram shows, it uses a base color and two secondary colors placed symmetrically around the base color's complement, forming a narrow triangle on the wheel. The result pairs one warm color with two cool ones, or one cool color with two warm ones.
  Unlike a direct complementary pair, a split-complementary scheme is comparatively balanced and gentle. The color at the triangle's narrow vertex generally serves as the dominant hue, while the other two are often used for lighting or accents. This creates a subtler palette with much of the visual effect of complementary color but less of its head-on collision. The wheel makes clear that split-complementary color is essentially a variation or branch of the complementary scheme. Its crucial difference is that the contrast is less intense and exaggerated.

Analogous Color Scheme

  The next scheme seems to combine the strengths of the two approaches above. It is less monotonous than a monochromatic palette but not as aggressive as a complementary one. Applied flexibly, it makes harmonious yet lively interfaces easy to design. What is it? We have arrived at our next scheme: analogous color.
  Analogous colors form a low-contrast group located close together on the color wheel. The scheme is remarkably versatile. Compare it first with monochromatic color. An analogous palette plainly contains more hues, yet it does not break the subtle harmony and balance among them. The result is richer and more colorful, making it useful when a design needs greater variety.
  At the same time, analogous colors are much softer than complementary ones. That makes the scheme a dependable all-rounder, and we see it used everywhere.

Triadic Color Scheme

  A triadic scheme uses three colors spaced evenly around the wheel, creating a degree of contrast among all three. All three can act as major colors, producing a bright, attention-grabbing effect. This approach demands particular care with color balance. Because each pair has a subtle contrast, triadic color is useful when a design needs strong differentiation among all three hues. Divide the image equally among them, however, and the impact can become so strong that beauty is lost.
  Are there exceptions? Yes. Equal shares work in an image whose very meaning suggests an even division—three buttons for three equivalent functions, for example. Once the composition becomes complicated, distributing all three colors equally tends to create disorder.
  To use a triadic palette well, choose one or two of the three as dominant hues and let them restrain the others. Make one color the main presence in the image and use the rest sparingly as accents. Another option is to use a softer tone to temper the other two.

Rectangular Color Scheme

  What happens if you select two pairs of opposing colors from the wheel? You get a rectangular, or tetradic, scheme—an approach even more unruly than triadic color. The four hues have no obvious hierarchy, but their paired contrasts still produce a bright, vivid result. Together, they can create a powerful visual impression, though achieving the best effect requires advance planning and careful design.
  The more colors a palette contains, the harder they generally are to reconcile. Rectangular schemes are more common in evenly divided situations such as four buttons. They can also be blended at lower contrast to create an intentionally intricate effect.

Color Psychology

  Now that we know some fundamentals of color schemes, how do we choose the right one? Before we begin working with color in earnest, we need some “color psychology.” Many people assume that color choice depends mainly on a designer's taste and aesthetic sense. The process is more complicated than it looks, and choosing well is vital to design. The table below shows that different colors tend to produce different feelings.
  Red, for example, is often associated with passion and fervor, but also with aggression and attack. It has two faces: love and confidence on one side, anger on the other. Either way, it is exceptionally conspicuous. In design, red is often an effective way to attract a user's attention.
  What image appears when you think of green? Even if it is not your first thought, green readily suggests dense forests and thriving grassland. It is a vigorous color and therefore ill suited to decorating a negative or pessimistic image. For the latter, we more often choose shades of gray.
  Color psychology describes the feelings of a majority, not a rule that applies to everyone. Some people see green and think of plague, disease, or death.
