  As for whether it tasted good… Sorry, that was outside the scope of consideration…

  But do not look down on steaming and boiling just because the food did not taste good, you fool. Even today, Western cooks rarely use “steaming.” Take France, whose cuisine is famous worldwide: some say its chefs do not even have a concept of “steaming.”

  Now let us turn to roasting. The Tang campaigns in the north brought large quantities of northern mutton into the empire, along with the soul of barbecue—cumin—from the Middle East. So people in the Tang could eat lamb skewers, and lamb was not the only meat they roasted.

Cumin ⬆

  The Tang physician Jiu Yin (who may have spent all day hanging around barbecue stalls) recorded several grilled dishes in the Shiyi Xinjian: mandarin duck, wild boar, eel, myna, and yellow hen.

Be sure to watch to the end!

  Thus, even if the Tang had woks, there was little use for them. They existed, but only in very small numbers. Woks did not begin to grow more common until the transition from the Tang to the Song.

  Salt and iron were often state monopolies in imperial China, and the Song was no exception. Mining and iron smelting were overseen by the government: local mine owners handled extraction, while a “professional team” took care of smelting.

  The “professional team” familiar to us today looks like this:

No explanation needed for this professional team

  The professional iron-smelting team of the time looked like this:

Illustration of wrought- and cast-iron production from *Tiangong Kaiwu*

  That professional team naturally came under the Salt and Iron administration, one of the Northern Song’s Three Financial Bureaus.

(Extra: after the Ming reorganization, during the Yongle reign...)

  The Baoyuan Bureau was originally a mint, the equivalent of a modern coin factory. Ancient currency was made of metal, but everyday pots, bowls, ladles, basins, hoes, rakes, shovels, and the like also required metal. Rather than trouble a second office, the state mint made these farm tools too. Its directors must have found the situation galling: a dignified national mint reduced to casting farm implements!?

  All right, back to the point. Someone is bound to complain: over the three hundred years between the Tang and Song, were those craftspeople doing nothing but eating? They could not even make something as simple as a wok. Put me in charge and the Tang would be eating stir-fries in minutes. (Insert doge face.)

  Hey, do not complain that this was slow. A wok “midwife” was nagging away the entire time, pushing for woks to be manufactured and used on a large scale and spurring the emergence of the new cooking method called “stir-frying.”

  There was more than one of these nags: there were two. One had been chattering without pause from the Han dynasty all the way to the Song, nearly a thousand years. The other began during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

  As for who these two “nags” were…

  I will write about that next time…

entry.title: The Novel Coronavirus 2019-nCoV
entry.content:
Author: Shenzhou
Reviewers: DClean and Weiming

  The novel coronavirus outbreak (hereafter 2019-nCoV; claims circulating online that the virus had been named “SARI” were false) has drawn widespread attention across China. For ordinary members of the public, whether or not we live in an affected area or have spent time in one, we must stay alert, take proper precautions, and not assume that we will simply be lucky. We should wear a mask whenever we go out, avoid crowded places wherever possible, and refrain from indoor activities in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces.

Transmission and Protection

  Some reports suggest that 2019-nCoV originated in bats or other wild animals, but no official source has confirmed this.

  Because 2019-nCoV is a new virus, anyone who has not previously been infected with the same virus is susceptible, regardless of age. It can spread from person to person, most likely through respiratory droplets and contact, with aerosol transmission also a possibility.

  Droplet transmission occurs when a source of infection releases pathogen-bearing secretions and droplets by coughing, sneezing, or speaking, and a susceptible person inhales them. Such transmission generally requires close contact with the source; beyond two meters, infectiousness largely disappears. It can readily occur in crowded places such as stations, schools, and large gatherings. Contact transmission occurs when a pathogen reaches a susceptible person through direct or indirect contact with a vehicle of transmission. In direct contact transmission, the pathogen passes straight from the source to a suitable portal of entry in the susceptible person; indirect contact transmission results from touching contaminated objects. Masks offer effective protection against droplet transmission, while rubber gloves can provide some protection against contact transmission.

Symptoms and Treatment

  At present, no effective treatment for pneumonia caused by 2019-nCoV has been validated in clinical trials; clinical care consists mainly of symptomatic and supportive treatment. Recent high-throughput drug-screening efforts have identified several drugs that may be effective against 2019-nCoV. Do not blindly trust online rumors or folk remedies. Any unofficial treatment circulated online should be assessed through scientific reasoning and careful research. Follow official information as it is released to avoid unnecessary problems.

  The main symptoms of pneumonia caused by 2019-nCoV infection are fever, cough, and fatigue, and more than half of patients experience difficulty breathing. Some people may not develop a fever. It should also be noted that patients infected with 2019-nCoV rarely show upper-respiratory symptoms, such as a runny nose, sneezing, or a sore throat, or intestinal symptoms.

  Sneezing is a response to irritation of the nasal mucosa, and much of the expelled air leaves through the nose. Coughing, by contrast, is a response to irritation of the trachea, bronchial mucosa, or pleura, and the expelled air leaves mainly through the mouth. The two should be distinguished. If upper-respiratory symptoms appear, an upper-respiratory infection rather than the novel pneumonia should be considered.

  Patients with similar symptoms that are not severe—a temperature below 38°C and no difficulty breathing—should first call a nearby community doctor. The doctor can visit the home wearing full protective equipment and then determine whether a trip to a designated hospital is necessary, reducing the risk of cross-infection while seeking care. Patients with severe symptoms should immediately call the local designated hospital and center for disease control and prevention, then put on the recommended protection and go to the hospital as instructed.

entry.title: Do We Get Overtime Pay in a Leap Year?
entry.content:
Author: 斎藤信
Reviewer: 白烟

  If I have counted correctly, this article will reach you on the first day of the Lunar New Year—or sometime afterward—making a conspicuous public appearance. Happy New Year to everyone! Publishing on the first day of the year is not easy. I will not ask for triple pay (or any pay at all); I only hope you will read carefully. A like, a comment, and a favorite—scratch that—and a share would be even better!

Happy New Year, and may everyone enjoy good health!

  You have probably heard that 2020 is a “double leap year.” The Year of the Rat has 384 days, so we have to put in an extra month’s work—an intercalary fourth lunar month. I understand the arithmetic, but why the overtime? Today, then, we will talk about intercalation in calendars.

  First, let us look at what a “calendar” is.

  A calendar is a system for calculating the lengths of days, months, and years and the relationships among them, thereby establishing the order of time. The lengths of some calendar months and years are determined by the cycles of the Sun and Moon; others are set by convention. The earliest calendars paid close attention to the waxing and waning of the Moon. Later, the needs of agriculture required calendars in which the seasons remained regular and seasonal markers followed a stable order. These rules kept the sequence of months and days in the calendar aligned with the apparent positions of the Sun and Moon in the sky. Without that alignment, seasons would be reversed and lunar phases would fall out of place.

  Next, let us examine “intercalation.”

  The tropical year is the cycle of the seasons, while the synodic month is the cycle of the lunar phases. A calendar must therefore determine both periods precisely. Yet neither the tropical year (365.2422 days) nor the synodic month (29.5306 days) is an integer, and the two are not simply commensurable. If years and months retained their exact astronomical lengths, their starting times would not fall at a fixed point within the day—and who knows what to do with 0.2422 of a day? That would be highly inconvenient for work and daily life. Calendars therefore define years and months as whole numbers of days. These are known as calendar years and calendar months. A discrepancy remains between them and the astronomical periods. If ignored, it accumulates and eventually throws the calendar into disorder. A calendar’s method for correcting that discrepancy is called intercalation.

  Most readers will know how intercalation works in the Gregorian calendar, the solar calendar in common use. A solar calendar takes the tropical year as its basic unit and has nothing to do with the synodic month. It treats the year as the primary component and aims to make the mean calendar year equal to the tropical year; the number of days in a month and the number of months in a year are conventional. Today’s worldwide civil calendar developed from the Julian calendar. The Julian calendar assigned 365.25 days to a tropical year and twelve months to each year. Odd-numbered months had 31 days; even-numbered months had 30, except February, which had 29 because it was then the month in which prisoners were executed. A leap day was inserted in February after every three ordinary years, giving it 30 days in a leap year. Later misunderstandings led to twelve leap years being inserted over a span of 33 years, three too many. The ruler of the time ordered two corrections. First, there would be no leap years for the next eleven years; once the three extra leap years had been offset, the four-year cycle would resume. Second, August, the month of his birth, would become a long month. The pattern of long and short months after August was reversed, and the extra day was taken from February. February consequently has 28 days in an ordinary year and 29 in a leap year.

  The Julian calendar was arguably the best calendar of its time. Several Christian countries in Europe adopted it together and, based on contemporary astronomical observations, stipulated that the vernal equinox must fall on March 21. The Julian year, however, is 0.0078 day longer than the tropical year. Over 1,257 years, this tiny difference accumulated into an error of about ten days, so that by 1582 the Sun was observed to pass the vernal equinox on March 11. Pope Gregory XIII therefore accepted a proposal by the Italian physician and philosopher Lilio and issued a decree: the ten days from October 5 through October 14 that year were removed, and the rule of one leap year every four years was replaced with 97 leap years every 400 years. This is the familiar modern rule: a year divisible by 100 is a century leap year only if it is also divisible by 400; every other year divisible by 4 is a leap year. The reformed calendar became known as the Gregorian calendar. It is far more accurate than the Julian calendar, although it still gains 1.2 days in 4,000 years. The years 4000 and 8000 should therefore not be leap years—unless a better calendar has been devised by then.

  To understand intercalation in the traditional Chinese calendar, we must first understand how that calendar is constructed. It is a lunisolar calendar, not the purely lunar calendar it is often called. A lunar calendar treats the month as its primary component and tries to make the synodic month the length of a calendar month. The length of its calendar year is conventional and unrelated to the tropical year. A synodic month lasts 29.5306 days. Lunar calendars therefore assign 30 days to odd-numbered months and 29 days to even-numbered months, beginning each month with the first appearance of the new Moon. Twelve months make a 354-day year. Twelve synodic months, however, last 354.3671 days, so over thirty years they exceed thirty calendar years by 11.013 days. This calendar follows the phases of the Moon, but each ordinary calendar year is about eleven days shorter than the tropical year. It falls behind by one month in three years, and after about seventeen years its sequence of months and seasons would be reversed. Such a system would be a poor guide to agriculture. The traditional Chinese calendar was developed to solve this problem.

  A lunisolar calendar gives equal weight to the year and the month. It uses the synodic month as the length of a calendar month and inserts leap months so that the tropical year determines the length of the calendar year. The tropical year contains about 12.368 synodic months. To keep the average calendar year close to the tropical year, an ordinary lunisolar year has twelve months and a leap year has thirteen. The additional month is the leap month. Calculation shows that seven leap months in nineteen years is a reasonable arrangement. It prevents the order of the months from becoming detached from the seasons. The insertion of leap months creates a large difference in year length: an ordinary year has 353 to 355 days, while a leap year has 383 to 384—so you really do receive another month’s salary; there is no need to feel cheated. The placement of the leap month is closely connected to the twelve principal solar terms among the twenty-four solar terms. Strictly speaking, the system contains twelve principal terms and twelve sectional terms. In a lunisolar calendar, every month normally contains a designated principal term, a point we will not explore further here. Nineteen tropical years contain 228 sectional terms and 228 principal terms, while nineteen lunisolar years contain 235 synodic months. Seven months must therefore lack a sectional term, and seven must lack a principal term. The rule eventually adopted makes a month without a principal term the leap month of that year. It takes the name of the preceding month with the word “leap” placed before it. Later calendar makers have continued to use this method to the present day.

  Why, then, have you never encountered a leap first month? In early July each year, Earth passes aphelion, roughly around the beginning of the sixth lunar month. Earth is then moving more slowly along its orbit, while the difference in the Sun’s apparent ecliptic longitude between successive principal terms remains 30°. The interval between two principal terms is therefore longer, increasing the probability of a leap month. As far as I know, no leap first month will occur between now and 2060. Until then, forget about getting a two-month winter vacation.

entry.title: Tumors Explained
entry.content:
Author: 绿水青山
Reviewers: 食野; 未名

  Most of us have encountered the word “tumor” in everyday life, but may not know its technical definition. The word often provokes an immediate sense of fear. Malignant tumors are generally difficult to cure and can have an enormous effect on a patient’s daily life. Today we will look at some basic facts about tumors.

  In biology, a tumor is a neoplasm formed through the abnormal proliferation of the body’s cells—in other words, a mass produced by the abnormal growth of body tissue. It commonly appears as a localized mass of abnormal tissue. Tumors form when various tumor-causing factors severely disrupt the regulation of cell growth.

  This definition tells us that a tumor should not exist when the body is functioning normally. What, then, characterizes neoplastic proliferation? First, it is uncoordinated with the body and is harmful. It is also generally clonal, and tumor cells lose the ability to differentiate and mature to varying degrees. Their original function, morphology, and metabolism usually become abnormal. At the same time, they grow vigorously, escape control, and acquire a degree of autonomy. Early in tumor formation, an external carcinogenic factor alters the genes of a cell. The cell escapes control and can pass its altered genes stably to the next generation. Even if the external factor is removed later, the tumor continues to proliferate autonomously. A tumor is generally composed of daughter cells descended from the same original cell.

  After understanding the characteristics of neoplastic proliferation, we can consider the usual morphology of tumors. A tumor mass is most often solitary, although several may appear at once. Tumors also take many shapes, including polypoid, papillary, cauliflower-like, nodular, and ulcerative forms. Their colors vary as well. A cut surface is generally gray-white or gray-red, but the color also depends on the blood content, pigments, and other factors. Lipomas, for example, are usually yellow, whereas hemangiomas are often dark red or purplish red. Tumors can also be classified as benign or malignant according to their growth. Medical naming conventions differ for the two. A malignant epithelial tumor is generally named for its “primary site” followed by “carcinoma,” whereas a benign tumor is named for its “location” followed by “tumor” or “-oma.” There are exceptions: a malignant tumor arising in mesenchymal tissue, for example, is called a “sarcoma.”

I. Benign tumors

  One clear distinction between benign and malignant tumors lies in how they grow. A benign tumor grows expansively and does not spread to other parts of the body. A malignant tumor grows invasively and may metastasize from its primary organ to other sites. At the cellular level, benign tumors show relatively few abnormal mitotic figures and grow more slowly. A benign tumor generally grows in a single location and is usually enclosed by a fibrous capsule. It therefore tends to cause less harm, and its damage to the body is generally limited to local compression or obstruction. Treatment is comparatively straightforward. Most benign tumors have a good prognosis and do not readily recur.

II. Malignant tumors (cancer)

  Malignant tumors are generally called cancer. Because they grow invasively, they can seriously affect surrounding tissues, extending into them much like tree roots. Abnormal mitotic figures are common in malignant tumor cells. Genetic changes also alter their adhesion, motility, and ability to degrade the extracellular matrix during metastasis, enabling the cells to break through the basement membrane and invade surrounding tissue. If they then enter blood or lymphatic vessels, leave those vessels at a suitable point, and continue proliferating elsewhere, the tumor has metastasized. This is a principal reason malignant tumors threaten patients’ lives. In addition to causing greater harm, malignant tumors require more complex treatment, and the outcome is generally less satisfactory.

  The growth rate of tumor cells is generally affected by the following factors:

  1. The doubling time of the tumor cells;
  2. The growth fraction—the proportion of cells in the population that are proliferating;
  3. The production and loss of tumor cells;

  Research has found that the doubling time of cells in most malignant tumors is similar to, or even longer than, that of normal cells. The rapid growth of malignant tumors therefore does not result from a shorter doubling time. The latter two factors have a greater influence on their growth rate.

  The distinction between benign and malignant is not absolute; it is a boundary drawn by people. Some tumors have tissue morphology and biological behavior that fall between the two. Such tumors generally have a tendency toward malignant transformation or display some features of malignancy. An ovarian borderline serous tumor, for example, lies between benign and malignant. Some benign tumors may also become malignant if they are not treated promptly. In exceptionally rare cases, a malignant tumor may stop growing or even regress spontaneously for reasons such as stronger immune function.

entry.title: The Feathered Sprites of My Campus
entry.content:
Author: 蜗牛
Reviewer: 一毫秒的永恒

  A winter morning is cold and quiet. The Sun has not yet laid its highlights across the surfaces around me, so everything retains its natural color. I like this hour: no noise, no distractions, no rush before the first class. I can leave home at an easy pace, clock in at work, and bring my binoculars along to see the birds on campus.

  Today begins well. Soon after leaving home, amid the calls of magpies in the small square by the water tower, I pick out a faint zi-zi among the sparrows’ chatter. Probably a tit. Through the binoculars, it looks like a great tit, though it could be a Japanese tit. I confuse those two every time I see them. Even familiar birds demand attention.

  Beyond the small central gate, the avenue of plane trees between the sports field and the shops is a veritable “path of angels”—or rather, angel droppings. Great patches of bird mess run together across the ground. Perhaps the birds hold a meeting here every day. Around the turn from spring to summer, many people have been challenged by azure-winged magpies along this road. First, a large bird appears on a low branch diagonally ahead, scolding with a stream of cries. The moment you walk a little past its perch, a gust brushes the back of your head. Turn around, and the magpie has already declared victory and withdrawn. It does not truly attack; it merely circles very close behind and above your head after you pass. I have no idea what kind of tactic that is. Once, I kept my head turned and watched the bird making the announcement. With me staring at it, it seemed too embarrassed to act. I finally walked backward out of its territory and spent quite some time privately delighted by the helpless look in its eyes.

Eurasian magpie

  Real attacks do happen, though not often. A close friend told me that she was playing with her son on this road when a young azure-winged magpie fluttered nearby. The two- or three-year-old went a little too close, and an adult bird dived at him. She hurried forward to shield the child. A day later, on the same stretch of road but without her son, the adult swooped from behind and pecked the top of her head. It genuinely hurt. She wore different clothes, so how had the bird recognized her? To us, birds of the same species and size can be almost impossible to distinguish. I do not know whether the bird I meet on the road is the same one I see outside my window. How, then, can a bird pick the same person in different clothes out of a crowd?

Spotted dove

  Even on this avenue ruled by azure-winged magpies, a dove will occasionally hide in silence. Whenever I see one, I look only at its collar. So far, campus has shown me spotted doves with black-and-white pearl necklaces, but never an Oriental turtle dove with a striped black-and-white collar. I will keep examining every dove I meet.

  After twenty-two years on this campus, I know every tree and every blade of grass. A tree at the southwest corner of the sports field became the “king of trees” because an underground pipe leaked nearby. The same leaking pipe later caused its crown to be cut off. But a tree king remains a tree king: it turned all its stored strength into the largest leaves we had ever seen and became the center of attention. This is also where I once encountered a grey-headed woodpecker and a flock of white-cheeked starlings stopping on their southward migration.

  Along Magnolia Avenue, red-billed blue magpies and light-vented bulbuls greet me cheerfully from the magnolias or the cedars in the rose garden. I know where they are going. The bulbuls will sing from the pines south of the western classroom building. The blue magpies will rummage secretly through the rubbish bin beside the western wall. Do they not know about the bin by the northeastern wall, or does that one belong to the crows?

  After clocking in at the office building, I can stroll over to the small garden in front of the western classroom building and try my luck. In the morning, that garden is luckier than the one in front of the eastern building; in the afternoon, the reverse is true. After thinking it through, I decided the reason must be sunlight. A row of tall cedars stands at the southern edge of the gardens, followed by the school wall. In the morning, those trees block all sunlight from the eastern garden, while sunshine stretches directly from the square before the office to the western garden. I have watched yellow-bellied tits hopping among willow branches here and, with students—on a winter morning, cold and quiet, before the Sun had laid highlights across the world, when everything kept its natural colors; an hour I love, without noise, distraction, or the tension of first period, when I can leave home calmly to clock in and bring binoculars to watch campus birds—secretly observed a crowned hoopoe. Even when luck brings nothing else, the light-vented bulbuls singing at full voice from the cedar tops do not disappoint. Their calls at this hour are endlessly varied and never grow tiresome. From the little garden I continue west to the wall, then turn north. Soon I will see my favorite sprite. The thought brings a little anticipation and a little excitement.

Daurian redstart

  First comes the Daurian redstart, a landmark in my life as a birdwatcher. Because of this little creature, I searched Baidu for two years and accidentally joined a QQ group for people who sell birds before finally finding the “Chinese Birdwatchers” group. These days I no longer search everywhere for the redstart’s hiding place. I need only hear its thin, crisp, metallic di to picture it bobbing its head and flicking its tail. In that respect, it resembles the wagtails that often exercise on the sports field.

Black-throated bushtit

  The other is the black-throated bushtit, affectionately called the “little redhead.” Seeing one of China’s smallest birds demands both patience and luck. I usually listen first for a very soft zi-zi. With experience, a quiet sound nearby becomes distinguishable from a loud one far away. I stand still and watch. Once something flickers among the branches, I raise the binoculars, and the little bird appears: a narrow white line around its neck above a black diamond-shaped patch. Then I examine the forehead. If the crown is not pure black but chestnut-red, it is my little redhead. Only when my arms and back ache from holding the binoculars for so long do I lower them and walk away content. Beside a bushtit barely visible to the naked eye, a large red-billed blue magpie makes the moment feel perfectly peaceful.

Chinese blackbird

  Farther on is the western dining hall, an excellent place. Birds can eat, drink, play, brawl, and quarrel there, with only a wall between them and the grove outside the school. It offers both an advance position and an escape route, so no wonder black drongos choose it as a base in early summer. I still wonder whether the great spotted woodpecker fills its stomach in the trees or on the ground in front of the dining hall. Two winters ago, a flock of light-vented bulbuls quarreled with a blackbird here so loudly that I heard them from twenty meters away. At first I could not see the blackbird and assumed an azure-winged magpie had upset the bulbuls. The magpies were not involved, and only then did I spot the blackbird. I saw no blackbirds for the rest of that winter or the next. I thought they had left the campus for good. Yet suddenly there they were before me: one, two, five—no, still more—a whole flock of at least seven or eight. At the sight of me, they scattered from a tree in the flower bed, to the great cedar by the dining-hall entrance, over the wall a few meters away, and back again to hide among privet leaves. One greedy bird on the ground refused to leave. Its orange-yellow bill gave it a charmingly foolish look. Standing still, it held its head high and alert. The moment it began walking, its anxiety showed: head lowered and stretched forward, a few hurried steps, then stillness with head raised, then neck out and head down for another quick dash. The pattern repeated until I was laughing inside. Compared with the magpie’s calm, unhurried stride, it made me spare a second’s sympathy for the pressures these birds face.

Eurasian tree sparrow

  This beautiful campus has been my home. Now I am about to leave the place where I have lived and worked for twenty-two years, and my heart is full of reluctance. I remember the pagoda tree between the dormitories with a flat, sesame-cake-shaped hornet’s nest. I remember the Oriental greenfinches calling from the crowns of white poplars. But do they remember me—the person who, before understanding the principles of birdwatching, once scared apart a mixed flock of sparrows and greenfinches feeding on the sports field, just to identify which bird belonged to which species more quickly?

The author’s school: Mianchi High School, Henan

entry.title: From Simple to Complex: Algebra, Part 1
entry.content:
Algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies numbers, quantities, relations, structures, and general methods for solving algebraic equations and systems, together with their properties. Elementary algebra is usually taught in secondary school. It introduces the subject’s basic ideas: what happens when we add or multiply numbers, what variables are, and how to construct polynomials and find their roots. Algebra studies not only numbers but all kinds of abstract structures.

  Author: delta

  Algebra is one of the most important branches of mathematics today. It has many branches of its own, including elementary algebra and higher algebra, while higher algebra divides into still more offshoots. If mathematics is Yggdrasil, then algebra is Asgard.

  Geometry is Vanaheim.

  Clearly, within Asgard, modern algebra wields power comparable to Odin’s in Valhalla. Our purpose on this journey is to seek an audience with Odin. Yet in any kingdom, no one can meet the king directly without first obtaining a pass from the gatekeeper. So let us at least step onto Bifrost and have a heart-to-heart with Heimdall—elementary algebra.

Origins

  Diophantus, a Greek mathematician of the third century BCE, is now widely regarded as the father of algebra, while its true founder is considered to be al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician of the medieval Arab Empire. Chinese students often make fun of the latter because of how his name sounds in Chinese.

  That ill-judged teasing has not brought al-Khwarizmi much fame, however. Only a small minority have heard of him. Diophantus, by contrast, is known to most people because of the elementary math-olympiad puzzle on his tombstone and the famous Diophantine equations.

  Amusingly, the story takes another dramatic turn: although many people have heard of Diophantine equations, far from being able to solve such problems, they do not even know what a Diophantine equation is.

  If you think this article is about to discuss Diophantine equations, you are quite mistaken. Since we are proceeding from the simple to the complex, we must begin with what is genuinely “simple.” A Diophantine equation is plainly not simple enough; its essence is.

  What is the essence of an equation? An equality.

  What lies at the heart of an equality? “={=}=”.

  Let us begin with the equals sign and enter Mímir’s well.

The Equals Sign

  First, we know that the following statements are true:

1=12=1+12×5−6=2×2\begin{aligned}1 &= 1 \\2 &= 1 + 1 \\2 \times 5 - 6 &= 2 \times 2\end{aligned}122×5−6​=1=1+1=2×2​

  Why are they true? Because Odin’s divine authority decrees it. We will have to wait until our audience with Odin to ask why he made that decree. For now, one thing is plain: we all know these statements are true.

  Yet the numbers on either side of these three equalities can be changed in infinitely many combinations. Our time is limited—the allure of video games is always in the air—so we need a way to describe numbers in general terms. This undertaking began as a search for substitutes for numbers, so we shall call it the “algebra project.”

  And so we obtain the following equalities, which are plainly also true:

x=x(a+b)x=ax+bx(a−b)x=ax−bx\begin{aligned}x &= x \\(a + b)x &= ax + bx \\(a - b)x &= ax - bx\end{aligned}x(a+b)x(a−b)x​=x=ax+bx=ax−bx​

  (Odin, speaking from behind the scenes: In fact, this is because (R−{0},+,⋅)(R - \{0\}, +, \cdot)(R−{0},+,⋅) is a commutative ring. Never mind my circular definition.)

  For the real numbers and the four basic arithmetic operations we are using, these equalities follow from those operations and several laws known as the “Thrud-commutative law,” the “Hildr-associative law,” and the “Olrun-distributive law.” Heimdall is the one who teaches you the rules for using these operations and laws.

  What? You have forgotten who Heimdall is? Do not forget that he plays the role of “elementary algebra” in this article!

  (Heimdall: That hurts my feelings. Sob, sob.)

  Because you forgot him, Heimdall now wants revenge. Asgard is a civilized realm, however, so his revenge is civilized too: Heimdall gives you several problems. If you cannot solve them, you will never reach Asgard for as long as you live.

  Heimdall’s question 1: Prove that (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2.

  Far too easy. With help from the Valkyries, you quickly solve the problem.

(a+b)2=(a+b)(a+b)=a(a+b)+b(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+ab+ab+b2=a2+2ab+b2.\begin{aligned}(a + b)^2 &= (a + b)(a + b) \\&= a(a + b) + b(a + b) \\&= a^2 + ab + ba + b^2 \\&= a^2 + ab + ab + b^2 \\&= a^2 + 2ab + b^2.\end{aligned}(a+b)2​=(a+b)(a+b)=a(a+b)+b(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+ab+ab+b2=a2+2ab+b2.​

  Heimdall refuses to concede and sets you another problem.

  Heimdall’s question 2: Prove that (a+b+e)2=a2+b2+e2+2ab+2be+2ca(a + b + e)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + e^2 + 2ab + 2be + 2ca(a+b+e)2=a2+b2+e2+2ab+2be+2ca.

  This problem is more complicated than the last because it has one more quantity, but with the Valkyries’ assistance, you still work it out.

The result follows at once and is plainly trivial; imitate the previous example. Left as an exercise, answer omitted; the proof is not difficult.
The converse is likewise identical, and the corollary follows naturally. The steps are omitted. QED. Hence proved.

  Just as Heimdall is reluctantly about to let you pass, you cannot resist asking, “Who are these three goddesses beside me who have been calling themselves Valkyries and helping me all this time?”

  The three Valkyries—the “Thrud-commutative law,” the “Hildr-associative law,” and the “Olrun-distributive law”—are most displeased that you have never read any Norse mythology (mathematics). So they detain you. While you are wondering how to escape, Heimdall offers a helping hand.

  There is, of course, no such thing as a free lunch. You must help Heimdall solve his problem first.

  Heimdall’s question 3: Prove that (∑i=1nai)2=∑i=1nai2+2∑1≤i<j≤naiaj.\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j.(∑i=1n​ai​)2=∑i=1n​ai2​+2∑1≤i<j≤n​ai​aj​.

  You now have two choices: admit that you do not know what ∑\sum∑ means, or prove the result.

  Then you suddenly remember:

∑i=1nai=a1+a2+Λ+an.∑1≤i<j≤naiaj=a1a2+a1a3+Λ+a1an+a2a3+a2a4+Λ+a2an+Λ+an−1an.\begin{aligned}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i &= a_1 + a_2 + \Lambda + a_n. \\[0.9em]\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j &= a_1 a_2 + a_1 a_3 + \Lambda + a_1 a_n \\[0.9em]&+ a_2 a_3 + a_2 a_4 + \Lambda + a_2 a_n \\[0.9em]&+ \Lambda \\[0.9em]&+ a_{n-1} a_n.\end{aligned}i=1∑n​ai​1≤i<j≤n∑​ai​aj​​=a1​+a2​+Λ+an​.=a1​a2​+a1​a3​+Λ+a1​an​+a2​a3​+a2​a4​+Λ+a2​an​+Λ+an−1​an​.​

  Now only the second path remains. But how should you handle the expansion of a squared sum with nnn terms?

  You suddenly remember (again): mathematical induction.

    Prove that the proposition holds when n=1n = 1n=1;

    assume it holds when n=mn = mn=m, and then show that it also holds when n=m+1n = m + 1n=m+1.

    The equality clearly holds for n=1,2,3n = 1,2,3n=1,2,3, so:

    Assume the proposition holds when n=mn = mn=m. When n=m+1n = m + 1n=m+1:

(∑i=1m+1ai)2=(∑i=1mai+am+1)2=(∑i=1mai)2+2∑i=1maiam+1+am+12=∑i=1mai2+2∑1≤i<j≤maiaj+2∑i=1maiam+1+am+12=∑i=1m+1ai2+2∑1≤i<j≤m+1aiaj.\begin{aligned}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m+1} a_i\right)^2 &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i + a_{m+1}\right)^2 \\[0.9em]&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\right)^2 + 2 \sum_{i=1}^m a_i a_{m+1} + a_{m+1}^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{i=1}^m a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le m} a_i a_j + 2 \sum_{i=1}^m a_i a_{m+1} + a_{m+1}^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{i=1}^{m+1} a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le m+1} a_i a_j.\end{aligned}(i=1∑m+1​ai​)2​=(i=1∑m​ai​+am+1​)2=(i=1∑m​ai​)2+2i=1∑m​ai​am+1​+am+12​=i=1∑m​ai2​+21≤i<j≤m∑​ai​aj​+2i=1∑m​ai​am+1​+am+12​=i=1∑m+1​ai2​+21≤i<j≤m+1∑​ai​aj​.​

  Heimdall is pleased, but this is not enough:

  Heimdall’s question 4: Prove that ∑1≤i<j≤n(ai−aj)2=n∑i=1nai2−(∑i=1nai)2.\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} (a_i - a_j)^2 = n \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2.∑1≤i<j≤n​(ai​−aj​)2=n∑i=1n​ai2​−(∑i=1n​ai​)2.

  In this equality, we need to count how many times each aaa occurs, so you search your memory once more.

  You suddenly remember (for the third time—the protagonist’s plot armor is getting rather strong): the Fubini principle.

  Also called double counting, it proves an equality by observing that two different methods of counting the same quantity must give the same result. The principle extends to the evaluation of multiple integrals, though it can also be confined to applications in combinatorics.

  Clearly, for a2a^2a2, the cases j=2,3,Λ,nj = 2,3,\Lambda,nj=2,3,Λ,n make it appear a total of n−1n - 1n−1 times;

  For aaa, the cases j=3,4,Λ,nj = 3,4,\Lambda,nj=3,4,Λ,n make it appear a total of n−2n - 2n−2 times, but when i=1i = 1i=1, there is also the case j=2j = 2j=2. Including that occurrence gives n−1n-1n−1 in all;

  similarly, every aia_iai​ occurs n−1n-1n−1 times. You therefore obtain:

∑1≤i<j≤n(ai−aj)2=(n−1)∑i=1nai2−2∑1≤i<j≤naiaj=n∑i=1nai2−(∑i=1nai)2.\begin{aligned}\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} (a_i - a_j)^2 &= (n-1) \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j \\[0.9em]&= n \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2.\end{aligned}1≤i<j≤n∑​(ai​−aj​)2​=(n−1)i=1∑n​ai2​−21≤i<j≤n∑​ai​aj​=ni=1∑n​ai2​−(i=1∑n​ai​)2.​

  This technique of proving an equality by counting how often terms occur is extremely convenient, so you glide effortlessly through the next problem:

  Heimdall’s question 5: Prove that (∑i=1nai)(∑j=1nbj)=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj+ajbi).\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\right) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (a_i b_j + a_j b_i).(∑i=1n​ai​)(∑j=1n​bj​)=21​∑i=1n​∑j=1n​(ai​bj​+aj​bi​).

  Observe that, for a fixed aia_iai​, every bjb_jbj​ will occur nnn times; the same conclusion holds for a fixed bjb_jbj​. Therefore:

(∑i=1nai)(∑j=1nbj)=∑i=1n∑j=1naibj=∑i=1n∑j=1najbi=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj+ajbi).\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_i b_j = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_j b_i = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (a_i b_j + a_j b_i).(i=1∑n​ai​)(j=1∑n​bj​)=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai​bj​=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​aj​bi​=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai​bj​+aj​bi​).

  As the saying goes, three strikes and that is enough. No one knows whether Asgard has the same proverb, but Qin Shi Huang’s planet-destroying warship technology was so advanced that perhaps it carried the saying from China’s anomalous zone all the way to Northern Europe. Heimdall agrees to rescue you.

  The moment you step out of the cell, however, you encounter the three Valkyries.

  Oh no—the Three Pillars.

  Rather than break his oath, Heimdall goes to war with the Valkyries. According to Lu Xun’s classic “the North always wins a civil war” theory (Lu Xun: I never said that), Heimdall, who serves the Northern Empire, ultimately prevails. (That is a story from another world—perhaps one found in a certain Tencent game.) There are plenty of examples supporting the theory, such as the American Civil War.

  The Valkyries agree to let Heimdall take you away, but, as ever, only if you solve one more problem:

  Valkyrie’s question: Prove that (∑i=1nai2)(∑i=1nbi2)≥(∑i=1naibi)2\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^2 \right) \ge \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \right)^2(∑i=1n​ai2​)(∑i=1n​bi2​)≥(∑i=1n​ai​bi​)2

  You know this one! Is that not Cauchy’s Wash-Socks—the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality?

  Wait. An inequality? Weren’t we supposed to be discussing equalities? How did inequalities enter the picture?

  (Odin, speaking from behind the scenes: Inequalities arise from equalities.)

  Oh, right. From equalities.

  Odin has inspired you. Clever as you are, you give it some thought.

  You suddenly remember (for the fourth time) Lagrange’s identity. Thanks to your earlier practice answering Heimdall’s questions, you quickly obtain:

(∑i=1nai2)(∑i=1nbi2)−(∑i=1naibi)2=∑i=1n∑j=1nai2bj2−∑i=1n∑j=1naibiajbj=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(ai2bj2+aj2bi2−2aibiajbj)=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj−ajbi)2=∑1≤i<j≤n(aibj−ajbi)2≥0.\begin{aligned}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^2 \right) - \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \right)^2&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_i^2 b_j^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_i b_i a_j b_j \\[0.9em]&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left( a_i^2 b_j^2 + a_j^2 b_i^2 - 2a_i b_i a_j b_j \right) \\[0.9em]&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left( a_i b_j - a_j b_i \right)^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \left( a_i b_j - a_j b_i \right)^2 \ge 0.\end{aligned}(i=1∑n​ai2​)(i=1∑n​bi2​)−(i=1∑n​ai​bi​)2​=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai2​bj2​−i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai​bi​aj​bj​=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai2​bj2​+aj2​bi2​−2ai​bi​aj​bj​)=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai​bj​−aj​bi​)2=1≤i<j≤n∑​(ai​bj​−aj​bi​)2≥0.​

  Remove the final “greater than or equal to zero,” and what remains is the proof of Lagrange’s identity. This fully demonstrates that inequalities, too, arise from equalities.

  There is likewise a way to prove the mean inequalities using an equality-based structure. The method is too involved to include in this popular-science article, however, so I will merely note that the proof can be found in Chen Ji’s Algebraic Inequalities.

  To keep you from being detained again, Heimdall also tells you a few stories from Norse mythology (mathematics):

  Abel transformation:

∑k=mnfk(gk+1−gk)=[fn+1gn+1−fmgm]−∑k=mngk+1(fk+1−fk)\sum_{k=m}^{n} f_k \left( g_{k+1} - g_k \right) = \left[ f_{n+1} g_{n+1} - f_m g_m \right] - \sum_{k=m}^{n} g_{k+1} \left( f_{k+1} - f_k \right)k=m∑n​fk​(gk+1​−gk​)=[fn+1​gn+1​−fm​gm​]−k=m∑n​gk+1​(fk+1​−fk​)

  where {fk}\{f_k\}{fk​} and {gk}\{g_k\}{gk​} are any two sequences.

  Schur’s inequality:

a,b,c>0, r∈R  ⟹  ar(a−b)(a−c)+br(b−c)(b−a)+cr(c−a)(c−b)≥0a,b,c>0,\ r\in\mathbb{R} \implies a^r(a-b)(a-c) + b^r(b-c)(b-a) + c^r(c-a)(c-b) \ge 0a,b,c>0, r∈R⟹ar(a−b)(a−c)+br(b−c)(b−a)+cr(c−a)(c−b)≥0

  This, too, is proved with an equality. The proof is left to the reader and is not difficult.

  At last, Heimdall leads you across Bifrost, the rainbow bridge. You have finally taken your first step toward an audience with Odin. Little do you know that Thor, Sif, and the trickster god Loki await you ahead…

entry.title: Sapiens: The Cognitive Revolution
entry.content:
Author: 自控力
Reviewer: Nancy

  The familiar “march of human evolution” is misleading. Human evolution was not the straight, single-track road shown in that image, but a flourishing tree with many branches. More than fifteen known species once belonged to the genus Homo. Neanderthals, Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis, and others shared the Earth with our ancestors, Homo sapiens, for long stretches of time.

  Where, then, did this deeply misleading linear image come from? It first appeared in the popular-science book Early Man, published in 1965. The book originally featured an elegant, elongated foldout showing hominins at different stages. Because the original illustration was so long, later layouts compressed and folded it to save space. The figures consequently looked as though they were walking forward in a line, eventually producing the linear version we know today.

  In the struggle for survival on the ancient Earth, Homo sapiens was not as strong as the Neanderthals, nor were we the most agile. Why, over the long course of time, did all our other “brothers and sisters” become extinct, while only we

  Researchers studying human origins generally hold that modern Homo sapiens arose in sub-Saharan Africa, centered on the East African Rift, where our ancestors gradually emerged several million years ago. Some fossils, however, suggest that members of the genus Homo may also have lived in other parts of the world during the same period. This evidence has led to two main theoretical frameworks in academia: the Out-of-Africa hypothesis and the multiregional hypothesis.

  Early human groups were not greatly different from one another. Many left Africa and evolved separately in different regions, gradually becoming distinct archaic human populations. The process resembles the way the cat family branched into lions, tigers, leopards, and other very different animals. Among the human species that evolved early were the robust Neanderthals and the diminutive Homo floresiensis. All of them had learned to think, but the expansion of the brain imposed a heavy cost on early humans.

  A mammal weighing about 60 kilograms generally has a brain volume of roughly 200 cubic centimeters, whereas early humans such as Homo habilis already had brains of about 600 cubic centimeters. It was as though they had installed an extra, highly efficient CPU. Humans then relied on their exceptional intelligence and struggled onward for tens of thousands of years, until at last—nothing happened. In the beginning, a more capable brain brought no obvious benefits. Instead, it made human life even harder.

  In other apes, the brain generally accounts for only 8 percent of total energy consumption. In humans of the same period, it consumed a full 25 percent. Ancient humans had only a limited amount of food each day, so where could they find the energy to cover this much larger bill? They reduced investment in physical strength and put all their skill points into intelligence. It was rather like a country at war diverting a large share of its budget into education.

  The enhanced brain was not entirely useless, however. Early on, it supplied two crucial abilities that kept ancient humans alive until the brain’s real advantages could emerge: comparatively efficient social organization and the ability to use tools. In the wartime-country analogy, education produced capable military personnel and scientists who could design weapons.

  Homo sapiens was not the only species to develop social organization and tools. On the contrary, many human species that appeared before us had already acquired both. Why, then, did only Homo sapiens reach the brain’s tipping point? Many social animals have organized groups, including wolves and lions. Ants, bees, and similar animals have even evolved what is known as “eusociality.” Primates such as chimpanzees also crack nuts with stones and extract termites with twigs. The brain merely strengthened these two human abilities.

  For two million years of human evolution, however, all this did little more than keep our populations from dying out. Around 800,000 years ago, humans learned to use fire. Cooked food then pushed brain evolution further. By roughly 400,000 years ago, some archaic humans could hunt large animals with reasonable consistency.

  Before our own ancestors appeared, other human species had already mastered the skills needed to survive and occupied habitable places across the Earth. It was like standing idle at the spawn point while everyone else had already bought their equipment and taken over every part of the jungle. Only about 300,000 years ago did our ancestors, Homo sapiens, emerge in Africa, the cradle of humankind. In appearance, these early sapiens were already much like people today.

  Early Homo sapiens quickly learned the survival skills possessed by other human species, but this was not enough to compete with them. In Harari’s account, a revolution 70,000 years ago set every later change in motion. It enabled Homo sapiens to sweep across the globe, drive other human species to extinction, and reach places none of them had ever entered. That transformative event was the Cognitive Revolution.

  According to Harari’s hypothesis, the early Cognitive Revolution began when Homo sapiens learned to “tell tall tales.” That one ability propelled our species to the top of the food chain and consigned many other organisms, including other human species, to the evolutionary dustbin.

  The development of the human Cognitive Revolution is generally thought to have appeared first in language. One explanation is the lion theory. In the same situation, human language can convey far more information. A vervet monkey may scream to warn its companions of a lion, prompting them to flee into the trees, but the warning is indiscriminate: the others do not know where the lion is or how many lions there are. The language used by early Homo sapiens as they left Africa and spread across the world was more complex and carried more information. Someone who spotted a lion could tell others where it was, what it was doing, and how many there were, allowing the group to decide whether to stalk and kill it or run away.

  Another explanation is the gossip theory. Once humans acquired language, they could evaluate other members of their group and quietly discuss their strengths and faults. That may seem pointless today, or even harmful to a tribe’s survival, but gossip still has benefits. It tells us who is reliable, who is clever, and who excels at hunting or making stone spears. This information makes the whole group more effective because it is difficult to get to know everyone individually. Gossip lets us learn about other members of the group more easily and cooperate with them. In a school relay, for example, hearing that one of our runners is the fastest sprinter in the school would reassure us. We may never have seen that person run, but gossip can still give us useful information.

  Whether the lion theory, the gossip theory, or some combination of the two is correct, the feature of language that ultimately carried the Cognitive Revolution forward was our ability to “tell tall tales.” This means confidently describing through language something that does not exist or could not happen. Humans thereby became animals capable of inventing things absent from reality. We might solemnly tell the rest of the tribe that a mountain is alive and embodies a spirit, and that without worshipping it we will catch no prey, find no edible fruit, and locate no suitable stone for tools.

  This ability to tell tall tales is, of course, the expression of imagination through language. We do not know whether our Homo sapiens ancestors first evolved language and then imagination, or first developed imagination and then learned to express it in words. What we do know is that once Homo sapiens could imagine, shared fictions such as a sacred mountain allowed cooperation on a much larger scale. Gossip alone can sustain groups of no more than 150 people, while wild chimpanzee communities generally contain only about 20 to 50 individuals.

Mount Kailash in Tibet, whose Tibetan name means "mountain of the gods"

  If neighboring groups shared a belief in the same sacred mountain, however, they could work together to maintain a hunting ground and drive away other tribes that entered it. With this stronger capacity for cooperation and imagination, Homo sapiens swept across the world like a flood 70,000 years ago and became its most powerful organism. So what happened to our other brothers and sisters? Genetic research now shows that it was not simply a massacre. Although most other human species became extinct, migrating Homo sapiens also had intimate encounters with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Most people alive today still carry a small amount of the blood of those brothers and sisters who disappeared tens of thousands of years ago. Homo sapiens did not replace them completely. We carried their traces with us as our species alone accelerated down evolution’s fast track.

entry.title: How Does Plasma Differ from Ordinary Solids, Liquids, and Gases?
entry.content:
Author: 阿白特尔
Reviewed by: 一毫秒的永恒

  When we think of states of matter, the first three that probably come to mind are solids, liquids, and gases. In a solid, particles are confined near fixed positions, where they vibrate randomly. The material therefore has a fixed volume and shape as a whole. As the kinetic energy of the particles’ random thermal motion increases, a point eventually comes when they break free from those fixed positions and begin to flow. The particles no longer occupy fixed locations, but attraction from their neighbors still prevents them from escaping the group. At the macroscopic scale, the material has a relatively fixed volume but no fixed shape: the familiar liquid state. Raise the temperature further and the particles’ thermal motion grows so intense that they almost completely overcome their mutual attraction and disperse freely. Matter with neither a fixed volume nor a fixed shape is called a gas. The essential distinction among solids, liquids, and gases, then, lies in the increasing extent to which thermal motion overcomes—or disrupts—interactions among particles.

  Once we know these three forms of matter, it is natural to ask whether there might be others. What happens if we raise the temperature still further? A gas has already escaped almost all the interactions among the particles, such as molecules, that directly make up the material, so further heating can disrupt only stronger and tighter bonds. In a molecular gas, the added heat may first break covalent or coordinate bonds, causing the atoms or atomic groups within each molecule to separate and gradually turning the molecular gas into an atomic one. Continue heating, and even the sturdy atom can no longer hold together: electrons continually escape the attraction of the atomic nucleus and become free particles independent of the atom. A formerly neutral atom loses negative charge and becomes positively charged, turning into an ion. When the density of electrons and ions in the gas reaches a level at which their collective effects dominate its properties, a fourth state of matter—plasma—emerges.

  The process just described is one way to create plasma: thermal ionization. Heating intensifies the thermal motion of electrons until they escape their atoms. Plasma produced this way is often in thermal equilibrium, meaning that its electrons and ions have the same temperature. The plasma in the Sun and in nuclear-fusion reactors is produced by this process and is in thermal equilibrium. Plasma in lightning and fluorescent tubes, by contrast, forms through electrical discharge. During a discharge, electrons emitted from an electrode strike gas atoms and knock electrons out of them, producing electron–ion pairs. Unlike heating, a discharge injects kinetic energy only into the electrons, so the electron temperature in the resulting plasma is far higher than the ion temperature.

  Having described how plasma forms, let us examine two of its unusual collective effects, neither of which occurs in ordinary matter. The first is called plasma oscillation. Plasma consists of large numbers of positive and negative charges. Under Coulomb’s law, each charge is continually acted on by all the others: like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Because a plasma contains roughly equal amounts of positive and negative charge, however, its attractive and repulsive forces are approximately equal, leaving the particles in statistical equilibrium. Any equilibrium can be disturbed. If all charges of one kind in a plasma shift some distance from their equilibrium positions, that balance is broken.

  Imagine an electron–ion plasma in which some disturbance makes the electrons shift together to the right. Their “departure” leaves behind a region where the ion density exceeds the electron density, giving it a net positive charge. Because electrons are negative and opposite charges attract, the displaced electrons feel a backward force trying to pull them home. But the story does not end there. When the electrons return, the attractive force disappears, yet they have accelerated on the way and cannot “brake” at the equilibrium position. Inertia carries them past it, so they depart again in the opposite direction. Once more, the positive charge attracts and pulls them home. A cycle emerges: electrons depart → ions pull them back → electrons depart in the opposite direction → ions pull them back again. Over time, the electrons display a collective oscillation, which we call a plasma oscillation. An ion has nearly 2,000 times the mass of an electron, so under an equal reaction force its acceleration is far smaller. While the electrons oscillate, the ions remain almost where they began; before they have time to move, the electrons are already on the other side.

  Plasma oscillations have many applications. One—arising from the difference between plasma and ordinary solid, liquid, and gaseous states—is a sound explanation for disruptions to shortwave radio communications during solar storms. Every oscillator has a natural frequency, and plasma is no exception. The natural frequency of plasma oscillation increases with the density of positive and negative charges. We also know that when the frequency of an external force approaches an oscillator’s natural frequency, resonance occurs. The oscillator absorbs as much energy as possible from the force and reaches its greatest amplitude. The electromagnetic waves used in radio communication are, in essence, continuously varying electric and magnetic fields. Charged particles such as electrons experience a force in an electric field. An electromagnetic wave passing through plasma is therefore equivalent to applying a periodic external force to its electrons. When this force has a frequency far above the natural frequency of the plasma oscillation, the electrons’ motion and the changes in the force are badly out of step. The force does almost no work on the electrons, allowing the wave to cross the plasma with almost no loss and carry communications, as it ordinarily does on Earth.

  Once a solar storm erupts, however, large numbers of charged particles enter Earth’s atmosphere and increase the density of positive and negative charges. As noted above, the plasma’s natural oscillation frequency rises with that density. When it reaches roughly the frequency of the electromagnetic waves used for shortwave communication, resonance occurs and as much wave energy as possible is transferred to the plasma. The electromagnetic wave then struggles to propagate through the plasma, and communication is interrupted. Because high-voltage alternating-current transmission also operates through periodically changing electric fields, a solar storm can in some cases cause widespread power outages as well.

Diagram of a solar storm and Earth's magnetic field | Credit: SOHO (ESA & NASA)

  Debye shielding is another curious story about charge. We might call it the way a charge becomes “invisible” in a plasma. Picture a mass of electron–ion plasma, where disturbances occasionally produce plasma oscillations like waves rolling across an ocean. Now throw a positively charged sphere into that ocean, and it is quickly submerged. Something remarkable happens. The positive sphere attracts negative electrons and repels positive ions, so the electron density around it exceeds the ion density. From a distance, the sphere looks like a steamed bun wrapped in an electron “skin.” Because the surrounding shell of electrons is negatively charged, its effect cancels that of the positive sphere, and the bun as a whole has only a weak net electrical effect on its surroundings. A positively charged sphere went in, and its positive charge seems to vanish in the plasma. This is the plasma’s “invisibility trick” for charge: Debye shielding.

  These effects are only the tip of the iceberg. Keep exploring, and you will discover many more of plasma’s secrets and wonders.

entry.title: Understanding Plague
entry.content:
The immune system keeps pathogens from invading the body. Having previously examined how our defenses work, we will now look at how pathogens attack. Today’s subject is one of history’s most notorious diseases: plague. Its immense harm to humanity deserves our attention. Plague is also known as the “Black Death” because many people who died from the disease developed dark purple or black discoloration.

Author: 神州
Reviewers: 未名 and Thinker

Introduction

  Where there is attack, there must be defense. The body’s immune system exists to block invading pathogens. Here, we will take the opposite perspective and examine how those pathogens mount an attack.

  We begin with the agent behind one of history’s best-known diseases: plague. The devastation it has caused is reason enough to take it seriously. Plague is also called the “Black Death,” a name associated with the dark purple or black discoloration seen in many of its victims.

Yersinia pestis
Credit: Rocky Mountain Laboratories, NIAID, NIH

  Its principal reservoirs are rodents, including marmots—the animals often loosely called “groundhogs” in everyday Chinese.

The “screaming marmot” meme

  In China, marmots are found mainly on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, making these areas important natural plague foci. For a time, marmots became popular online, and their awkwardly cute appearance made many people eager to approach them. Most, however, did not recognize the risk of infectious disease.

  Some people assume that they are safe as long as a marmot does not bite them. That is not true. Plague is extremely dangerous and highly contagious. Its main route of transmission is not an attack by a rodent, but fleas moving from an infected rodent to a new host after feeding. Skinning and butchering rodents can also bring a person into direct contact with Yersinia pestis and cause infection. Humans generally have little resistance to plague, and the great majority of people invaded by the pathogen become ill.

  Symptoms differ according to the part of the body the bacterium infects. The main primary forms are bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic plague. Less common forms include ocular, cutaneous, and meningeal plague.

  After a person is bitten by an infected flea, the bacteria enter through the skin and travel through lymphatic vessels to nearby lymph nodes. They multiply there, causing inflammation and swelling: primary bubonic plague. Medical treatment should be sought immediately. If the infection is allowed to progress, the bacteria can enter the bloodstream and cause sepsis. Severe disease may produce extensive mucosal bleeding and tissue necrosis.

  Once the pathogen reaches the bloodstream and causes sepsis, the patient may develop chills, high fever, and altered consciousness. Without prompt care, a person with these symptoms can die from hemorrhage and tissue necrosis within two or three days. Intravascular clotting and gangrene of the extremities can leave the body dark purple or black—the origin of the name “Black Death.”

  Plague spreads from person to person mainly through respiratory droplets. Inhaling enough bacteria can produce disease in the lungs, most often primary pneumonic plague. Within one or two days of onset, the patient may develop severe chest pain, coughing, blood-streaked sputum, and difficulty breathing. Without timely treatment, respiratory or heart failure may prove fatal by the third day.

  Plague is therefore an exceptionally dangerous disease that demands strict precautions. Anyone with suspected or confirmed plague must seek medical care and be isolated promptly, both for their own sake and to prevent the disease’s high transmissibility from causing wider harm. Never assume that approaching a marmot is a risk worth taking.

  For all its dangers, plague is highly curable when treatment begins in time. Historically, its mortality was high because it develops rapidly and has a short incubation period, but modern health-care systems offer new hope. That short incubation period and its conspicuous symptoms also make large outbreaks less likely in modern society. Even so, everyone needs to remain alert to infectious disease and seek medical attention as soon as symptoms appear.

entry.title: The Solar System—Our Home and Our Origin
entry.content:
Author: Kon
Reviewed by: Xiao

  The Solar System that humanity inhabits contains planets, moons, comets, and other celestial bodies of every size. The Sun itself is a thoroughly ordinary member of the Milky Way’s “family of stars.” This raises two questions:

  1. Is our existence unique?
    In more specific astronomical terms: are planetary systems like the Solar System common throughout the universe?
  2. How did the Solar System on which we depend come into being?

  Before humanity could search for exoplanets on a large scale, it was difficult to answer either question satisfactorily. Without a substantial set of comparison samples, the Solar System itself was our only model for understanding planetary systems. The two questions are also linked to some extent: once the mechanism of planetary-system formation is established, it can in turn predict whether such systems should be common. Historically, several theories have sought to explain “planet formation”:

  The first theory holds that planet formation is connected to the formation of a planet’s host star. Soon after the star forms, a residual “disk of gas and dust” remains around it, and planets form within that disk. This theory naturally implies that planets are relatively common.

  Other theories argue that planet formation is unrelated to star formation and is instead triggered by separate events. The “tidal stripping hypothesis,” for example, proposes that when two stars pass close to one another, tidal forces “strip” some gas from a star and that planets then form from the stripped gas. Even in a region as densely populated with stars as the Milky Way, however, the number density of stars in space is remarkably low. The tidal stripping hypothesis therefore implies that planets are exceedingly rare.

  Even before the search for exoplanets began, most people nevertheless tended to believe that planetary systems like the Solar System were common. Modern science seems to favor making anything connected with humanity as unspecial as possible. The Copernican Revolution and the Curtis–Shapley debate both drove humanity away from the “most central and exceptional” position and into increasingly inconspicuous places. This, however, leads into questions in the philosophy of science that lie beyond the scope of this article.

  Thanks to the launch of the Kepler space telescope, exoplanets began to be detected in large numbers after 2010. By 2026, more than 6,000 exoplanets had been confirmed. Current observations show that even the stars in the Sun’s immediate neighborhood host so many planets. Extrapolating to the whole Milky Way, a space artist’s depiction of the “hot Jupiter” 51 Pegasi-b (left) and its host star 51 Pegasi (right)—the first “hot Jupiter” discovered in human history—the number of stars within it is on the order of hundreds of billions. Seen in that context, planets are naturally very common.

  As for the second question, the mainstream theory of planet formation holds that a newly formed star does not draw in all the gas and dust around it. The remaining material forms a “protoplanetary disk” around the star. Within that disk, planets grow through collisions, beginning as micrometer-sized grains and becoming kilometer-scale planetesimals. Because a protoplanetary disk extends across a large region, matter is distributed differently at different distances from the Sun. The “snow line” marks the boundary beyond which the disk is cool enough for water and other volatile substances to condense into ice. Inside the snow line, planetesimals consist mostly of rock; outside it, most are mixtures of rock and ice. Beyond the snow line, the gravitational feeding zone is larger and icy solids are more abundant, so the solid cores of planetesimals “grow” extremely quickly. Once they reach a certain mass, they can rapidly capture the gas left in the protoplanetary disk and eventually become enormous gas planets. Inside the snow line, planetesimals have smaller feeding zones and fewer icy solids, leaving them with less massive solid cores. They therefore struggle to accrete large quantities of gas and usually must wait until the gas in the protoplanetary disk has gradually dispersed before growing through collisions with other planetesimals. Their increase in mass is consequently very limited, and their atmospheres are also extremely thin.

  This conclusion was originally developed in an effort to “reconstruct” the Solar System’s present distribution of planets: small, low-mass solid planets dominate the inner region, while large, high-mass gaseous planets dominate the outer region. Since the first “hot Jupiter”—a Jupiter-mass gas giant orbiting very close to its host star—was discovered in 1995, however, many more hot Jupiters have been found. Their discovery has called the original theory of planet formation into question to some extent. The discovery of the Kuiper Belt also seems to suggest that the Solar System’s actual formation history was far more dramatic than we had thought.

  The image below illustrates the evolution of a star and its planetary system. Under gravity, diffuse gas in space collapses to form a star. The gas and dust left around the newly formed star create a “protoplanetary disk,” in which planets then form. Late in its evolution, the star returns some of its material to interstellar space. If that residual gas gathers together, it may form a new star.

Diagram of the evolution of a star and its planetary system

entry.title: How Does the Body Repair an Injury?
entry.content:
Author: 绿水青山
Reviewers: 食野; 未名

  Throughout our lives, we are inevitably affected by things in the surrounding environment. The body naturally responds by first trying to adapt. If a stimulus is too strong, however, the body may be injured. Today we will look at how the body repairs that damage.

  An injury is the destruction or loss of some of the body’s cells and tissues; repair is the process of mending and restoring what is missing. Repair generally takes one of two forms: regeneration or fibrous repair. In regeneration, cells of the same type divide at the injured site and restore the tissue’s original function. This form of repair is usually more complete and can restore all function. Fibrous repair uses fibrous connective tissue. It produces a scar and does not completely restore function.

  The body’s regenerative capacity has several general characteristics. Tissues that are frequently injured or continually renewed regenerate more readily than other tissues, and less differentiated cells regenerate more readily than highly differentiated ones. Regenerative capacity also varies with an organism’s evolutionary path and species. Salamanders, geckos, many plants, and other organisms have especially strong regenerative abilities.

  Tissue regeneration can be broadly divided into complete and incomplete regeneration. In complete regeneration, the repaired tissue functions much as it did before. In incomplete regeneration, fibrous connective tissue replaces the original tissue. The cells used for repair differ from those in the original tissue, some function is lost, and a scar forms.

  Different tissues and different parts of the body generally regenerate in different ways after injury. Let us consider several examples.

Epithelial tissue

  The cells in epithelial tissue are labile cells. Because they divide frequently, they have a strong capacity for regeneration. Their ability to regenerate also depends on surrounding connective tissue and other factors. If the connective tissue remains intact, complete regeneration is likely and the original function can be restored relatively well. If that connective tissue is destroyed and can no longer provide its supporting framework, the body instead undertakes fibrous repair. Fibrous repair is often incomplete and cannot restore the original function.

Fibroblasts

  Connective tissue repair relies mainly on fibroblasts. When tissue is injured, these cells are activated and increase in number. They begin producing large amounts of collagen and other “supporting materials,” gradually filling the damaged area. The newly formed structures then stabilize, cellular activity declines, and relatively dense fibrous tissue develops to complete the repair.

Blood vessels

  Blood-vessel regeneration can be divided into the regeneration of small and large vessels. Small vessels such as capillaries generally regenerate by sprouting and joining surrounding vessels to form a network, and the repair is usually complete. Large vessels have more difficulty regenerating completely. Severe damage may require surgical suturing before their function can be restored.

  Now that we have a general picture of how several tissues regenerate, let us examine what happens after an ordinary injury, using a common wound as an example.

  Immediately after tissue is damaged, severed blood vessels bleed. The blood mixes with exudate and detached epithelial cells around the wound and coagulates into a scab. The scab adheres to the wound surface, so forcibly tearing it off may enlarge the wound, expose it to the air again, and increase the risk of infection.

  Granulation tissue then begins to fill and surround the wound. This tissue is rich in newly formed capillaries and immune cells, which help remove pathogens and suppress infection. Because granulation tissue contains so many capillaries, the wound bleeds very easily at this stage.

  In the next stage, fibroblasts inside the wound begin forming scar tissue, which contracts and reduces the wound. Finally, epithelial cells cover the tissue again, completing the repair process.

entry.title: Mars One, Ready for Launch!
entry.content:
Author: 白書
Reviewers: 蜗牛; 一毫秒的永恒
Note: “Mars One” was later officially renamed “Tianwen-1.” It successfully completed the three major stages of Mars exploration: orbiting, landing, and roving.

  On October 11, 019, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation published photographs of the physical spacecraft for China’s second Mars probe on its official Weibo account. It was the first time the public had seen the probe in its finished form; the mission was scheduled for launch the following year.

“Mars One” | Credit: China National Space Administration

  According to Ye Peijian, chief scientist for space science and deep-space exploration at the China Academy of Space Technology, a subsidiary of the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, preparations for China’s Mars mission were complete and the launch was planned for 2020. The probe was provisionally named “Mars One” (and was later officially renamed “Tianwen-1”). The mission would carry an orbiter, a lander, and a rover, completing three stages at Mars: orbiting, landing, and roving. First, it would conduct global observations of the entire planet; second, it would land on Mars; and third, the rover would deploy and survey the surface. Under the plan, Tianwen-1 would travel to Mars aboard a Long March 5 launch vehicle in July 2020 and land near the Martian equator before the centenary of the founding of the Communist Party of China in July 2021.

  The latest progress in China’s Mars program was exciting, but the country had already attempted one unsuccessful Mars mission: Yinghuo-1. Here, we look back at the probe’s ill-fated life.

  Yinghuo-1 measured about 75 centimeters in both length and width and 60 centimeters in height. Its two deployed solar panels spanned approximately 7.85 meters. The probe had a mass of 110 kilograms, a designed operating life of two years, an average power output of 90 W, and a data-transmission rate of 8,192 bit/s. It carried four types of payload: a plasma-detection package, an optical imager, a fluxgate magnetometer, and a radio-occultation receiver. It was intended to spend one year observing Mars from orbit. Its objectives included studying the planet’s magnetic field, ionosphere, particle distributions, and the ways they change; measuring the escape rate of ions from the Martian atmosphere; surveying Martian terrain, landforms, and dust storms; and investigating the gravitational field around the Martian equator.

  Yinghuo-1 was originally scheduled to launch with Russia’s Phobos-Grunt spacecraft aboard a Zenit-2SB launch vehicle from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan in October 2009. On September 29, 2009, however, Russia postponed the launch until October 2011 to further ensure the project’s reliability.

  On November 9, 2011, Yinghuo-1 launched together with Russia’s Phobos-Grunt probe and soon entered Earth orbit successfully. Three engine burns were then supposed to send the two probes onto a Mars-bound trajectory. The entire journey was expected to take about 300 days.

  After launch, Yinghuo-1 remained mounted on Phobos-Grunt, and the two were to enter Mars orbit as a combined spacecraft. Yinghuo-1, installed atop Phobos-Grunt, would separate after three orbits of Mars. Phobos-Grunt would transfer into a circular Martian orbit, wait for an opportunity to land on Phobos, collect soil samples, and return them to Earth. Yinghuo-1, meanwhile, would carry out its Mars mission in a highly elliptical orbit with a periapsis of 800 kilometers, an apoapsis of 80,000 kilometers, and an inclination of less than 5°.

Yinghuo-1

  The day after launch, however, Vladimir Popovkin, head of the Russian Federal Space Agency, announced that Phobos-Grunt had failed to change orbit as planned. “It has been a very difficult night,” he said. “For a long time we could not locate the spacecraft. We eventually established its position and found that its propulsion system had not operated; both engine burns had failed.” This also meant that China’s first Mars-probe mission had ended in failure.

  On January 15, 2012, Alexei Zolotukhin, a spokesperson for the Aerospace Defense Forces of the Russian Ministry of Defense, told the media that debris from Phobos-Grunt would fall into the Pacific Ocean at around 21:45 Moscow time (01:45 Beijing time on January 16). According to information from the Space Surveillance Center of the Aerospace Defense Forces’ Space Command, the unburned debris—about 200 kilograms—ultimately fell into the Pacific Ocean 1,250 kilometers west of Wellington Island, an island in southern Chile.

  The Yinghuo-1 mission had long since ended, but new explorers were ready to depart.
