entry.title: Did You Know? Even Moderate Drinking Can Be Comparable to Smoking
entry.content:
Author: 一毫秒的永恒

  A British study found that the additional cancer risk associated with drinking one bottle of wine per week was roughly equivalent to smoking 5 cigarettes per week for men and 10 for women. The study used data from nonsmokers and converted the risks through an epidemiological model.

  Published in the British journal BMC Public Health on March 28, 2019, it was one of the first studies to estimate the relationship between alcohol and cigarettes in terms of cancer risk.

Credit: Shutterstock

  The study aimed to communicate the cancer risks of moderate drinking more effectively. Moderate alcohol consumption is widely believed to be less harmful than smoking, but research in the United States and the United Kingdom has found that many people are unaware of the relationship between alcohol and cancer. A 2017 survey by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, for example, found that roughly 70% of Americans did not know that drinking alcohol was a carcinogenic risk factor.

  “We estimated the number of cigarettes that would carry the same cancer risk as a bottle of wine,” said Dr. Theresa Hydes of gastroenterology and hepatology at University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, the study’s lead author. “This lets us communicate the potential cancer risk of drinking more intuitively by drawing on what people already know about the harms of smoking. By using cigarettes as a comparison, we hope to help people make better-informed lifestyle choices.” The comparison is an inventive and useful way to help people see the carcinogenic risk of alcohol more accurately.

  It is important to note, however, that the study did not claim that the carcinogenic risk of moderate drinking was identical to that of smoking. It considered only the cancer risk of drinking and did not account for effects on other health conditions. It also assessed the lifetime cancer risk of the general population, which may differ from the cancer risk faced by an individual who smokes or drinks.

Alcohol and Cigarettes

  The study set out to answer a question: in terms of cancer risk, how many cigarettes are equivalent to drinking one bottle of wine, containing approximately 80 grams of pure alcohol? Using data on cancer risk in the general British population and previously published research on the relationships among alcohol, smoking, and cancer, the researchers estimated that among nonsmokers, drinking one bottle of wine per week increased men’s lifetime cancer risk by 1.0% and women’s by 1.4%. Put differently, if 1,000 men and 1,000 women each drank a bottle of wine every week, about 10 of the men and 14 of the women might develop cancer because of their drinking later in life. The higher risk among women was mainly due to the close association between alcohol consumption and breast cancer. The effect was equivalent to smoking 5 cigarettes per week for men and 10 for women.

A “Carcinogen We All Know”

  “Most people know that cigarettes cause cancer,” Seitz said. “It is useful for the public to hear that a certain amount of alcohol carries the same cancer risk as a certain number of cigarettes.” He also observed that although alcohol is a known carcinogen, the cancer risks associated with it are rarely discussed. Some dietary guidelines even recommend a daily amount of alcoholic drinks. “If I did not call it alcohol, wine, beer, or cocktails and simply called it a carcinogen,” Seitz said, “no one would ask how many glasses of carcinogen you plan to drink.”

  The researchers also noted that because the study considered only cancer risk, it did not account for other illnesses associated with smoking or drinking, such as respiratory, cardiovascular, or liver disease.

  Although 5 to 10 cigarettes per week may not sound like many, smokers typically consume far more. British smokers, for example, average about 80 cigarettes per week, while smokers in the United States consume about 100 per person each week. Nevertheless, the researchers emphasized that “these findings show that the health risks of moderate drinking are an important public-health issue.”

Reference

  1. https://www.livescience.com/65092-alcohol-cigarettes-cancer-risk.html

entry.title: Earth's Spring Equinox Seen from Space
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

At Earth's spring equinox, the illuminated and dark hemispheres are almost equal in area. | Credit: NOAA; NOAA Environmental Visualization Laboratory

  On March 20, 2019, a GOES satellite photographed Earth at the spring equinox. In the image, half the planet is illuminated while the other half lies in darkness, like a black-and-white cookie.

  This beautiful symmetry will not surprise anyone familiar with astronomy and geography. A real photograph—especially an astronomical one—can nevertheless be more powerful than the theories we learn, inspiring wonder at the universe’s extraordinary beauty. In Latin, “equinox” means “equal night.” Geography teachers tell us that the spring and autumn equinoxes occur in March and September each year, when day and night are nearly equal in length at every latitude.

  Earth’s rotation axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane. The subsolar point moves between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, so sunlight is usually distributed unevenly across Earth. Depending on Earth’s position in its orbit around the Sun, day and night are generally unequal in length in either the Northern or Southern Hemisphere.

  “At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres receive essentially the same amount of daylight,” said C. Alex Young, associate director for science in the Heliophysics Science Division at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. In other words, at noon on an equinox, the Sun is directly above the equator.

  The 2019 spring equinox occurred at 5:58 a.m. Beijing time on March 21, marking the first astronomical day of spring in the Northern Hemisphere. The image above was taken by the GOES-East satellite at 8:00 p.m. Beijing time on March 20, 2019.

  The GOES series—the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite system—is a network of Earth-observation satellites operated by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). One satellite is positioned at 75° west longitude and another at 135° west—hence the names GOES-East and GOES-West. Together they cover roughly one-third of the globe and provide continuous meteorological observations of the Western Hemisphere 24 hours a day.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/65057-spring-equinox-from-space.html

entry.title: Suicide—the Only Serious Philosophical Problem
entry.content:
Author: Guanfu · Juntian

  At the opening of The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus declares that suicide is the only serious philosophical problem, because judging whether life is worth living is itself an answer to a philosophical question. This shows that Camus’s philosophy centers on individual life rather than merely discussing the external world.

  A clarification is necessary here: when Camus says that “suicide is the only serious philosophical problem,” he is absolutely not encouraging anyone to take their own life. He once wrote: “The absence of hope is not the same as despair; lucidity does not lead to submission. A person should recognize that life is their only wealth: it must inevitably pass away, yet it can also be developed to the fullest possible extent. A person should, and can, find the courage to live in this world—even happiness.” Camus offered these words to people who were considering giving up their lives. He raised the question of suicide to make people think about the meaning of life and about how to face the absurd—the world’s impenetrability and strangeness.

  The subtitle of The Myth of Sisyphus is “An Essay on the Absurd.” What, then, is the absurd?

  In the second chapter of The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus calls the absurd “a wall.” He writes: “Rising, streetcar, four hours in the office or the factory, meal, streetcar, four hours of work, meal, sleep; Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, according to the same rhythm—this path is easily followed most of the time. But one day the ‘why’ arises, and everything begins in that weariness tinged with amazement.”

  “Why?” I believe many people have asked themselves that question. The absurd often lies in the conflict between the human desire for meaning and the world’s inability to satisfy it. A person who can still ask “why” has encountered the absurd, but has also opened a door through which to resist it.

  Unfortunately, more of the people around us usually do not ask “why.” The Stranger begins with a famous line: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday.” Many people spend their whole lives as outsiders to everything they do, including their own lives.

  I often hear people around me say that even a wretched life is better than a good death. Camus would answer that even while living wretchedly, a person will still ask questions. The question no one can escape is: Why am I alive? “The world’s impenetrability and strangeness—this is the absurd.”

Three Possible Responses to the Absurd

  Camus believes that a person facing the absurd has three possible responses:

  The first is straightforward: suicide, bringing one’s life to an end. If someone believes that their life has no meaning or value, they can choose suicide. In Camus’s view, however, suicide does not resolve the absurd. It makes the person disappear and thereby evades the problem. This is the way of a coward, not an act of genuine revolt.

  The second is to seek a transcendent world in religion. For Camus, responding to the absurd with a transcendent explanation means abandoning the courage to confront it; this is “philosophical suicide.” He regards this approach as another form of self-destruction. Overcoming the absurd through religion is not a viable course.

  The third possibility is to accept the absurd. For Camus, this is the only authentic and effective solution. Here, “acceptance” does not mean passive submission. It means embracing the absurd with open eyes and creating one’s own meaning and value within meaninglessness. Camus wrote: “There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.” This maxim captures the heart of Sisyphus’s attitude: even if fate is fixed, a person can still rise above it through their stance toward it. As Sisyphus walks back down the mountain, he knows that the stone will roll down again, yet he still chooses to climb once more. It is precisely where resistance appears impossible that a person can still resist. Put another way, Sisyphus’s actions embody humanity’s ultimate revolt against fate.

entry.title: Meet the Particle Family
entry.content:
Author: 一毫秒的永恒

  Physics is full of particles such as neutrons and photons, but it also contains particles stranger than most people imagine. They have different properties and sizes, and many bear evocative names, from supersymmetric particles to the “God particle.” Today, let us meet some of the coolest members of this almost indescribable family.

Higgs Boson

  The Higgs boson is enormously important to physics. Often nicknamed the “God particle,” it is associated with the origin of mass for many elementary particles. In 1964, physicists were trying to understand why some particles were more massive than others and where that mass came from. Peter Higgs proposed what became known as the Higgs mechanism. The Higgs boson is associated with the Higgs field, which the mechanism assumes permeates the universe. Together, the field and its boson are thought to account for the masses of many fundamental particles. Scientists hoped the mechanism would solve this puzzle and complete the Standard Model, our existing description of known particles. In 2012, experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) confirmed the discovery of a particle whose properties were consistent with those of the Higgs boson, providing crucial support for the Standard Model. The LHC continues to collect data so that researchers can investigate the Higgs field and Higgs boson in greater detail.

A visualization reconstructing particle tracks after a collision at the Large Hadron Collider | Credit: CERN

Neutrino

  Neutrinos are subatomic particles with extremely little mass that interact only rarely with ordinary matter. They usually travel at close to the speed of light. Trillions pass through your body at any given moment, yet so few interact with normal matter that they produce almost no detectable effect. Neutrinos are created by the Sun, cosmic rays, and radioactive decay inside Earth. They also have antiparticles called antineutrinos; under certain conditions, neutrinos and antineutrinos can annihilate one another.

A solar flare at the moment of eruption, imaged at a wavelength of 94 ångströms | Credits: NASA/SDO/GSFC

Sparticle

  “Sparticle” is short for “supersymmetric particle,” a term from supersymmetry. The theory proposes that every known particle has an undiscovered partner: every fermion should have a bosonic partner, and every boson a fermionic one. The electron’s supersymmetric partner, for example, is the selectron; the quark’s partner is the squark.

  As of 2026, no sparticle has been found experimentally. Why do we not observe these particles in the universe? Scientists think they may be far more massive than ordinary particles, and massive unstable particles generally decay very quickly. In essence, a sparticle would disappear almost as soon as it was created. Producing one requires extraordinarily high energies of the kind present shortly after the Big Bang, although a large particle accelerator such as the LHC might be able to recreate them. As for why sparticles should be so heavy, physicists have suggested that some hidden sector of the universe, beyond our ability to detect directly, may cause supersymmetry to break. We could neither see nor touch such a sector, sensing it only through its interactions.

Fermilab's CDF (Collider Detector at Fermilab) | Credit: Fermilab

Graviton

  The graviton is a hypothetical particle in theories of quantum gravity and a possible carrier of the gravitational interaction. In quantum field theory, fundamental interactions can often be described through the exchange of particles. Electromagnetism, for example, is mediated by photons, massless particles that carry the electromagnetic force. By analogy, scientists have proposed that gravity may be mediated by particles called gravitons.

  As of 2026, no graviton has been detected experimentally, and its existence remains theoretical. Because gravitons would interact so weakly with matter, detecting a single one directly is thought to be almost impossible under real physical conditions. One study, for example, calculated that even a detector as massive as Jupiter, operating at 100% efficiency in a close orbit around a neutron star, would detect only about one graviton every ten years under the most favorable conditions.

Artist's impression of gravitational waves | Credit: NASA

Antimatter

  Antimatter is matter composed of antiparticles, the counterparts of particles in ordinary matter. When matter and antimatter meet, they annihilate one another, releasing enormous energy in accordance with E=mc². The process has an exceptionally high energy density. Scientists believe that every ordinary particle has a corresponding antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge. The positron, for example, is the electron’s antiparticle: it carries the same magnitude of electric charge but the opposite sign.

Artist's concept of antimatter produced by a thunderstorm | Credits: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center

Quark

  Quarks are elementary particles proposed by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig. They participate in the strong interaction and are the basic constituents of hadrons such as protons and neutrons. Gell-Mann took the word “quark” from a line in James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake: “Three quarks for Muster Mark.” Quarks always occur in combinations because the force binding them grows as the distance between them increases. Pulling them apart would require so much energy that free quarks do not occur in nature. Six types, or “flavors,” of quark are known: up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm ©, bottom (b), and top (t). A proton, for example, contains two up quarks and one down quark, while a neutron contains two down quarks and one up quark. Up and down quarks are the least massive. Heavier quarks rapidly turn into up or down quarks through particle decay. Because those heavier quarks are generally unstable, strange, charm, top, and bottom quarks can be produced only in high-energy particle collisions, such as those involving cosmic rays or particle accelerators, and decay soon afterward.

A reconstructed lead-nucleus collision recorded by the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.The experiment studies quark–gluon plasma, a state of matter that existed moments after the Big Bang | Credits: CERN

  That concludes our tour of these remarkable particles. Which one is your favorite? Does the sheer variety of the universe feel a little more astonishing now? If you want answers to every question, keep searching for them yourself.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/13593-exotic-particles-sparticles-antimatter-god-particle.html
  2. Wikipedia: “Higgs boson,” “Quark,” “Superpartner,” “Neutrino,” “Antimatter,” and “Graviton”

entry.title: Did Neptune's Tiny Moon Come from Proteus?
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

“The Moon That Should Not Exist”

Artist's concept of Hippocamp, the tiny moon discovered by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2013. This is the first evidence that a moon may be an offshoot of a comet's collision with a larger parent body. | Credit: NASA, ESA and J. Olmsted (STScI)

  After several years of analysis, a team of planetary scientists has finally explained the mysterious moon orbiting Neptune that they discovered with the Hubble Space Telescope in 2013.

  The small moon, named Hippocamp, lies unusually close to a much larger Neptunian moon, Proteus. Under normal circumstances, a moon like Proteus should use its gravity to sweep smaller moons aside or swallow them as it orbits.

  Why, then, does such a small moon still exist? Hippocamp is probably a fragment of the larger moon, broken off in a collision with a comet billions of years ago. Only 20 miles (about 34 kilometers) in diameter, the tiny moon has just one-thousandth the mass of Proteus, which is about 260 miles (about 418 kilometers) across.

  “The first thing we realized was that you would not expect to find such a tiny moon right next to Neptune’s largest inner moon,” said Mark Showalter of the SETI Institute in Mountain View, California. “In the distant past, as the larger moon slowly migrated outward, Proteus was once where Hippocamp is now.”

  Images taken by Voyager 2 in 1989 support this idea. They show an enormous impact crater on Proteus, almost large enough to have shattered the moon. “In 1989, we thought the huge depression must simply be a crater,” Showalter said. “With Hubble, we now know that a small piece of Proteus was left behind—the object we know today as Hippocamp.” The moons’ orbits are now separated by 7,500 miles (about 12,070 kilometers).

Observations of Hippocamp (inside the white square). The Hubble Space Telescope took the images in sequence in a. 2004, b. 2005, c. 2009, and d. 2016.

  The “developmental history” of Neptune’s moon system has been remarkably violent and convoluted. Billions of years ago, Neptune captured its large moon Triton from the Kuiper Belt—a densely populated annular region beyond Neptune’s orbit filled with icy and rocky bodies. Triton’s gravity disrupted Neptune’s original system of moons before Triton settled into a relatively stable circular orbit. Fragments of the shattered moons then recombined to form Neptune’s second-generation moon system. Continued bombardment by comets, however, broke apart those second-generation moons and may have produced Hippocamp, which could be regarded as a third-generation moon.

  “Based on estimates of the enormous number of comets, it is fairly clear that other moons in the outer Solar System have been struck and disrupted by comets many times, then reassembled, in a cycle that repeats over and over,” said Jack Lissauer of NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, California, a coauthor of the new study. “Proteus and Hippocamp provide a somewhat dramatic example of how moons are sometimes broken into several pieces by comets.”

Diagram of the orbits of Neptune's moons, with Hippocamp's orbit highlighted. | Credit:NASA, ESA, and A. Feild (STScI) | From:https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocamp_(moon)#/media

  Hippocamp, originally designated S/2004 N 1, is a small moon of Neptune about 34 kilometers (20 miles) in diameter. It orbits the planet in less than one Earth day. Its discovery on July 1, 2013, brought Neptune’s number of known moons to 14. When the Voyager 2 space probe flew past Neptune and its moons in 1989, Hippocamp was too dim to be observed. Mark Showalter of the SETI Institute discovered the moon by analyzing archival Hubble Space Telescope images of Neptune taken between 2004 and 2009.

  The moon was formally numbered Neptune XIV on September 25, 2018, and named Hippocamp in February 2019.

  The word Hippocamp comes from the horse-headed, fish-tailed creature of Greek mythology. The scientific name of the seahorse is Hippocampus, which is also the name of the important brain region associated with memory. The International Astronomical Union requires Neptune’s moons to be named after creatures from the undersea worlds of Greek and Roman mythology.

References

  1. ScienceDaily: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/02/190221095033.htm
  2. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocamp_(moon)

entry.title: SpaceX Rocket Launches the First Privately Funded Lunar Lander
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

  At 9:45 a.m. Beijing time on February 22, 2019, just as the Moon rose above the horizon, a Falcon 9 rocket began its journey toward it.

  On the evening of February 21, 2019, a previously flown SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket successfully launched an Israeli lunar lander and an Indonesian communications satellite from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in the United States. After placing both payloads into orbit, Falcon 9’s first stage returned to Earth and landed successfully on the uncrewed vessel Of Course I Still Love You in the Atlantic Ocean.

  Although the mission’s primary payload was Indonesia’s Nusantara Satu satellite, the small lunar lander traveling as a secondary payload stole the spotlight. It became not only Israel’s first spacecraft to venture beyond Earth orbit, but also the first privately funded lunar lander.

Concept art of the Beresheet lander on the lunar surface | Credit: SpaceIL

  Today’s launch marks an important moment for Israel. Apart from several communications and Earth-observation satellites, the country has never launched a mission beyond Earth orbit.

  The lander is named Beresheet—Hebrew for “in the beginning.” It was built by SpaceIL, an Israeli nonprofit that entered the mission in 2011 as a contestant in the Google Lunar X Prize. The international competition offered 30 million US dollars to any privately funded team that could land a robotic spacecraft on the Moon. If no team met the deadline, the competition would have no winner.

  “Our vision is to show the world the best that Israel has to offer,” SpaceIL donor Sylvan Adams said at a briefing in Orlando, Florida, on February 20, 2019. “Israel is about to become the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon. That is an extraordinary achievement.”

Beresheet will orbit Earth repeatedly for about 27 days to build the momentum it needs.

  Beresheet will take seven weeks to reach the Moon. Before it arrives, it will circle Earth several times, using Earth’s gravity to gain the momentum needed to reach its destination. If Beresheet makes a successful soft landing, Israel will become the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon, following the United States, Russia, and China. In 1966, the Soviet spacecraft Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon. Later that year, NASA’s Surveyor 1 landed on the lunar surface. China’s Chang’e 3 lander and Yutu rover joined them in 2013.

  When Beresheet approaches the lunar surface, it will aim to land in the region known as Mare Tranquillitatis, SpaceIL spacecraft program manager Yigal Harel said at the briefing. The spacecraft, however, will be able to operate for only about two days before running out of power. During that time, it will study the Moon’s magnetic field and photograph the lunar surface.

  Even after those two days, the defunct spacecraft will not be entirely useless. Beresheet carries a laser retroreflector, a mirror-like device that requires no power and enables space-to-ground communication through NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN). NASA provided the device for the mission, and the agreement will allow the startup to use the DSN for its lunar mission.

  The reflector is not the only payload aboard Beresheet designed to endure. SpaceIL also built a time capsule filled with digital files about the spacecraft and a range of Israeli mementos. They include the Hebrew Bible, Hebrew songs, artwork created by Israeli children, and photographs of Ilan Ramon, Israel’s first and only astronaut. Inside the time capsule is a vast digital database known as the “Lunar Library,” a project of the nonprofit Arch Mission Foundation. “The library holds millions of documents from around the world, including many different dictionaries and encyclopedias, as well as three laser-etched coins,” said SpaceIL cofounder Yonatan Winetraub. “It will be the most information-dense artifact ever to reach the Moon, and it will remain there in 2019 so that future generations can see what life on Earth was like.”

This small coin is part of the time capsule aboard Beresheet. The entire Hebrew Bible is laser-etched onto its surface. | Credits: Hanneke Weitering/Space.com

  Beresheet and Nusantara Satu were launched on a Falcon 9 booster that had already flown two separate missions to space, making this its third successful launch and landing. SpaceX had first flown and recovered the same first-stage booster for a third time during the SSO-A mission in December 2018; the Nusantara Satu mission was the company’s second time reaching that milestone. The booster may also be refurbished for a historic fourth flight. Reusing rocket boosters can drastically reduce the cost of spaceflight, a central goal of SpaceX.

Note: Beresheet attempted to land on April 11, 2019, but lost contact after its main engine failed during the final stage of descent. It ultimately crashed on the lunar surface in the early hours of that day, Beijing time.

entry.title: Underwater Archaeologists Find Surprising Artifacts from a Roman Naval Battle
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

The Naval Battle

  Archaeologists have explored the site of a naval battle fought between Rome and Carthage 2,200 years ago. They found clues to how the battle may have unfolded, along with several unsolved mysteries.

Archaeologists found numerous helmets while surveying the Roman–Carthaginian battlefield. This 3D model of one helmet was created by William M. Murray. | Credit: Courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

  The discoveries suggest that Carthage reused captured Roman warships in the battle, and that Carthaginian sailors may have made a desperate attempt to escape Roman pursuit by throwing their cargo into the sea.

  According to historical records, the naval battle took place on March 10, 241 BCE, near the Aegadian Islands off Sicily in the Mediterranean. A Carthaginian fleet attempting to carry supplies to Carthaginian forces on Sicily was intercepted by the Roman navy, which then destroyed most of its ships. Rome ultimately won a decisive victory, forcing Carthage to sue for peace and accept terms favorable to Rome.

  Over the past decade, underwater archaeologists have surveyed the battlefield and found bronze rams, metal helmets, and fragments of ceramic vessels. The final field season of 2018 alone uncovered six bronze rams, several helmets, and pottery fragments.

Carthaginian and Roman Ships in Combat

A Roman bronze ram found during the survey of the battlefield. | Credit: Photo by William M. Murray, courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

  Carthage appears not to have fought the Romans in an all-out engagement, but to have entered the battle with a fleet composed partly of captured Roman ships. “Of the 19 bronze rams already found in this area, I believe 11 are Roman,” said team member William Murray, professor of Greek history at the University of South Florida. Many helmets found at the site are also of a design archaeologists call the Montefortino type. The helmet was so popular in Rome that the Romans decorated some of their bronze rams with its image.

  The many Roman rams and Montefortino-style helmets have left archaeologists with a puzzle. “You would expect the Carthaginians, who lost the battle, to have suffered heavy casualties,” Murray said. “But you might also expect the bronze rams from some warships to have ended up on vessels crewed by the Carthaginians.”

  “Carthage probably used ships that it had captured from the Romans in an earlier naval battle,” Murray said. Historical records show that Carthage captured 93 Roman ships in a naval battle several years before the Battle of the Aegadian Islands. Why so many Montefortino helmets are present remains a mystery. “One explanation is that the Carthaginians hired mercenaries from Gaul and Iberia to crew many of the ships in their fleet, and soldiers from those regions sometimes used Montefortino helmets,” Murray said.

A Roman bronze ram found during the survey bears the image of a winged woman. She is Victoria, the Roman goddess of victory. | Credit: Photo by William M. Murray, courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

Did the Sailors Throw Their Cargo into the Sea?

  The archaeologists also found amphorae—oval, two-handled ceramic jars often used to store liquids—scattered around the remains of Roman ships. Murray said this was strange because jars that fell from storage aboard a ship should have been clustered together. “It is as if they were thrown into the sea, which separated them before they sank to the seabed,” Murray said. “One possible explanation is that the Carthaginian sailors realized during the battle that their mission would fail and jettisoned their cargo—the supplies intended for Carthaginian forces in Sicily—to make their ships lighter, faster, and better able to escape the Roman fleet.”

Wasted Food?

  “Besides being widely scattered, none of the amphorae has the tar-like lining that would keep liquids from evaporating during storage,” Murray said. This means that most of the liquid would have evaporated by the time the jars reached Sicily. Even if the Carthaginian fleet had reached Sicily, therefore, part of its cargo would have gone to waste. Although amphorae could also store grain, he said, ancient accounts of unloading cargo from ships suggest that grain was more commonly carried in sacks.

  “Perhaps the Carthaginians were in such a hurry to supply their army that they had no time to choose suitable containers,” Murray said. “Another possibility is that they did not have many sacks available, so they decided to carry dry goods to Sicily in amphorae.” Scientists are conducting chemical tests in an effort to determine what the containers held.

  Murray and other members of the research team presented their findings in a paper at the joint annual meeting of the Archaeological Institute of America and the Society for Classical Studies, held in San Diego from January 3 to 6.

  The project surveying and excavating the underwater site is jointly conducted by Sicily’s Soprintendenza del Mare and the RPM Nautical Foundation, with scientists from several other institutions also participating. They plan to conduct another field expedition in 2019.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/64734-underwater-rome-carthage-battle-artifacts.html

entry.title: Farewell, Opportunity: Remembering a Pioneer of Mars Exploration
entry.content:
Author: 一毫秒的永恒

  A record-setting NASA mission on Mars has come to an end. One of the longest-running and most successful achievements in interplanetary exploration, NASA’s Opportunity rover mission concluded after nearly fifteen years on the Martian surface. The mission laid a foundation for NASA’s return to Mars.

  In June 2018, a severe planet-wide dust storm covered Opportunity’s location on Mars. The rover then stopped communicating with Earth. Engineers at the Space Flight Operations Facility at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) sent more than 1,000 recovery commands in an effort to reestablish contact, but none succeeded. The solar-powered rover’s final communication arrived on June 10, 2018.

  NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine said, “It is because of trailblazing missions such as Opportunity that there will come a day when our brave astronauts walk on the surface of Mars.” He added, “And when that day arrives, some portion of that first footprint will be owned by the men and women of Opportunity, and a little rover that defied the odds and did so much in the name of exploration.”

  Opportunity was designed to operate for only 90 days and travel 1,000 meters. Its endurance, scientific value, and lifetime exceeded every expectation. It lasted sixty times longer than planned, and by the time it reached its final resting place on Mars, Perseverance Valley, it had traveled more than 45 kilometers.

  Thomas Zurbuchen, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, said, “For more than a decade, Opportunity has been an icon in the field of planetary exploration, teaching us about Mars’ ancient past as a potentially habitable planet, and revealing uncharted Martian landscapes.” He continued, “Whatever loss we feel now must be tempered with the knowledge that the legacy of Opportunity continues—both on the surface of Mars with the Curiosity rover and InSight lander—and in the clean rooms of JPL.”

During a presentation, Opportunity principal investigator Steve Squyres points to a strange rock that the rover found on January 8, 2014, named "Pinnacle Island." The image on the left side of the screen was taken by Opportunity on December 26, 2013. The rover on the right is Curiosity, the first nuclear-powered Mars rover. | Credit: NASA/JPL

  JPL Mars Exploration Rover project manager John Callas said, “We have made every reasonable engineering effort to try to recover Opportunity and have determined that the likelihood of receiving a signal is far too low to continue recovery efforts.”

  Opportunity landed in Mars’s Meridiani Planum region on January 24, 2004, seven months after launching from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. Its twin rover, Spirit, had landed more than twenty days earlier in the 166-kilometer-wide Gusev Crater on the other side of Mars. Spirit traveled nearly eight kilometers before its mission ended in May 2011.

  From the day Opportunity landed, a team of mission engineers, rover drivers, and scientists on Earth worked together to overcome one challenge after another and move the rover between geological sites on Mars. They plotted workable paths across rough terrain so that the 174-kilogram Martian explorer could maneuver around rocks and boulders. At times it climbed gravel-covered slopes as steep as 32 degrees, a record beyond Earth, explored crater floors and hilltops, and crossed what may have been dry riverbeds. Its final journey took it to the western edge of Perseverance Valley.

  JPL Director Michael Watkins said, “I cannot think of a more appropriate place for Opportunity to endure on the surface of Mars than one called Perseverance Valley. The records, discoveries and sheer tenacity of this intrepid little rover are a testament to the ingenuity, dedication and perseverance of the people who built and guided her.”

  Opportunity had already lost steering in one front wheel in 2005. A stuck heater severely restricted the power available to the rover, and a Martian sand ripple nearly trapped it permanently. Two years later, a dust storm that lasted two months placed the rover in danger. Opportunity lost its 256-megabyte flash memory in 2015 and steering in its other front wheel in 2017. Whenever the rover met an obstacle, the team on Earth found a way around it and kept the vehicle operating. The enormous dust storm that formed in the summer of 2018, however, was more than even the most experienced Mars explorer in history could withstand.

  Callas said, “When I think of Opportunity, I will recall that place on Mars where our intrepid rover far exceeded everyone’s expectations. But what I suppose I’ll cherish most is the impact Opportunity had on us here on Earth. It’s the accomplished exploration and phenomenal discoveries. It’s the generation of young scientists and engineers who became space explorers with this mission. It’s the technical legacy of the Mars Exploration Rovers, which is carried aboard Curiosity and the upcoming Mars 2020 mission. Farewell, Opportunity, and well done.”

Distances traveled by Opportunity and other extraterrestrial vehicles, as of February 13, 2019. Opportunity ranks first at 45.16 kilometers.Second: the Soviet Union's Lunokhod 2, which landed on the Moon in 1973 and held the off-world driving record for many years.Third: the United States' Apollo 17 lunar rover.Fourth: the United States' Apollo 15 lunar rover.Fifth: the United States' Apollo 16 lunar rover.Sixth: the United States' Curiosity Mars rover.Seventh: the Soviet Union's Lunokhod 1.Eighth: the United States' Spirit Mars rover.Ninth: the United States' Sojourner Mars rover.Tenth: China's Yutu 2.Eleventh: China's Yutu 1.Credit: MARS.NASA.GOV

  2. https://www.space.com/mars-rovers-after-opportunity.html
